docs.title: About this book
docs.text: A student's plain-English guide to how a digital chip goes from an idea to manufactured silicon — flow, concepts, tools, file formats, standards, companies and careers. Every topic is explained with an everyday analogy, a worked example, step-by-step mechanics, and a table of the concepts, tools (commercial and open source), file formats, standards and companies you need to know.

docs.title: Chapter 1: Chip Design Foundations
docs.text: Before you write a line of Verilog or open a layout tool, you need the big picture: what a custom chip is, how a transistor works, how logic gates become flip-flops and state machines, and why timing and power rule every decision. This chapter builds that foundation from zero and then walks through the whole journey from an idea on a whiteboard to a packaged chip on a circuit board. It ends with the business side: who does what in the industry, and why a chip can cost millions before the first one is sold.

docs.title: 1.1 What Is an ASIC? (vs FPGA, CPU, GPU and SoC)
docs.text:
An ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit) is a chip designed to do one particular job extremely well, such as decoding video, mining a cryptocurrency or running a phone. Once it is manufactured its circuits are fixed forever. Other chips trade that efficiency for flexibility: a CPU runs any software, a GPU runs many parallel calculations, and an FPGA is a chip whose wiring you can reprogram after manufacture.

CPU vs FPGA vs ASIC

CPU / MCU FPGA ASIC Flexibility Any software Reprogrammable logic Fixed at manufacture Perf per watt Lowest Medium Highest Unit cost at volume Medium High Lowest Up-front NRE Almost none Low Millions of dollars Time to product Weeks Weeks to months 1-2+ years Fixing a bug Software update New bitstream Respin or workaround

Moving right buys efficiency and low unit cost at the price of NRE, time and flexibility.

Think of it like…

A CPU is a Swiss Army knife, an FPGA is a box of LEGO you can rebuild any time, and an ASIC is a custom-forged chef's knife: it does one job, but faster and cheaper per cut than anything else.

Real-world example

Northwind Audio sells wireless earbuds. Their first prototype used a small FPGA to run the noise-cancelling filter, but it drained the battery in two hours. Once the design was proven, they turned it into an ASIC: the same filter now uses one-tenth of the power and costs 40 cents per chip instead of 9 dollars. The catch was a 3 million dollar up-front cost and 14 months of work.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Decide what the chip must do and how fast, how cheap and how low-power it must be.
  2. If volumes are small or the design will change, an FPGA or off-the-shelf processor is usually better.
  3. If volumes are high or power/performance requirements are extreme, an ASIC pays off.
  4. Modern ASICs are usually SoCs: CPU cores, memory, accelerators and interfaces on one die.
  5. Some products start on FPGA for prototyping and move to ASIC for mass production.

Who uses it

Chip companies like Apple, NVIDIA, Qualcomm, Broadcom and Google, plus thousands of start-ups and automotive, medical and IoT companies, design ASICs.

Key takeaway

Interviewers love the question 'ASIC or FPGA?': answer with volume, unit cost, power, performance, NRE and time-to-market.

Going deeper

  • Implementing the same logic in an FPGA instead of standard cells typically costs tens of times more area, several times more delay and roughly an order of magnitude more dynamic power, because LUTs and routing switches replace fixed gates.
  • Most modern ASICs are SoCs whose die area is dominated by licensed or reused IP and SRAM; the company's own differentiating logic is often a minority of the gates.
  • The ASIC decision weighs volume, unit cost, power, performance, NRE, schedule, risk and IP protection; a fixed chip is also much harder to copy than an FPGA bitstream.
  • Hybrid options exist: FPGA prototypes before tapeout, embedded FPGA (eFPGA) fabric inside an ASIC from vendors such as Achronix, and structured ASICs that customise only a few layers.
  • Digital ASICs today are almost entirely standard-cell designs; full-custom layout survives for SRAM bit cells, analog and I/O circuits, and a few of the fastest CPU datapaths.
  • Each market adds its own rules: automotive ASICs need AEC-Q100 qualification and ISO 26262 safety work, medical implants need extreme reliability, and data-centre chips chase performance per watt.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming an ASIC always beats an FPGA: at low volume or with changing requirements, NRE and schedule risk make FPGAs or standard chips the better business choice.
  • Confusing SoC with ASIC: SoC describes what is integrated, ASIC describes how and for whom the chip is built — a phone SoC is both.
  • Expecting an FPGA design to port straight to ASIC: vendor primitives, clocking, initial values and memories must be reworked, and DFT must be added.

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies
docs.text: Name What it does Example ASIC (Application-Specific Integrated Circuit)General industry term · Concept · Whole flow A chip custom-designed for one application, with fixed circuits that give the best power, performance and unit cost. Bitcoin mining chips, Google's TPU and the image processor inside a phone camera are ASICs. FPGA (Field-Programmable Gate Array)AMD (Xilinx), Altera, Lattice, Microchip · Device A chip full of configurable logic blocks and wiring that can be reprogrammed with a new design in seconds. An engineer loads a new image-filter design onto an AMD Artix board to test it before committing to silicon. CPU (Central Processing Unit)Intel, AMD, Arm-based designs, RISC-V · Device A general-purpose processor that runs any software by executing instructions one after another, very flexibly. A laptop's CPU runs a browser, a spreadsheet and a game, all from software instructions. GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)NVIDIA, AMD, Intel, Arm, Imagination · Device A processor with thousands of simple cores that perform the same calculation on lots of data at once. GPUs render 3D games and train AI models because both need millions of parallel multiplications. SoC (System on Chip)General industry term · Concept · Spec/Architecture A single chip that integrates CPUs, GPU, memory controllers, accelerators and I/O interfaces: a whole computer on one die. A smartphone application processor is an SoC with CPU cores, GPU, modem, camera ISP and AI engine. Structured ASIC / eASICIntel (eASIC, discontinued), various · Concept A halfway house where most layers are pre-made and only a few metal layers are customised, lowering NRE. A company once used a structured ASIC to move an FPGA design into cheaper silicon with lower mask cost. Full-custom vs semi-custom (standard-cell) designGeneral industry term · Methodology · Whole flow Full-custom draws every transistor by hand; standard-cell design builds digital logic from a pre-made library of gates. Analog blocks and SRAM bit cells are full-custom; a 50-million-gate digital controller is built from standard cells. ASSP (Application-Specific Standard Product)General industry term · Concept A chip built for one application but sold to many customers, unlike an ASIC built for one company. A USB-to-Ethernet bridge chip sold by a catalogue vendor to hundreds of product makers is an ASSP. Accelerator / NPUGeneral industry term · Concept · Spec/Architecture A specialised hardware block or chip that speeds up one class of work, such as neural networks, far beyond a CPU. The NPU in a laptop chip runs background-blur in video calls using a fraction of CPU power. Die, wafer and chipGeneral industry term · Concept · Fabrication A wafer is a round silicon disc; it is cut into many rectangular dies; a packaged die is what people call a chip. One 300 mm wafer might hold about 600 dies of 100 square millimetres each. Microcontroller (MCU)STMicroelectronics, NXP, Microchip, Renesas, Raspberry Pi · Device A small, cheap chip combining a CPU core, flash, SRAM and peripherals for embedded control. An STM32 or RP2040 in a thermostat reads a temperature sensor and switches a relay. DSP (Digital Signal Processor)Texas Instruments, Cadence Tensilica, CEVA · Device A processor optimised for fast multiply-accumulate on streams of samples, used for audio, radio and sensor processing. A hearing aid's DSP filters and amplifies sound thousands of times per second using very little power. Digital, analog and mixed-signal ICsGeneral industry term · Concept · Whole flow Digital chips process 0s and 1s; analog chips handle continuous signals; mixed-signal chips combine both on one die. A sensor-interface chip combines an analog amplifier, an ADC and a digital filter with an SPI interface. Performance per wattIndustry metric · Concept Useful work delivered per unit of power; fixed-function ASICs often beat general processors by an order of magnitude or more. A video-encoder ASIC compresses 4K video at a few watts where a CPU would need tens of watts.

docs.title: 1.2 Semiconductor Basics: Silicon, Doping and the MOSFET
docs.text:
Silicon is a semiconductor: it conducts electricity better than glass but worse than copper, and we can control exactly how well. Adding tiny amounts of other elements (doping) creates N-type silicon with spare electrons or P-type silicon with 'holes' (missing electrons). A MOSFET transistor uses a voltage on its gate to turn a channel of current on or off, acting as an electrically controlled switch.

A chip in cross-section. Transistors sit at the bottom; a dozen or more copper wiring layers above connect them.

Think of it like…

A MOSFET is like a garden hose with a tap: the gate voltage is your hand on the tap, and the current is the water flowing from source to drain.

Real-world example

In a 1.0 V chip, when Priya's design puts 1.0 V on the gate of an NMOS transistor, a thin channel of electrons forms under the gate and current flows from drain to source: the switch is ON. When the gate is at 0 V, the channel disappears and the switch is OFF. Billions of these switches flipping billions of times a second are what make a processor compute.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Start with very pure crystalline silicon.
  2. Dope regions with phosphorus or arsenic (N-type) or boron (P-type) to control conductivity.
  3. Build a gate electrode separated from the silicon by a thin insulating layer (the gate oxide or high-k dielectric).
  4. Apply voltage to the gate: above the threshold voltage (Vt) a conducting channel forms between source and drain.
  5. NMOS turns on with a high gate voltage; PMOS turns on with a low gate voltage.

Who uses it

Device physicists, process engineers and analog designers work at this level daily; digital designers need the basics for power, timing and interview questions.

Key takeaway

Remember: NMOS passes a strong 0, PMOS passes a strong 1, which is why CMOS uses PMOS to pull up and NMOS to pull down.

Going deeper

  • Operating regions: below Vt a transistor is in subthreshold (small, exponential leakage current); above Vt it conducts in the linear region at low drain voltage and saturates at higher drain voltage.
  • Subthreshold swing is ideally about 60 mV per decade of current at room temperature, so every ~60-100 mV cut in Vt raises off-state leakage roughly tenfold.
  • Leakage rises steeply with temperature, so a chip at 105 °C leaks many times more than at 25 °C; leakage power is therefore signed off at hot corners.
  • Short-channel effects such as drain-induced barrier lowering weaken gate control as channels shrink; FinFET and gate-all-around structures wrap the gate around the channel to restore it.
  • 300 mm wafers are standard for advanced logic, 200 mm remains common for analog, power and MEMS, and the industry abandoned a 450 mm transition in the mid-2010s.
  • Core supply voltages fell from 5 V in the 1980s to roughly 0.7-0.9 V at leading-edge nodes; they cannot drop much further because Vt cannot shrink without leakage exploding.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing '3 nm' describes a 3 nm feature: node names are marketing labels, so compare density, speed and power data instead.
  • Assuming an off transistor draws no current: leakage across billions of devices can dominate standby power.
  • Mixing up carrier types: NMOS conducts with electrons and turns on with a high gate; PMOS conducts with holes and turns on with a low gate.

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies
docs.text: Name What it does Example SemiconductorPhysics / materials science · Concept · Fabrication A material whose conductivity sits between a conductor and an insulator and can be precisely controlled. Silicon is the dominant semiconductor; gallium nitride and silicon carbide are used in power chips. Doping (N-type and P-type)Semiconductor fabrication · Process · Fabrication Adding impurity atoms to silicon: phosphorus or arsenic gives extra electrons (N), boron gives holes (P). The source and drain of an NMOS transistor are heavily N-doped regions in a P-type well. MOSFETMetal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor · Concept · Fabrication A transistor with gate, source, drain and body terminals, where gate voltage controls current between source and drain. A modern CPU contains tens of billions of MOSFETs acting as tiny switches. NMOS and PMOSMOSFET types · Concept NMOS conducts when its gate is high using electrons; PMOS conducts when its gate is low using holes. In an inverter, the PMOS connects the output to VDD and the NMOS connects it to ground. Threshold voltage (Vt)Device physics · Concept The gate voltage at which a transistor starts to conduct strongly; lower Vt is faster but leaks more. Libraries offer low-Vt (fast, leaky) and high-Vt (slow, low-leakage) versions of each cell. Gate oxide / high-k metal gate (HKMG)Introduced in volume by Intel at 45 nm (2007) · Concept · Fabrication The insulator under the gate; high-k materials like hafnium oxide replaced silicon dioxide to reduce gate leakage. Every node since about 45 nm uses a high-k dielectric with a metal gate electrode. Channel length and 'process node'Industry naming · Concept · Fabrication Node names like '3 nm' were once gate lengths; today they are marketing labels for a technology generation. A TSMC N3 transistor has no feature that actually measures 3 nanometres. Leakage currentDevice physics · Concept Small current that flows through a transistor even when it is switched off, wasting power. A phone chip in standby still drains the battery slowly because of leakage in billions of transistors. Silicon waferWafer makers: Shin-Etsu, SUMCO, GlobalWafers, Siltronic, SK Siltron · Concept · Fabrication A thin, polished disc sliced from a single-crystal silicon ingot; leading fabs use 300 mm diameter wafers. A 300 mm wafer is about 0.775 mm thick and becomes hundreds of chips. Moore's LawGordon Moore (1965, revised 1975) · Concept The observation that transistor counts on a chip double roughly every two years. Chips grew from 2,300 transistors (Intel 4004, 1971) to over 100 billion in today's largest GPUs. Carrier mobility (electrons vs holes)Device physics · Concept How easily charge carriers move; in silicon, electrons are roughly two to three times more mobile than holes. Library inverters make the PMOS wider than the NMOS so rising and falling outputs switch at similar speeds. On-current and Ion/Ioff ratioDevice physics · Concept Ion sets how fast a transistor charges loads; the Ion/Ioff ratio measures how good a switch it is. Engineers comparing two nodes check both how much faster Ion is and how much worse Ioff leakage became. Wells and substrateCMOS process structure · Concept · Fabrication Doped regions hosting transistors: NMOS sit in P-type substrate or P-well, PMOS in an N-well, each tied to a supply. Tap cells in every standard-cell row connect wells to VDD and ground, preventing latch-up. Interconnect (metal wires and vias)BEOL wiring · Concept · Fabrication Copper wiring layers above the transistors that connect them; at advanced nodes wire delay rivals gate delay. A modern SoC may have more than a dozen metal layers, thin at the bottom and thick near the top.

docs.title: 1.3 CMOS Logic: Inverters, NAND and NOR Gates
docs.text:
CMOS (Complementary MOS) logic pairs PMOS and NMOS transistors so that, in a steady state, one network is on and the other is off. That means almost no current flows except while switching, which is why CMOS dominates. The simplest gate is the inverter (NOT); NAND and NOR are built from series and parallel transistors and can make any logic function.

Three basic CMOS gates

Inverter NAND2 NOR2 Transistors 2 4 4 PMOS pull-up 1 2 in parallel 2 in series NMOS pull-down 1 2 in series 2 in parallel Output is 0 when A = 1 A = 1 and B = 1 A = 1 or B = 1 Universal gate? No Yes Yes Relative speed Fastest Good Slower (series PMOS)

Series and parallel transistor networks are mirror images in the pull-up and pull-down.

Think of it like…

A CMOS gate is like two doors at either end of a corridor: one leads to VDD (logic 1) and one to ground (logic 0), and they are wired so exactly one is open at a time.

Real-world example

A two-input NAND gate has two PMOS in parallel to VDD and two NMOS in series to ground. The output only goes low when both inputs are 1, because then both NMOS are on and both PMOS are off. With any input at 0, at least one PMOS pulls the output high. Draw this on paper: it is a classic interview question.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Inverter: one PMOS from VDD to output, one NMOS from output to ground, gates tied together.
  2. NAND: PMOS in parallel (pull-up), NMOS in series (pull-down).
  3. NOR: PMOS in series (pull-up), NMOS in parallel (pull-down).
  4. Complex gates (AOI, OAI) combine series/parallel networks in one cell for efficiency.
  5. Standard-cell libraries package hundreds of these gates in different sizes (drive strengths).

Who uses it

Standard-cell library designers, circuit designers and every VLSI student meet CMOS gates; digital designers use them through the library.

Key takeaway

NAND is usually preferred over NOR in CMOS because series NMOS (fast electrons) hurt less than series PMOS (slower holes).

Going deeper

  • Static CMOS gates are naturally inverting: one stage can only build NAND, NOR or AOI-style functions, so an AND gate is a NAND plus an inverter and is slower.
  • Series stacks slow gates down, so libraries rarely offer gates wider than four inputs; synthesis builds wide functions as trees of two- and three-input cells.
  • Gate delay is roughly on-resistance times load capacitance; doubling a cell's drive strength halves its resistance but doubles the input capacitance seen by the previous stage.
  • The fan-out-of-4 (FO4) inverter delay is a technology-neutral yardstick; designers describe clock periods in FO4 units, for example roughly 15-25 FO4 per high-performance pipeline stage.
  • Standard-cell libraries hold hundreds to over a thousand cells: logic in several sizes and Vt flavours, flip-flops, clock buffers, clock-gating cells, plus filler, tie and tap cells.
  • Short-circuit current flows while both networks conduct during a slow input transition, which is one reason tools enforce maximum transition (slew) limits.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming NAND and NOR are equally good: NOR's series PMOS use slower holes, so NAND-based logic is usually preferred in CMOS.
  • Forgetting AND and OR need an extra inverter stage in CMOS, making them larger and slower than NAND and NOR.
  • Thinking bigger cells are always faster: upsizing a gate loads the gate driving it and can slow the whole path.

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies
docs.text: Name What it does Example CMOS (Complementary MOS)Invented by Frank Wanlass, Fairchild (1963) · Concept Logic style using complementary PMOS pull-up and NMOS pull-down networks, drawing almost no static current. Nearly every digital chip made today, from watches to supercomputers, is CMOS. Inverter (NOT gate)Basic CMOS cell · Concept The simplest CMOS gate, using one PMOS and one NMOS to output the opposite of its input. Chains of inverters are used as buffers to drive long wires and as ring oscillators to measure speed. NAND gateBasic CMOS cell · Concept Outputs 0 only when all inputs are 1; universal, so any logic can be built from NANDs alone. A NAND2 cell is often the unit used to count design size in 'gate equivalents'. NOR gateBasic CMOS cell · Concept Outputs 1 only when all inputs are 0; also universal but slower in CMOS due to series PMOS. The Apollo Guidance Computer was built entirely from NOR gates. AOI / OAI complex gatesStandard-cell libraries · Concept AND-OR-INVERT and OR-AND-INVERT cells combine several functions in one compact, fast gate. Synthesis maps the expression NOT((A AND B) OR C) to a single AOI21 cell. Transmission gateCMOS circuit technique · Concept A PMOS and NMOS in parallel acting as a switch that passes both 0 and 1 cleanly. Multiplexers and flip-flops inside standard-cell libraries often use transmission gates. Gate equivalent (GE)Industry metric · Concept Design size measured as the area of an equivalent number of NAND2 gates, independent of technology. A small RISC-V core might be about 20,000 gate equivalents. Drive strength (X1, X2, X4...)Standard-cell libraries · Concept · Synthesis Larger transistor versions of a cell that can charge bigger loads faster, at the cost of area and power. A BUF_X8 drives a long net to 40 flip-flops that a BUF_X1 would drive too slowly. Fan-in and fan-outDigital design terms · Concept Fan-in is the number of inputs to a gate; fan-out is how many gate inputs one output drives. A signal with fan-out of 200 needs a buffer tree, or it will switch very slowly. SPICEUC Berkeley (1973); commercial and open versions · Tool · Open source Circuit simulator that computes voltages and currents in transistor netlists; the basis of analog and cell characterisation. Students simulate an inverter in ngspice to see its switching threshold and delay. XOR / XNOR gateBasic CMOS cell · Concept XOR outputs 1 when inputs differ, XNOR when they match; essential for adders, parity and comparators, but larger than NAND. A 32-bit parity generator is a tree of 31 two-input XOR gates. Static vs dynamic (domino) logicCMOS circuit styles · Concept Static CMOS always drives its output; dynamic logic precharges then evaluates, faster but harder to design and verify. Some older high-speed CPUs used domino logic in ALUs; standard-cell ASICs use static CMOS. Logical effortSutherland, Sproull and Harris (1999 book) · Methodology A pencil-and-paper method for estimating path delay and choosing gate sizes to minimise it. Logical effort shows a large load is best driven through a chain of inverters each growing about four times. Noise margin and transfer curveCMOS circuit analysis · Concept An inverter's output-vs-input voltage curve; noise margins show how much interference a gate tolerates before misreading. Students plot the transfer curve in ngspice and read the switching threshold near VDD/2.

docs.title: 1.4 Digital Logic Refresher: Gates, Flip-Flops and State Machines
docs.text:
Digital circuits come in two kinds. Combinational logic (adders, multiplexers, decoders) produces outputs that depend only on current inputs. Sequential logic (latches and flip-flops) remembers values, so outputs depend on history; a clock tells flip-flops when to capture new values. Combine both and you get finite state machines (FSMs), the brains of every controller.

Traffic-light FSM. A 2-bit state register steps round the four states each time the timer expires.

Think of it like…

Combinational logic is a calculator that answers instantly; a flip-flop is a notepad that only updates when the teacher rings the bell (the clock edge).

Real-world example

A traffic-light controller at Elm Street has four states: NS-green, NS-yellow, EW-green, EW-yellow. A 2-bit register holds the current state, combinational logic decides the next state based on a timer, and on each clock edge the register updates. The light outputs are decoded from the state. This tiny FSM is a classic first Verilog exercise.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Combinational logic computes outputs from inputs through gates (no memory).
  2. A latch is level-sensitive: it is transparent while enable is high and holds when low.
  3. A D flip-flop is edge-triggered: it captures D only at the rising (or falling) clock edge.
  4. Registers are groups of flip-flops; pipelines put registers between stages of logic.
  5. An FSM = state register + next-state logic + output logic (Moore or Mealy style).

Who uses it

Every RTL designer and verification engineer works with these building blocks every day.

Key takeaway

Know the difference between a latch and a flip-flop cold, and be able to draw a Moore vs Mealy FSM.

Going deeper

  • A flip-flop is usually two latches in master-slave arrangement: the master is transparent while the clock is low and the slave while it is high, giving edge-triggered behaviour.
  • Library flip-flops are characterised for clock-to-Q delay, setup time and hold time at every corner; these numbers live in Liberty files used by synthesis and STA.
  • FSM design flow: draw the state diagram, list transitions, choose an encoding, code the state register, next-state logic and output logic, and add a safe default for unused states.
  • Pipelining raises throughput but adds latency: a five-stage pipeline delivers one result per cycle once full, yet each instruction still takes five cycles to complete.
  • Synthesis minimises logic automatically with algorithms far beyond K-maps (for example ABC's and-inverter-graph rewriting), so K-maps matter for understanding and interviews rather than daily work.
  • The synchronous design rule — every flop on a clean clock edge, only combinational logic between flops, no combinational loops — is what makes static timing analysis possible.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Creating combinational loops (an output feeding its own input without a flop); they oscillate or latch unpredictably and break timing analysis.
  • Inferring latches by accident through incomplete combinational code; use flip-flops unless a latch is truly intended.
  • Using a combinational or glitchy signal as a clock or asynchronous reset; a glitch can create a false edge.

docs.title: Try it: A D flip-flop with synchronous reset in Verilog
docs.text:
module dff (input clk, input rst, input d, output reg q);
  always @(posedge clk)
    if (rst) q <= 1'b0;
    else     q <= d;
endmodule

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies
docs.text: Name What it does Example Combinational logicDigital design fundamentals · Concept · RTL Design Logic whose outputs depend only on present inputs, with no memory or clock. A 32-bit adder that outputs A+B as soon as A and B settle is combinational. Sequential logicDigital design fundamentals · Concept · RTL Design Logic containing memory elements, so outputs depend on stored state as well as inputs. A counter that increments every clock cycle is sequential. D flip-flopDigital design fundamentals · Concept Edge-triggered storage element that copies its D input to Q at each active clock edge. A pipeline register in a CPU is a row of D flip-flops capturing results each cycle. LatchDigital design fundamentals · Concept Level-sensitive storage element: transparent while enabled, holding its value while disabled. Clock-gating cells use a latch internally to prevent glitches on the gated clock. Finite state machine (FSM)Digital design fundamentals · Concept · RTL Design A circuit with a fixed set of states that moves between them based on inputs, one step per clock. A UART receiver FSM moves through IDLE, START, DATA and STOP states. Moore vs Mealy machineEdward Moore (1956), George Mealy (1955) · Concept Moore outputs depend only on state; Mealy outputs depend on state and current inputs, reacting a cycle sooner. A Moore traffic light shows colours per state; a Mealy detector flags a pattern in the same cycle it arrives. Multiplexer (MUX)Digital design fundamentals · Concept A selector that passes one of several inputs to its output based on control bits. A 4:1 MUX chooses which of four registers feeds the ALU. Adder (ripple-carry, carry-lookahead)Digital design fundamentals · Concept Circuits that add binary numbers; faster designs compute carries in parallel at the cost of area. Synthesis tools pick a fast parallel-prefix adder on a critical path and a small ripple adder elsewhere. PipeliningComputer architecture technique · Methodology · Spec/Architecture Splitting long logic into stages separated by registers so a higher clock frequency is possible. A 5-stage RISC-V pipeline fetches, decodes, executes, accesses memory and writes back in parallel. Boolean algebra and Karnaugh mapsGeorge Boole (1847), Maurice Karnaugh (1953) · Concept Mathematics of true/false logic and a visual method to simplify small logic expressions. Students reduce a 4-variable truth table to a minimal sum-of-products with a K-map. Decoder and encoderDigital design fundamentals · Concept A decoder activates one of 2^n outputs from an n-bit code; an encoder does the reverse. An address decoder uses four address bits to select one of 16 peripheral registers. Shift registerDigital design fundamentals · Concept A chain of flip-flops that moves bits one position per clock, used for serial I/O and delays. A UART transmitter shifts out its eight data bits one at a time on each baud tick. CounterDigital design fundamentals · Concept · RTL Design A register plus incrementer that counts clock cycles or events; the basis of timers, PWM and baud-rate generators. A 16-bit counter divides a 50 MHz clock to produce a 1 kHz timer tick. Glitch (hazard)Digital design fundamentals · Concept A brief unwanted pulse on a combinational output while inputs change at slightly different times. Glitches are harmless when sampled by flops but dangerous on clocks, resets or asynchronous outputs.

docs.title: 1.5 Binary Numbers and Arithmetic for Hardware
docs.text:
Hardware stores every value in a fixed number of bits. You need to read binary and hexadecimal, represent negative numbers with two's complement, know what happens when a result overflows its width, and use fixed-point or floating-point formats for fractions. Getting widths and signs right is a daily part of RTL design.

Making −5 in 8-bit two's complement. Invert and add one; adding the result to +5 overflows to exactly zero.

Think of it like…

A fixed-width register is like a car's odometer: it has a set number of digits, and after 99999 it rolls over to 00000.

Real-world example

Wen designs an audio volume block. Samples are 16-bit signed two's complement, from -32,768 to +32,767. Multiplying by a signed 8-bit gain gives a 24-bit product, so she keeps all 24 bits, rounds, and saturates back to 16 bits. Without saturation, loud samples would wrap to large negative values and the speaker would crackle.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Binary: each bit is a power of two; hexadecimal groups four bits per digit (8'hA5 = 1010_0101).
  2. Unsigned n bits hold 0 to 2^n − 1; two's complement holds −2^(n−1) to 2^(n−1) − 1.
  3. Negate in two's complement by inverting every bit and adding 1.
  4. An n-bit plus n-bit sum needs n+1 bits; an n-bit by m-bit product needs n+m bits.
  5. For fractions use fixed-point (Q format) or floating-point (IEEE 754, bfloat16, FP8).

Who uses it

RTL designers, DSP and AI-accelerator engineers, and verification engineers writing reference models use these skills every day.

Key takeaway

In Verilog and SystemVerilog, mixing signed and unsigned operands makes the whole expression unsigned — a classic interview trap and a common silicon bug.

Going deeper

  • Two's complement is universal because one adder handles both signs: A − B is computed as A + ~B + 1, with the +1 entering through the carry-in.
  • Overflow rules: unsigned addition overflows when there is a carry-out; signed addition overflows when both operands share a sign and the result's sign differs.
  • DSP datapaths track Q formats: multiplying Q1.15 by Q1.15 gives Q2.30, which is then rounded and saturated back to Q1.15 for storage.
  • AI accelerators favour narrow formats such as INT8, FP8 and block-scaled FP4 because multiplier area grows roughly with the square of the operand or mantissa width.
  • IEEE 754 defines subnormals, ±infinity, NaN and several rounding modes; many hardware units flush subnormals to zero to save area, which must be documented and verified.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing signed and unsigned operands in Verilog: the whole expression becomes unsigned, so negative values compare as huge positives.
  • Dropping the carry by assigning an n-bit sum to an n-bit signal; size results using width-growth rules.
  • Truncating instead of rounding in DSP chains, which adds a systematic negative bias that accumulates and degrades signal quality.

docs.title: Try it: Signed vs unsigned surprises in SystemVerilog
docs.text:
logic signed [7:0]  a = -8'sd3;   // stored as 8'hFD
logic        [7:0]  b = 8'd2;
logic signed [15:0] w;

initial begin
  w = a;                            // sign-extends to 16'hFFFD (-3)
  $display("%0d", a < b);           // 0: unsigned compare, 253 < 2 is false
  $display("%0d", a < $signed(b));  // 1: signed compare, -3 < 2
end

docs.title: 1.6 Timing Basics: Clocks, Delay, Setup and Hold
docs.text:
Every synchronous chip runs to the beat of a clock. Between two flip-flops, a signal must travel through logic and arrive before the next clock edge (setup time) and stay stable for a short time after it (hold time). If logic is too slow, the chip fails at that frequency; if it is too fast, data can race through and corrupt the next stage.

Tomás's 1 GHz timing budget. Clock-to-Q, logic and setup must fit inside the 1,000 ps period; what is left over is slack.

Think of it like…

It is like a relay race: the runner (data) must reach the next runner before the whistle (clock edge), and the next runner must not leave before taking the baton properly (hold).

Real-world example

Tomás designs a block for 1 GHz, so the clock period is 1,000 picoseconds. The worst path has 50 ps clock-to-Q delay, 870 ps of logic and 40 ps setup time: 960 ps total, leaving 40 ps of positive slack. When a colleague adds a multiplier to that path, the delay grows to 1,150 ps and slack becomes negative 150 ps, so Tomás must pipeline the multiplier.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. The clock period T = 1 / frequency (1 GHz gives 1 ns).
  2. Setup check: clock-to-Q + logic delay + setup time must be no more than T (adjusted for skew).
  3. Hold check: clock-to-Q + minimum logic delay must be at least the hold time.
  4. Slack = required time minus arrival time; negative slack means a violation.
  5. Clock skew (different arrival times at flops) and jitter eat into the timing budget.

Who uses it

RTL designers, synthesis, physical design and STA engineers all speak in terms of slack and critical paths.

Key takeaway

Setup violations can be fixed by slowing the clock; hold violations cannot, so they must be fixed in the design.

Going deeper

  • Setup check: Tclk-q + Tlogic,max + Tsetup ≤ Tperiod + Tskew − Tuncertainty, where skew is the capture clock's arrival minus the launch clock's arrival.
  • Hold check: Tclk-q + Tlogic,min ≥ Thold + Tskew. The clock period does not appear, so hold violations fail at any frequency and must be fixed in the design.
  • Positive skew (capture clock arriving later) helps setup but hurts hold; physical designers exploit this deliberately as 'useful skew' during clock tree synthesis.
  • Timing is checked at many process-voltage-temperature corners: slow corners (low voltage, slow transistors) for setup and fast corners for hold.
  • Daily timing metrics are WNS (worst negative slack), TNS (total negative slack) and the count of failing endpoints; teams track them across every implementation run.
  • Wire delay grows with each node because thin wires are resistive, so early estimates without wires are optimistic and long nets need repeaters.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trying to fix hold violations by lowering the clock frequency; hold does not depend on the period, so add delay to the short path instead.
  • Trusting synthesis timing alone: paths that pass before placement can fail once real wires, clock skew and crosstalk are included.
  • Treating metastability as an STA problem: asynchronous inputs need synchronisers, not tighter constraints.

docs.title: Try it: Telling tools about a 1 GHz clock (SDC)
docs.text:
# 1 GHz clock on port clk (units: ns)
create_clock -name clk -period 1.0 [get_ports clk]
# Reserve 50 ps for jitter and estimated skew
set_clock_uncertainty 0.05 [get_clocks clk]
# Outside logic uses 300 ps of the cycle on each side
set_input_delay  0.3 -clock clk [get_ports data_in*]
set_output_delay 0.3 -clock clk [get_ports data_out*]

docs.text: Name What it does Example Clock and clock periodDigital design fundamentals · Concept A regular square wave that synchronises flip-flops; period is the time of one cycle. A 2 GHz clock has a period of 500 picoseconds. Propagation delayDigital design fundamentals · Concept The time for a change at a gate's input to appear at its output. A NAND2 in an advanced node might switch in about 5-15 picoseconds depending on load. Setup timeFlip-flop timing parameter · Concept · Signoff How long data must be stable before the clock edge for a flip-flop to capture it reliably. A flop with 30 ps setup time needs data settled 30 ps before the rising edge. Hold timeFlip-flop timing parameter · Concept · Signoff How long data must stay stable after the clock edge so the flop does not capture the next value. Tools insert delay buffers on very short paths to fix hold violations. SlackStatic timing analysis · Concept · Signoff Required time minus arrival time on a path; positive means it meets timing, negative means it fails. A report showing WNS of -0.05 ns means the worst path is 50 ps too slow. Critical pathStatic timing analysis · Concept The slowest register-to-register path, which limits the maximum clock frequency. In many CPUs the critical path runs through the ALU bypass and cache tag compare. Clock skewClock distribution · Concept · Physical Design Difference in clock arrival time between two flip-flops, caused by unequal wire and buffer delays. CTS aims to keep skew between related flops below a few tens of picoseconds. Clock jitterClock generation · Concept Random cycle-to-cycle variation in clock edge timing, usually from the PLL and noise. STA subtracts jitter as 'clock uncertainty' from the available period. MetastabilityDigital design fundamentals · Concept · RTL Design An unstable in-between state when a flop samples changing data, which may resolve late or randomly. Signals from another clock domain pass through a two-flop synchroniser to make metastability failures vanishingly rare. Fmax (maximum frequency)Digital design fundamentals · Concept The highest clock frequency at which all paths still meet setup timing. If the critical path needs 1.25 ns, Fmax is 800 MHz. Clock-to-Q delayFlip-flop timing parameter · Concept The time from the active clock edge until a flip-flop's output actually changes. With 45 ps clock-to-Q, new data leaves the launching flop 45 ps after each rising edge. Launch and capture flip-flopsStatic timing analysis · Concept · Signoff Every register-to-register path starts at a launching flop's clock edge and ends at a capturing flop on the next edge. A path from the ALU result register to the write-back register launches at edge 1 and is captured at edge 2. Setup and hold equationsStatic timing analysis · Concept Setup: clock-to-Q + max logic + setup ≤ period + skew − uncertainty. Hold: clock-to-Q + min logic ≥ hold + skew. With 1,000 ps period, 50 ps clock-to-Q, 40 ps setup and no skew, logic may take at most 910 ps. STA vs timing simulationVerification practice · Concept · Signoff Static timing analysis checks every path mathematically without test vectors; timing simulation only checks paths a test exercises. Signoff relies on STA because no simulation could toggle all billions of paths in a large SoC.

docs.title: 1.7 Power Basics: Dynamic, Leakage and P = αCV²f
docs.text:
Chips consume power in two main ways. Dynamic power is used each time a wire switches between 0 and 1, charging and discharging tiny capacitances. Leakage (static) power trickles through transistors even when nothing switches. Because heat and battery life limit almost every chip, power is as important as speed.

Energy per operation (45 nm). Approximate figures from Horowitz (ISSCC 2014): fetching data from DRAM costs far more than computing on it.

Think of it like…

Dynamic power is like the fuel a car burns while driving; leakage is like a slow fuel leak that drains the tank even when parked.

Real-world example

Ana's IoT sensor chip runs at 0.9 V and 100 MHz. Using P = αCV²f with activity α = 0.1 and switched capacitance C = 1 nF, dynamic power = 0.1 × 1e-9 × 0.81 × 1e8 ≈ 8 mW. Dropping the voltage to 0.7 V cuts it to about 4.9 mW, almost 40 % saved, because voltage is squared. She also uses high-Vt cells to cut leakage while the sensor sleeps.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Dynamic power = α × C × V² × f (activity × capacitance × voltage squared × frequency).
  2. Short-circuit power flows briefly when both PMOS and NMOS are partly on during a transition.
  3. Leakage power depends on threshold voltage, temperature and transistor count; it grows sharply when hot.
  4. Lowering voltage is the most powerful lever; lowering frequency and activity also help.
  5. Techniques: clock gating, power gating, multi-Vt cells, DVFS (covered later).

Who uses it

Low-power architects, RTL designers, power-analysis and physical design engineers, especially in mobile, wearables and data-centre AI chips.

Key takeaway

Memorise P = αCV²f and explain why halving voltage gives roughly a 4x dynamic power saving.

Going deeper

  • Dynamic power has three parts: capacitive switching (αCV²f), short-circuit current during transitions and wasted glitching; in well-designed logic, capacitive switching dominates.
  • Leakage comes mainly from subthreshold conduction, plus gate-oxide tunnelling (reduced by high-k dielectrics) and junction leakage; all of them increase with temperature.
  • Halving frequency halves power but not energy per task; lowering voltage cuts energy per operation, which is why DVFS lowers voltage together with frequency.
  • The clock network often burns a third or more of dynamic power because it toggles every cycle and reaches every flop, making clock gating the first optimisation.
  • Power drives package and cooling cost, IR drop in the power grid, electromigration limits and, for data centres, electricity bills — not just battery life.
  • Power is estimated at every level: spreadsheets during architecture, RTL power tools using simulation activity, then gate-level and signoff analysis including wire parasitics.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming halving frequency halves energy: the task just takes twice as long; only lowering voltage greatly cuts energy per operation.
  • Ignoring leakage in mostly idle chips: an always-on device that rarely switches can be dominated by leakage, especially when hot.
  • Estimating power with default toggle rates; realistic activity from real workloads (SAIF or FSDB files) can change results dramatically.

docs.title: Try it: Dynamic power P = αCV²f in Python
docs.text:
alpha, C, f = 0.1, 1e-9, 100e6   # activity, farads, hertz
for V in (0.9, 0.7):
    P = alpha * C * V**2 * f
    print(f"{V} V -> {P*1e3:.1f} mW")
# 0.9 V -> 8.1 mW
# 0.7 V -> 4.9 mW

A CPU throttles one busy core when its local junction temperature approaches its limit.

docs.title: 1.8 The RTL-to-GDSII Flow: The Whole Journey
docs.text:
Designing a chip follows a long assembly line. You write a specification, design an architecture, describe it in a hardware description language (RTL), prove it works (verification), turn it into gates (synthesis), add test logic (DFT), arrange and wire the gates (physical design), check everything (signoff) and send the final layout file (GDSII/OASIS) to the factory: that hand-off is tapeout. Then come fabrication, packaging, testing and bring-up in the lab.

RTL-to-GDSII at a glance. Each stage hands specific files to the next; problems found late often loop back to earlier stages.

Think of it like…

It is like building a skyscraper: requirements, architect's drawings, detailed blueprints, structural checks, construction plans, inspections, then construction, fit-out and move-in day.

Real-world example

Bluewave Labs builds a Wi-Fi chip. Product managers write the spec in January; architects finish the block diagram in March; 40 RTL designers and 80 verification engineers work until November; the physical design team floorplans from August and closes timing by February; signoff and tapeout happen in March. Wafers return in June, packaged parts in July, and the first board boots Linux in August.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Front end: specification, architecture, RTL design, functional verification.
  2. Logic synthesis turns RTL into a gate-level netlist using a standard-cell library; DFT inserts scan and BIST.
  3. Back end: floorplan, power plan, placement, clock tree synthesis, routing, optimisation.
  4. Signoff: STA, power/IR, physical verification (DRC/LVS), equivalence checks, then tapeout of GDSII/OASIS.
  5. Fab makes masks and wafers; OSAT packages and tests; the team does post-silicon validation and bring-up.

Who uses it

Each stage has its own specialist roles (RTL, DV, synthesis, DFT, PD, STA, CAD), coordinated by project leads and program managers.

Key takeaway

Be able to recite the flow in order in an interview, and name one tool and one file format for each step.

Going deeper

  • Hand-offs are concrete files: RTL plus SDC and UPF into synthesis; netlist, Liberty and LEF into place-and-route; DEF and SPEF into signoff; GDSII or OASIS to the foundry.
  • The flow is iterative, not linear: timing, congestion or power problems found during layout frequently send teams back to RTL changes or even architecture decisions.
  • Verification usually outweighs design effort; industry studies such as the Wilson Research Group survey report as many or more verification engineers as designers on ASIC projects.
  • Key milestones are spec freeze, RTL freeze, netlist freeze, timing closure, tapeout, first silicon and production release, each gated by a sign-off checklist.
  • A mid-size SoC typically takes one to two years from specification to tapeout, followed by roughly two to four months of fabrication before first silicon returns.
  • Commercial flows rely mainly on Synopsys and Cadence tools, with Siemens EDA strong in verification and physical verification; open flows like LibreLane cover the same steps for mature nodes.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking tapeout ends the work: bring-up, validation, characterisation, qualification and production test continue for months afterwards.
  • Treating stages as isolated: RTL that ignores timing, power or testability causes painful late iterations in physical design.
  • Confusing ASIC 'front end' with web front-end development; here it means specification, RTL design and verification.

docs.title: Try it: Synthesise the PWM example with Yosys (synth.ys)
docs.text:
# run with:  yosys synth.ys
read_verilog pwm.v
synth -top pwm          # generic gate-level netlist
stat                    # print cell counts
write_verilog -noattr pwm_netlist.v

docs.title: 1.9 Levels of Abstraction and Design Trade-offs
docs.text:
Chips are far too complex to design transistor by transistor, so engineers work at levels of abstraction: system, architecture, RTL, gates, transistors and layout. Each level hides detail from the one above. Tools translate downward automatically, and at every level designers trade power, performance and area against each other.

Levels of abstraction. Tools translate each level into the one below; detail and accuracy rise as you go down, speed falls.

Think of it like…

It is like a map app: you plan the trip on the country map, then zoom into city streets and finally the exact lane, and each zoom level hides what you do not need yet.

Real-world example

An architect at Kestrel Semi models a new AI accelerator in Python to decide it needs 256 multiply units. RTL designers code those units in SystemVerilog. Synthesis turns the RTL into 40 million gates; place-and-route turns gates into polygons. When power came in 20 % over budget at layout, the team went back up to architecture and cut the multiplier count to 192.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. System/algorithm level: C++, Python, MATLAB or SystemC models of what the chip computes.
  2. Architecture level: block diagrams, pipelines, memories and buses.
  3. RTL: cycle-accurate description in an HDL.
  4. Gate level: netlist of standard cells.
  5. Transistor and layout level: actual devices and polygons on mask layers.

Who uses it

Architects work high; RTL and verification engineers in the middle; physical design, circuit and layout engineers low; all must understand the levels around them.

Key takeaway

The earlier a problem is found (higher abstraction), the cheaper it is to fix: a bug costs dollars in RTL and millions in silicon.

Going deeper

  • Simulation speed falls by orders of magnitude at each step down: TLM models can boot an OS, RTL simulation of a big SoC crawls, and SPICE handles only small circuits.
  • Formal checks link the levels: equivalence checking proves the netlist matches the RTL, and LVS proves the layout matches the netlist, so every translation can be trusted.
  • PPA trade-offs: more pipeline stages raise frequency but add area, power and latency; more parallel units raise throughput but cost area; lower voltage saves power but slows logic.
  • Leverage is highest at the top: architecture choices can change power or performance several-fold, while back-end optimisation typically yields tens of percent.
  • SystemC TLM-2.0 models in loosely-timed or approximately-timed styles let software and architecture work start many months before RTL is ready.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Micro-optimising gates before the architecture is settled; low-level tuning cannot rescue a poor architecture.
  • Trusting high-level estimates blindly: models ignore wires and physical effects, so keep margin and run early synthesis.
  • Letting the golden model and RTL diverge after spec changes, so tests compare the design against wrong answers.

docs.title: Try it: One 1-bit add slice at three levels (alternatives, not one file)
docs.text:
// 1) Behavioural RTL
assign {c1, s0} = a[0] + b[0];

// 2) Structural: wire up a full-adder module
full_adder fa0 (.a(a[0]), .b(b[0]), .cin(1'b0), .s(s0), .cout(c1));

// 3) Gate level, as synthesis would emit it
XOR2_X1 u1 (.A(a[0]), .B(b[0]), .Z(s0));
AND2_X1 u2 (.A(a[0]), .B(b[0]), .Z(c1));

Performance (frequency, throughput, latency)Industry metric · Concept How fast the chip works: clock rate, operations per second and delay for one result. A network chip is judged by 51.2 Tb/s throughput and nanoseconds of port-to-port latency. Shift-leftIndustry term · Methodology · Whole flow Moving checks earlier in the flow so problems are found while they are still cheap to fix. Running power estimates on RTL instead of waiting for the final layout is a shift-left. Hardware/software co-designIndustry practice · Methodology · Spec/Architecture Deciding together which functions run in hardware and which in software to meet goals. A team moves video encoding into hardware but keeps the bitrate controller in firmware. Golden reference modelVerification practice · Concept · Verification A trusted high-level model (often C/C++ or Python) whose outputs the RTL must match. Every RTL test of a crypto engine compares its output with a C reference implementation. Algorithmic model (Python, MATLAB, C++)Architecture practice · Methodology · Spec/Architecture An untimed model proving the maths works before any hardware decisions are made. A DSP team tunes filter coefficients in MATLAB, then freezes them as the reference for RTL. Cycle-accurate modelArchitecture practice · Concept · Spec/Architecture A model matching the hardware clock-by-clock but running faster than RTL, used to measure exact stalls and latencies. Architects use a cycle-accurate model to count pipeline stalls on real benchmark traces. Design-space explorationArchitecture practice · Methodology · Spec/Architecture Systematically trying many architecture or implementation options to find the best power, performance and area trade-off. A team sweeps cache size, bus width and core count in a model before choosing the final configuration. Cost of a bug by stageEngineering rule of thumb · Concept Fixing a bug costs roughly ten times more at each later stage, from minutes in RTL to a respin in silicon. A wrong FIFO depth caught in review costs an hour; found in silicon it costs months and a new mask set.

docs.title: 1.10 Who Does What: Fabless, Foundry, IDM, EDA, IP and OSAT
docs.text:
Very few companies do everything themselves. Fabless companies design chips but own no factories; foundries manufacture chips for others; IDMs (integrated device manufacturers) design and build their own. EDA vendors sell the design software, IP vendors license ready-made blocks, and OSATs package and test the finished dies.

The semiconductor value chain. A fabless company owns the design; everyone else supplies tools, blocks, factories or services.

Think of it like…

It is like the book industry: authors (fabless) write, printers (foundries) print, some publishers own their own presses (IDMs), and others sell the word-processing software (EDA) or license famous characters (IP).

Real-world example

When a fabless start-up called Lumen AI builds an inference chip, it licenses an Arm CPU and Synopsys PCIe IP, designs with Cadence and Synopsys tools, sends the layout to TSMC for wafers, has ASE package the dies with HBM memory, and tests them on Advantest testers. Lumen owns none of the factories but owns the design and the brand.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Fabless design house creates the chip using EDA tools and licensed IP.
  2. Foundry manufactures wafers using its process and PDK.
  3. OSAT (or the foundry's advanced packaging line) dices, packages and tests.
  4. Distributors or direct sales deliver chips to system makers (OEMs).
  5. IDMs like Intel, Samsung, TI and Infineon do several of these steps in-house.

Who uses it

Students should know this map because job titles, salaries and locations follow it: design jobs at fabless firms, process jobs at foundries, test jobs at OSATs.

Key takeaway

TSMC is the world's largest foundry by far; NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Broadcom and MediaTek are famous fabless companies.

Going deeper

  • Business models blur: Intel runs Intel Foundry for outside customers, Samsung designs Exynos chips while manufacturing for others, and hyperscalers design chips without selling them.
  • Margins differ sharply: fabless, IP and EDA firms are asset-light, while leading foundries spend tens of billions of dollars a year on new fabs and equipment.
  • Design teams cluster in the US, Europe, Israel, India, Taiwan and China; leading-edge logic fabs in Taiwan, South Korea and the US; OSAT capacity in Taiwan, China and South-East Asia.
  • EDA is concentrated: Synopsys and Cadence hold the majority of the market with Siemens EDA third, while Arm and Synopsys lead semiconductor IP licensing.
  • One chip programme involves many contracts: EDA licences, IP licences and royalties, a foundry wafer agreement, OSAT services, test-equipment time and distribution.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming fabless companies ignore manufacturing: they still own yield, test, qualification and supply-chain relationships.
  • Thinking IDMs make everything in-house: many use foundries for some products and OSATs for packaging.
  • Confusing foundry with fab: a fab is a factory building, a foundry is a business that manufactures chips for customers.

docs.title: 1.11 Worked Example: A Tiny Chip Through the Whole Flow
docs.text:
Seeing one small design go end to end makes every later chapter easier. Here we follow a simple 8-bit PWM (pulse-width modulation) LED controller from idea to a working chip using open-source tools and an open PDK, the same steps a big SoC uses, just smaller.

Leila's PWM chip, step by step. The same stages as a commercial SoC, run with free tools on an open PDK.

Think of it like…

It is like learning cooking by making one simple omelette from shopping to plating before attempting a banquet.

Real-world example

Student Leila writes a 60-line Verilog PWM module, simulates it in Icarus Verilog and views the waveform in GTKWave. She runs Verilator lint, synthesises with Yosys to about 150 SKY130 cells, then uses LibreLane to floorplan, place, build a clock tree and route. KLayout shows her layout, Magic and Netgen pass DRC and LVS, and she submits the GDS to a Tiny Tapeout shuttle. Months later she plugs the demo board into USB and her LED fades smoothly.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Spec: 8-bit duty cycle register, 10 MHz clock, one PWM output pin.
  2. RTL + testbench: write Verilog and simulate; check waveforms and assertions.
  3. Synthesis: Yosys maps RTL to standard cells using an SDC clock constraint.
  4. Place and route: floorplan, place cells, CTS, route; OpenSTA checks timing.
  5. Signoff and tapeout: DRC, LVS, final GDS; then fab, package, test on a board.

Who uses it

Universities, hobbyists and new graduates use exactly this flow to get hands-on experience before industry.

Key takeaway

Putting a real taped-out design (even a Tiny Tapeout tile) on your CV is a strong differentiator for entry-level jobs.

Going deeper

  • Tiny Tapeout designs follow a fixed template: a top module named tt_um_<name> with dedicated input, output and bidirectional pin buses plus clock, reset and enable, so every tile fits one shared harness.
  • A single Tiny Tapeout tile holds roughly a thousand digital gates in SKY130 — plenty for a PWM, UART, small state machine or tiny CPU experiment.
  • Every step writes reports: Yosys cell counts, OpenROAD utilisation and congestion, OpenSTA worst slack, and DRC/LVS summaries; learning to read them is the real skill.
  • The steps map directly to commercial tools: Icarus becomes VCS or Xcelium, Yosys becomes Design Compiler or Genus, OpenROAD becomes Innovus or Fusion Compiler, Magic and KLayout become Calibre.
  • Open PDKs available for practice include SkyWater SKY130 (130 nm), GlobalFoundries GF180MCU (180 nm) and IHP SG13G2 (130 nm SiGe BiCMOS); Tiny Tapeout runs shuttles on all three.
  • Silicon takes months to come back from a shuttle, so simulate thoroughly and, if possible, test the design on an FPGA board before submitting.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Skipping simulation because the design is tiny: a bug found after tapeout costs a whole shuttle cycle of months.
  • Ignoring flow warnings: an unconstrained clock or hidden DRC error can ruin the chip even when the flow 'completes'.
  • Forgetting reset: without one the counter powers up unknown; simulation shows X while silicon behaves randomly.

docs.title: Try it: Minimal PWM module in Verilog
docs.text:
module pwm (input clk, input rst_n, input [7:0] duty, output pwm_out);
  reg [7:0] cnt;
  always @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) cnt <= 8'd0;
    else        cnt <= cnt + 8'd1;
  assign pwm_out = (cnt < duty);
endmodule

docs.text: Name What it does Example Icarus VerilogStephen Williams (open source) · Tool · Verification · Open source The first tool Leila runs: it compiles her Verilog RTL and testbench and simulates them, writing a waveform file. iverilog -o sim pwm.v tb.v && vvp sim runs her PWM test in under a second. GTKWaveOpen-source project · Tool · Verification · Open source Waveform viewer for VCD/FST files produced by simulators. Leila zooms into the PWM output to check it is high for 64 of 256 cycles. YosysYosysHQ (Claire Xenia Wolf) · Tool · Synthesis · Open source In this flow, Yosys reads the PWM RTL and maps it onto SKY130 standard cells, reporting the cell count. Yosys turns the 8-bit counter and comparator into about 150 cells, mostly flops, adders and gates. LibreLaneFOSSi Foundation (successor to OpenLane 2) · Tool · Physical Design · Open source The push-button flow script that drives every step here, from synthesis to signed-off GDS, from one config file. Running librelane config.json takes Leila's design from Verilog to a final GDS in minutes. OpenROAD places Leila's 150 cells, builds a small clock tree and routes them on SKY130 metal layers. She toggles metal layers in KLayout to see how the clock net was routed across her tile. SKY130 PDKSkyWater Technology and Google (2020) · Standard · Fabrication · Open source The open 130 nm process kit used in this example, supplying the cells, rules and models for every step. Because SKY130 is open, Leila can inspect every cell and rule file her layout depends on. Tiny TapeoutTiny Tapeout (Matt Venn and team) · Resource · Whole flow The low-cost shuttle that turns Leila's small tile into real silicon by sharing one chip among many designs. She buys one tile on a SKY130 shuttle and months later receives a demo board containing her design. The Tiny Tapeout board uses a microcontroller to select which user design is active. TestbenchVerification practice · Concept · Verification A non-synthesisable module that drives clock, reset and inputs into the design and checks its outputs. Leila's testbench sets duty to 64, counts high cycles over 256 clocks and prints PASS or FAIL. Leila sets CLOCK_PERIOD to 100 ns for 10 MHz, and the timing report shows plenty of slack. One DRC error for metal spacing appears; Leila reruns routing with a lower density and it clears. GitHub Actions build (Tiny Tapeout template)Tiny Tapeout project template · Methodology · Whole flow Tiny Tapeout's template repository runs the hardening flow automatically on every push, producing GDS and reports. Each time Leila pushes Verilog, a green tick confirms her tile still hardens and passes checks. Flow reports (area, timing, power)EDA practice · Concept · Whole flow Summary files from each step: cell count, core utilisation, worst slack and estimated power. Leila's final report shows about 150 cells, 40 % utilisation and positive slack at 10 MHz.

docs.title: 1.12 Cost, NRE and Time-to-Market
docs.text:
A chip has two kinds of cost. NRE (non-recurring engineering) is the one-time cost to design it: engineers, EDA licences, IP licences and mask sets. Unit cost is what each manufactured chip costs: silicon, packaging and test. ASICs only make sense when the volume is high enough to spread the NRE thin, or when no off-the-shelf chip can do the job.

Fernhill: FPGA vs ASIC yearly cost. At 100k units the FPGA is cheaper; at 1M units the ASIC's 4 million dollar NRE pays back many times over.

Think of it like…

It is like opening a restaurant: kitchen fit-out and permits are one-time costs (NRE), while ingredients for each meal are the per-unit cost.

Real-world example

Fernhill Robotics compares options for a motor controller. An FPGA costs 25 dollars per unit with almost no NRE. A 28 nm ASIC would cost 2 dollars per unit but 4 million dollars NRE. At 100,000 units a year, the FPGA costs 2.5 million versus the ASIC's 4.2 million, so the FPGA wins. At 1 million units a year, the ASIC saves about 19 million dollars.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Estimate NRE: engineering salaries, EDA/IP licences, masks, prototypes and qualification.
  2. Estimate unit cost: wafer price / good dies per wafer + packaging + test.
  3. Find the break-even volume where ASIC total cost beats the alternative.
  4. Add time-to-market risk: a respin can cost months and lost sales.
  5. Consider MPW shuttles and older nodes to cut prototype cost.

Who uses it

Product managers, executives, ASIC programme managers and start-up founders make these calculations; engineers should understand them.

Key takeaway

Mask sets for leading-edge nodes cost many millions of dollars, which is why first-time-right design and thorough verification matter so much.

Going deeper

  • NRE usually comprises engineering salaries (often the largest part), EDA licences, IP licence fees, mask sets, prototype wafers, package design, test-program development and qualification.
  • Unit cost = wafer cost ÷ good dies per wafer, plus package, test and royalties; because yield falls as dies grow, cost per good die rises faster than area.
  • Mask costs climb with each node because more layers need masks and EUV or multi-patterning masks are complex; leading-edge mask sets cost many millions of dollars.
  • Cost levers: MPW shuttles for prototypes, mature nodes for analog and I/O, reuse of silicon-proven IP, chiplets that mix nodes, and metal-only ECOs instead of full respins.
  • Automotive and industrial chips spread NRE over 10-15 years of supply but pay extra for AEC-Q100 qualification and ISO 26262 functional-safety work.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing unit prices alone; ignoring NRE, schedule risk and respin probability makes an ASIC look far cheaper than it is.
  • Assuming cost scales linearly with die area; yield losses make large dies disproportionately expensive.
  • Forgetting royalties and test time: a few cents per chip becomes millions of dollars at high volume.

docs.title: Try it: Break-even volume in Python
docs.text:
nre = 4_000_000            # ASIC one-time cost ($)
asic_unit, fpga_unit = 2.0, 25.0
break_even = nre / (fpga_unit - asic_unit)
print(f"ASIC pays off above {break_even:,.0f} units")
# ASIC pays off above 173,913 units

docs.text: Name What it does Example NRE (Non-Recurring Engineering)Industry term · Concept · Whole flow One-time costs to design and prepare a chip for production, independent of how many are made. Industry estimates put advanced-node SoC development in the hundreds of millions of dollars. Mask set costFoundries / mask shops · Concept · Fabrication Cost of the photomasks needed for every layer; rises steeply at advanced nodes with more layers. A mature 180 nm mask set may cost tens of thousands of dollars; a leading-edge set costs millions. Unit costIndustry term · Concept Cost to produce one good, packaged, tested chip. Wafer cost 6,000 dollars / 500 good dies = 12 dollars, plus 3 dollars package and test. Break-even volumeBusiness analysis · Concept The production quantity at which an ASIC's total cost equals the alternative's. If NRE is 2 million and each chip saves 10 dollars, break-even is 200,000 units. Time-to-marketBusiness term · Concept Time from project start to product shipping; missing a market window can kill a chip. A phone chip that misses the autumn launch season may lose a whole year of sales. A university pays a few thousand euros for a small slot on a 65 nm MPW run. Splitting one huge die into four chiplets can raise good-die yield dramatically. Teams spend more on verification than design partly to be first-time-right. Automotive customers demand 10-15 years of supply for an ASIC. A simple QFN costs cents per unit, while a large AI package with HBM costs far more.

docs.title: 1.13 Scaling, Nodes and Why Chips Keep Getting Better
docs.text:
For decades, each new manufacturing generation (node) made transistors smaller, faster and cheaper. Today scaling is harder and more expensive, so progress also comes from new transistor shapes (FinFET, gate-all-around), new ways of delivering power (backside power), and stacking or combining many smaller chips (chiplets and 3D packaging).

Milestones in transistor scaling. Progress now comes from new transistor shapes, lithography and power delivery, not just shrinking.

Think of it like…

When you cannot fit more houses on a street by making them smaller, you start building upwards and putting the plumbing underground.

Real-world example

A smartphone SoC moved from 7 nm to 5 nm to 3 nm over five years. Each step gave roughly 10-20 % more speed or 20-30 % less power, plus more transistors per square millimetre. But each step also raised wafer cost, so the company kept its Wi-Fi and power-management chips on cheaper 12-28 nm processes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Planar transistors scaled until about 28-20 nm.
  2. FinFETs (3D fin-shaped channels) dominated from about 22/16 nm to 3 nm.
  3. Gate-all-around nanosheets arrived with Samsung's 3 nm and at 2 nm-class nodes (TSMC N2, Intel 18A, Samsung SF2).
  4. Backside power delivery (Intel PowerVia, TSMC Super Power Rail in A16) moves power wires under the transistors.
  5. Chiplets and 3D stacking add capability without one giant die.

Who uses it

Architects choose nodes; foundry, process and packaging engineers drive scaling; every designer feels its effects on rules and tools.

Key takeaway

Leading-edge isn't always best: most chips by volume are made on mature nodes (28 nm and above) because they are cheaper and good enough.

Going deeper

  • Dennard scaling ended around 2005: supply voltage stopped falling, so clock frequency stalled and gains came from parallelism, specialisation and better transistors instead.
  • A new node now typically brings roughly 10-15 % more speed at equal power or 20-30 % less power at equal speed, plus a density gain — far less than the near doubling of earlier eras.
  • Lithography drives scaling: 193 nm immersion DUV with multi-patterning reached 7 nm, EUV at 13.5 nm entered volume production in 2019, and High-NA EUV targets nodes beyond 2 nm.
  • Logic, SRAM, analog and I/O scale at different rates, so chiplet designs put compute on the newest node and I/O, analog or extra cache on cheaper processes.
  • Node choice is an economic decision: design cost, mask cost, wafer price and IP availability all rise steeply at each leading-edge node.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing node names across foundries directly: Intel 18A, TSMC N2 and Samsung SF2 differ in real density and performance.
  • Assuming the newest node suits every chip: analog, high-voltage and cost-sensitive designs often do better on 28-180 nm.
  • Thinking scaling is only about transistors: wires, SRAM, power delivery and packaging now limit gains as much as devices.

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies
docs.text: Name What it does Example Process nodeFoundry naming · Concept · Fabrication A named generation of manufacturing technology with its own rules, devices and performance. TSMC N3, Samsung SF2, Intel 18A and GF 22FDX are process nodes. Planar transistorClassic MOSFET structure · Concept · Fabrication A flat transistor where the gate sits on top of the channel; used until about 20-28 nm. Most 28 nm and older chips, including many microcontrollers, use planar transistors. FinFETFirst in volume: Intel 22 nm (2011) · Concept · Fabrication A transistor whose channel is a raised fin wrapped by the gate on three sides for better control. Phone chips from about 2015 to 2024 used FinFETs at 16 nm down to 3 nm. Gate-all-around (GAA) / nanosheetSamsung MBCFET (3 nm, 2022), TSMC N2, Intel RibbonFET (18A) · Concept · Fabrication Transistors with stacked horizontal sheets fully surrounded by the gate, reducing leakage further. TSMC N2 entered volume production in late 2025 using nanosheet transistors. Backside power deliveryIntel PowerVia (18A); TSMC Super Power Rail (A16) · Concept · Fabrication Routing power wires on the back of the wafer, freeing front metal for signals and cutting IR drop. Intel's 18A Panther Lake processors are the first high-volume products with backside power. FD-SOISTMicroelectronics, GlobalFoundries (22FDX), Samsung · Concept · Fabrication Planar transistors on a thin insulating layer, offering low leakage and body-bias tuning at lower cost. IoT and automotive radar chips use 22 nm FD-SOI for low power. Transistor density (MTr/mm²)Industry metric · Concept Millions of transistors per square millimetre, a rough way to compare nodes. Leading 3 nm-class logic exceeds 200 million transistors per square millimetre in dense blocks. Mature nodeIndustry term · Concept An older, cheaper and well-characterised process, typically 28 nm and above. Power-management chips, sensors and car microcontrollers often use 40-180 nm. More than MooreITRS/IRDS roadmap term · Concept Adding value through integration of sensors, RF, power and packaging rather than shrinking transistors. An MEMS microphone with on-package signal processing is a More-than-Moore product. IRDS (International Roadmap for Devices and Systems)IEEE (successor to ITRS) · Resource Industry roadmap forecasting devices, lithography and packaging needs for the next 15 years. Students read IRDS chapters to understand when new transistor types are expected. Interconnect scaling problemDevice and BEOL scaling · Concept Thinner wires grow more resistive each node, so wire delay and IR drop increasingly limit performance. Designers promote critical nets to thicker upper metal layers because lower layers are too resistive. SRAM scaling slowdownIndustry trend · Concept · Fabrication SRAM bit cells have shrunk far less than logic at recent nodes, so caches take a growing share of die area. TSMC's N3E high-density SRAM cell is about the same 0.021 µm² as N5's. Cost per transistorManufacturing economics · Concept For decades each node cut cost per transistor; since roughly 28 nm the savings have shrunk and are debated. A company keeps its IoT chip on 22 nm because moving to 5 nm would raise cost per useful function. Ångström-era node namesFoundry naming · Concept · Fabrication Below 2 nm, foundries label nodes in ångströms (0.1 nm), such as Intel 18A, Intel 14A and TSMC A16. Intel 18A is marketed as an 18-ångström (1.8 nm-class) node, though no feature measures 1.8 nm.

docs.title: Chapter 8: EDA Industry, Open-Source Silicon, Analog, AI-in-EDA & Careers
docs.text: The final chapter zooms out to the ecosystem around chip design: the big three EDA companies and their products, the open-source tools and open PDKs that let anyone tape out a chip, the basics of analog and mixed-signal design, and how AI agents are changing EDA in 2026. It then turns to you: how FPGAs can be a stepping stone, the Linux, Tcl and Python scripting skills every chip engineer uses, what each ASIC job role really does, a practical learning path with books, courses and websites, the interview questions you should be ready for, and how to land your first chip job.

docs.title: 8.1 The Big Three EDA Vendors: Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA
docs.text:
Three companies supply most of the world's chip design software: Synopsys, Cadence and Siemens EDA (formerly Mentor Graphics). Each offers tools covering almost the whole flow, but each has particular strengths. Most chip companies use a mix, choosing the best tool for each step and the one their foundry certifies.

Flagship tools by flow step

Synopsys Cadence Siemens EDA Simulation VCS Xcelium Questa Formal VC Formal Jasper Questa Formal Emulation ZeBu Palladium Veloce Synthesis Design Compiler, Fusion Compiler Genus Catapult (HLS) Place and route Fusion Compiler, ICC2 Innovus Aprisa Timing signoff PrimeTime Tempus — Extraction StarRC Quantus Calibre xACT Physical verification IC Validator Pegasus Calibre DFT and ATPG TestMAX Modus Tessent Custom and analog Custom Compiler, PrimeSim Virtuoso, Spectre Solido, AFS

Most chip companies mix these columns, picking the best tool for each step.

Think of it like…

The big three are like the major car makers: each sells a full range of vehicles, but drivers often have favourite models from different brands.

Real-world example

At Northgate Semi, verification runs on Xcelium and Jasper (Cadence), synthesis and P&R on Fusion Compiler (Synopsys), timing signoff on PrimeTime (Synopsys), DFT on Tessent (Siemens), and physical verification on Calibre (Siemens). The CAD team maintains scripts that pass data between all three vendors' tools using standard formats.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn which tool each vendor offers for each flow step.
  2. Understand that companies mix vendors based on PPA, foundry support and price.
  3. Know the key product names; they appear in every job advert.
  4. Use university programmes to get student access to commercial tools.
  5. Follow vendor news: acquisitions and product renames are frequent.

Who uses it

Every ASIC engineer uses these tools; CAD engineers, EDA application engineers and EDA developers work closely with the vendors.

Key takeaway

Map one flagship product per vendor per step, e.g. synthesis: Fusion Compiler/DC vs Genus; P&R: Fusion Compiler/ICC2 vs Innovus vs Aprisa; STA: PrimeTime vs Tempus.

Going deeper

  • Synopsys and Cadence each earn several billion US dollars a year; Siemens EDA sits inside Siemens Digital Industries Software after Siemens bought Mentor Graphics in 2017.
  • Mixed-vendor flows work because of shared formats (Verilog, Liberty, LEF/DEF, SDC, SPEF, UPF, GDSII/OASIS) and the OpenAccess database, plus vendor interoperability programmes.
  • The big vendors also sell semiconductor IP, with Synopsys and Cadence among the largest interface-IP suppliers, and hardware such as emulators and FPGA prototyping systems.
  • Licences are usually time-based multi-year agreements pooled on licence servers; token schemes let teams switch between tools, and cloud options absorb short peaks.
  • Foundries certify each vendor's tools for every new node; engineers check certification status and reference flows before choosing tools for advanced-node work.
  • Consolidation continues: Synopsys closed its Ansys purchase in July 2025, Siemens bought Altair in 2025, and Cadence bought Hexagon's design and engineering business (MSC Nastran, Adams) in February 2026.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Writing just 'Cadence tools' on a CV; name the exact tools and what you did with them.
  • Assuming a company uses one vendor for everything; most mix best-in-class tools step by step.
  • Thinking EDA vendors sell only software; IP, emulation hardware and services are large parts of their businesses.
