docs.title: 8.2 Other EDA and IP Players
docs.text:
Beyond the big three, many smaller companies offer specialised tools: lint and CDC, RF and high-frequency design, TCAD and device simulation, analog automation, design data management and more. China also has a fast-growing domestic EDA industry. Knowing these names helps you read job adverts and understand niche roles.

Specialist niches around the big three. Each niche has its own leaders, and many niche start-ups are later acquired by the big three.

Think of it like…

If the big three are department stores, these companies are specialist boutiques that do one thing extremely well.

Real-world example

An RF front-end team designs its power amplifier in Keysight ADS, its digital control in Cadence tools, and checks CDC with Real Intent Meridian. A foundry's device team uses Synopsys Sentaurus TCAD and Silvaco tools to model new transistors. A Chinese design house adopts Empyrean tools for analog layout and flat-panel display design.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Identify specialist needs: RF, TCAD, CDC, data management, analog automation.
  2. Evaluate niche tools for accuracy, integration and support.
  3. Integrate them with main-vendor flows via standard formats.
  4. Track acquisitions, as big vendors often buy successful specialists.
  5. Consider regional and open-source alternatives where appropriate.

Who uses it

CAD managers, RF/analog designers, TCAD engineers, methodology teams.

Key takeaway

Many big-three products began as start-ups (e.g. SpyGlass from Atrenta, Verdi from Novas, Jasper from Jasper Design Automation).

Going deeper

  • Many big-three flagships began as start-ups: SpyGlass (Atrenta, bought by Synopsys in 2015), Jasper (Cadence, 2014), Solido (Mentor, 2017), Aprisa (Avatar, Mentor, 2020) and OneSpin (Siemens, 2021).
  • Keysight grew in EDA by acquiring Cliosoft for design data management and Synopsys's optical solutions business, adding to its RF and high-speed digital tools.
  • Silvaco listed on Nasdaq in 2024 and supplies TCAD, analog/custom tools and IP; TCAD is a niche career linking device physics with design.
  • China's EDA vendors such as Empyrean, Primarius and X-Epic have grown quickly with government support, especially in analog, display and point tools.
  • AI-native start-ups raised significant funding in 2024-2026 to build agents for RTL, verification and debug; established vendors both partner with and compete against them.
  • Deals keep reshaping this list: GlobalFoundries took over Synopsys's ARC processor IP (June 2026), Arteris bought security-verification firm Cycuity (January 2026), and Siemens agreed to buy Defacto and Precision Innovations (July 2026).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Only applying to the big three; smaller EDA and IP firms often give broader responsibility and faster learning.
  • Assuming niche tools are second-rate; many are the industry standard in their niche, such as CDC signoff or RF simulation.
  • Forgetting integration cost: every extra tool needs format conversion, scripts and support in the flow.

docs.title: 8.3 Open-Source EDA: Yosys, OpenROAD, LibreLane, Magic, KLayout, Verilator
docs.text:
A complete open-source chip design flow now exists: Verilator and Icarus for simulation, Yosys for synthesis, OpenROAD for place and route, OpenSTA for timing, Magic, KLayout and Netgen for physical verification, all orchestrated by flows like LibreLane and OpenROAD-flow-scripts. They are free, scriptable and perfect for learning, research and small tapeouts.

An open-source RTL-to-GDS flow. LibreLane or OpenROAD-flow-scripts runs all of these steps from one configuration file.

Think of it like…

Open-source EDA is like a community kitchen with good, free equipment: you might not cook a 10-course banquet there, but you can learn every technique and serve real meals.

Real-world example

Priya, a second-year student, installs LibreLane with Nix, takes a small SPI peripheral, and in one evening goes from Verilog to GDS on SKY130. She opens the layout in KLayout, checks timing with OpenSTA, and reads OpenROAD logs to understand placement and CTS. Six months later her design is on a Tiny Tapeout chip and in her CV.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Install tools (package managers, Nix, Docker or the OSS CAD Suite builds).
  2. Simulate and lint with Icarus/Verilator; test with cocotb.
  3. Run a flow (LibreLane or ORFS) on an open PDK.
  4. Inspect results: timing, congestion, layout in KLayout or the OpenROAD GUI.
  5. Submit to a shuttle (Tiny Tapeout, wafer.space, ChipFoundry, IHP).

Who uses it

Students, researchers, hobbyists, start-ups prototyping, and companies contributing to open tools.

Key takeaway

Open-source tools teach the same concepts as commercial ones; put an open-source tapeout project on GitHub to stand out.

Going deeper

  • Licences are mostly permissive or weak copyleft, such as ISC (Yosys), BSD (OpenROAD, OpenRAM), Apache 2.0 (LibreLane), GPL (KLayout) and LGPL/Artistic (Verilator), so companies can use them commercially.
  • Open flows reach tapeout quality on 130-180 nm open PDKs; at advanced nodes commercial tools dominate because foundry certification and PDK access require NDAs.
  • Installation options include Nix (LibreLane's recommended route), Docker images such as IIC-OSIC-TOOLS and pre-built OSS CAD Suite archives; always pin versions for reproducibility.
  • Communities meet at FOSSi events (ORConf, Latch-Up), on GitHub and in chat servers; maintainers usually welcome newcomers who file clear, minimal bug reports.
  • Industry uses open tools too: Verilator for fast simulation, KLayout as a GDS viewer and scripting engine, and Yosys inside formal and FPGA flows.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Following old OpenLane 1 tutorials without checking; LibreLane commands and configuration keys differ in places.
  • Leaving PDK and tool versions unpinned, so a design that passed last month fails today.
  • Expecting commercial-grade PPA at advanced nodes from open tools; use them to learn concepts, then map to commercial tools.

docs.title: Try it: Run a LibreLane flow on an example design
docs.text:
# after installing LibreLane (see librelane.readthedocs.io)
librelane --pdk sky130A config.json
# then open the result
klayout runs/<run_tag>/final/gds/<design>.gds

docs.title: 8.4 Open PDKs and Shuttles: SKY130, GF180MCU, IHP and Tiny Tapeout
docs.text:
Open PDKs remove the NDA barrier so anyone can design a real chip, and shuttle programmes make fabrication affordable. After Efabless shut down in early 2025, the ecosystem regrouped: Tiny Tapeout continued with IHP and GF180 runs, ChipFoundry (founded by former Efabless leaders) restarted SKY130 shuttles, and wafer.space launched low-cost GF180MCU runs.

The open-silicon movement. In six years, real chip fabrication went from NDA-only to something a student can do.

Think of it like…

Open PDKs and shuttles are like community recording studios: once only big labels could afford to record an album; now anyone can book a slot.

Real-world example

A university club designs four student projects. Two go on a Tiny Tapeout shuttle for under a few hundred dollars each. One analog project uses IHP SG13G2 because it needs SiGe bipolar transistors. A start-up member puts a larger mixed-signal prototype on a wafer.space GF180MCU run, receiving about 1,000 chips per slot, enough for a small product trial.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick a PDK matching your needs: SKY130 (130 nm), GF180MCU (180 nm), IHP SG13G2 (130 nm BiCMOS).
  2. Choose a shuttle: Tiny Tapeout (small tiles), ChipFoundry, wafer.space, IHP or university programmes.
  3. Use the shuttle's template and flow, and pass its precheck.
  4. Submit before the deadline; wait several months for chips.
  5. Test on the demo board and share results openly.

Who uses it

Students, educators, researchers, hobbyists and early-stage start-ups.

Key takeaway

Shuttle schedules change; always check the provider's website for current runs, prices and supported PDKs.

Going deeper

  • SKY130 offers a local-interconnect layer plus five metal layers and devices from 1.8 V upward; GF180MCU offers 3.3-6 V devices; IHP SG13G2 adds SiGe HBTs with fT around 350 GHz.
  • Caravel, the SKY130 harness, gives each project a user area of about 10 mm² with 38 GPIOs, a Wishbone bus and logic-analyser probes driven by a RISC-V management core.
  • Tiny Tapeout projects start from a GitHub template; a GitHub Action runs the flow, and on the chip a multiplexer connects one selected tile at a time to the shared pins.
  • Expect six to nine months or more from submission to chips; shuttle dates can slip, as the 2025 Efabless closure showed.
  • Costs range from tens or hundreds of dollars for Tiny Tapeout tiles to thousands for a full shuttle slot, far below the cost of a private mask set.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating shuttle dates as guaranteed; build slack into course or project schedules.
  • Skipping gate-level simulation or ignoring precheck warnings; there is no second chance once the chip is fabricated.
  • Thinking an open PDK means relaxed rules; DRC, LVS and antenna checks are just as strict.

docs.title: 8.5 〰️ Analog and Mixed-Signal Basics
docs.text:
Not everything on a chip is digital. Analog circuits handle continuous signals: amplifiers, data converters (ADCs/DACs), PLLs, voltage regulators, sensors and radio front-ends. Mixed-signal chips combine analog and digital blocks. Analog design is done mostly by hand at the transistor level, with careful simulation and layout, and it is a highly valued skill.

A mixed-signal signal chain. Bandgap references, regulators and a PLL support every block in this chain.

Think of it like…

Digital is like a light switch (on/off); analog is like a dimmer that can be set anywhere, which makes it more flexible but much more sensitive to noise and variation.

Real-world example

A fitness-tracker chip contains a heart-rate sensor front-end amplifier, a 16-bit ADC, a Bluetooth radio, a PLL, a DC-DC converter and an LDO, plus digital logic and a CPU. Analog designer Hana draws the ADC schematic in Virtuoso, simulates it with Spectre across 45 corners and Monte Carlo runs, then works closely with a layout engineer to match transistors and avoid noise coupling from the digital logic.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Specify performance: gain, bandwidth, noise, linearity, power, area.
  2. Design schematics and size transistors using hand analysis and simulation.
  3. Simulate across corners, temperature and Monte Carlo variation.
  4. Create careful layout: matching, symmetry, guard rings, shielding.
  5. Post-layout simulation with parasitics; mixed-signal verification with digital.

Who uses it

Analog designers, RF designers, mixed-signal verification engineers, analog layout engineers.

Key takeaway

Analog skills are scarce and well paid; Razavi's textbook is the standard starting point.

Going deeper

  • In saturation a MOSFET's current is roughly ½·µCox·(W/L)·(Vgs − Vth)²; at advanced nodes designers prefer the gm/Id method with simulated lookup tables.
  • kT/C noise equals √(kT/C), about 64 µV rms for 1 pF at 300 K, so higher resolution needs larger capacitors and therefore more power.
  • ADC architectures trade speed for resolution: flash (fastest), pipeline, SAR (efficient mid-range) and sigma-delta (highest resolution, lower bandwidth); ENOB = (SINAD − 1.76)/6.02.
  • Analog scales poorly: lower supply voltages shrink signal headroom and short transistors have low intrinsic gain, so analog often stays on older nodes or becomes digitally assisted.
  • Many PLLs at advanced nodes are all-digital (ADPLL), using a time-to-digital converter and a digitally controlled oscillator instead of a charge pump.
  • Mixed-signal chips isolate noisy digital logic from sensitive analog using separate supplies, guard rings, deep N-wells and careful floorplanning.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Simulating only the typical corner; analog circuits must work across process, voltage, temperature and mismatch.
  • Treating analog blocks as ideal in SoC verification; real-number models must include power-up, enables and calibration.
  • Ignoring layout: parasitics, mismatch and substrate coupling can ruin a schematic that simulated perfectly.

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies
docs.text: Name What it does Example Op-amp / OTAAnalog building block · Concept · RTL Design Amplifiers that boost voltage differences; the workhorse of analog circuits. A two-stage OTA buffers a reference voltage for an ADC. ADC and DACData converters · Concept · RTL Design Convert analog signals to digital numbers (ADC) and back (DAC). A 12-bit SAR ADC samples a temperature sensor 1 million times per second. PLL building blocks (PFD, charge pump, VCO)Analog/mixed-signal circuit design · Concept · RTL Design Feedback loop of phase detector, charge pump, loop filter, VCO and divider; loop bandwidth trades jitter against lock time. An analog designer sizes the loop filter so a 2.4 GHz PLL locks within 20 µs while meeting its jitter budget. LDO and DC-DC convertersPower-management building blocks · Concept · RTL Design Regulators that provide stable supply voltages from a battery or main supply. An on-chip LDO supplies a clean 0.9 V to a sensitive analog block. Bandgap referenceAnalog building block · Concept · RTL Design Circuit producing a stable reference voltage independent of temperature and supply. A 1.2 V bandgap feeds the ADC and regulators. SerDesMixed-signal building block · Concept · RTL Design Serialiser/deserialiser transmitting very high-speed serial data with equalisation and clock recovery. A 112G PAM4 SerDes uses DSP-based receivers to recover the data. SerDes equalisers and clock-data recovery (FFE, CTLE, DFE, CDR)Mixed-signal building blocks inside every SerDes PHY · Concept · RTL design Transmit FFE plus receive CTLE and DFE undo channel loss, while clock-data recovery extracts timing from the data stream itself. During link training a 112G receiver adapts its CTLE peaking and DFE taps until the pre-FEC error rate meets the standard's target. Monte Carlo simulationAnalog verification · Methodology · Verification Running many simulations with random device variation to estimate yield. 1,000 Monte Carlo runs show the comparator offset stays under 5 mV. Matching and analog layoutAnalog layout practice · Methodology · Physical Design Layout techniques (common-centroid, interdigitation, dummies) to make devices identical. Input transistors of a differential pair are laid out common-centroid. Mixed-signal verification (AMS, real-number modelling)Verilog-AMS, SystemVerilog real-number models (wreal) · Methodology · Verification Verifying analog and digital together using co-simulation or simplified real-number models. An ADC is modelled with SystemVerilog real numbers in the SoC UVM testbench. BCD and RF processesFoundry specialty processes · Process · Fabrication Processes optimised for power management (Bipolar-CMOS-DMOS) or radio frequencies. A motor-driver IC uses a 130 nm BCD process with 40 V transistors. Current mirrorAnalog building block · Concept · RTL Design Transistor pair copying a reference current into other branches; used to bias almost every analog circuit. A 10 µA reference current is mirrored to bias amplifiers across the chip. Differential pairAnalog building block · Concept · RTL Design Two matched transistors amplifying the difference between their inputs while rejecting noise common to both. An op-amp's input stage is a differential pair, rejecting supply noise that hits both inputs equally. Noise (thermal, flicker, kT/C)Analog fundamentals · Concept · RTL Design Random device signals that set the smallest detectable signal; kT/C noise limits how small sampling capacitors can be. A 1 pF sampling capacitor adds about 64 µV rms of kT/C noise at room temperature. Data-converter metrics (ENOB, SNR, INL/DNL)IEEE 1241 and industry practice · Concept · RTL Design Numbers describing converter quality: effective number of bits, signal-to-noise ratio and static linearity errors. A '12-bit' ADC with 68 dB SINAD has an ENOB of about 11 bits.

docs.title: 8.6 Analog Design Tools: Virtuoso, Spectre, HSPICE, ngspice, Xschem
docs.text:
Analog designers draw schematics, simulate them with SPICE-class simulators, and lay out transistors by hand or with assistance. Cadence Virtuoso is the dominant commercial environment, with Spectre for simulation. Synopsys offers Custom Compiler and PrimeSim (including HSPICE), and Siemens offers Solido and Analog FastSPICE. Open-source options include Xschem, ngspice, Xyce, Magic and KLayout.

The analog design loop and its tools. Analog design iterates: post-layout results often send the designer back to the schematic.

Think of it like…

Analog tools are like an artist's studio: a sketchpad (schematic), a physics lab (simulator) and a precision drawing table (layout editor).

Real-world example

In industry, Raj designs an LDO in Virtuoso Schematic Editor, runs Spectre across corners with the ADE Assembler, and checks variation with Solido. On an open-source project, his student cousin draws the same LDO in Xschem using the IHP PDK, simulates with ngspice, and lays it out in KLayout with PDK PCells.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Draw the schematic with PDK symbols.
  2. Set up testbenches and simulate (DC, AC, transient, noise) across corners.
  3. Run statistical and variation analysis.
  4. Draw layout; run DRC, LVS and extraction.
  5. Re-simulate with parasitics and iterate.

Who uses it

Analog, RF and mixed-signal designers; analog layout engineers; CAD support.

Key takeaway

Virtuoso is the most requested analog tool in job adverts; Xschem plus ngspice is the best free way to practise.

Going deeper

  • SPICE simulators solve circuit equations accurately but slowly; FastSPICE tools partition and simplify circuits to handle memories and full-chip analog at some accuracy cost.
  • Virtuoso stores designs in the OpenAccess database and is automated with the SKILL language; most commercial PDK PCells are written in SKILL.
  • RF and PLL design adds periodic steady-state (PSS) and periodic noise (PNoise) analyses to the usual DC, AC, transient and noise simulations.
  • SRAM and other heavily replicated cells need high-sigma verification, around 6 sigma; tools such as Solido use statistical methods instead of billions of brute-force Monte Carlo runs.
  • The open analog stack (Xschem, ngspice or Xyce, Magic or KLayout, Netgen) is bundled in containers such as IIC-OSIC-TOOLS for SKY130, GF180MCU and IHP PDKs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting results without checking simulator accuracy settings, convergence and time steps.
  • Stopping at schematic simulation; post-layout simulation with extracted parasitics is mandatory.
  • Using the wrong model library section or corner set from the PDK, which invalidates every result.

docs.title: Try it: Run an ngspice simulation in batch mode
docs.text: ngspice -b inverter.cir -o inverter.log

docs.title: 8.7 AI in EDA: From Design-Space Optimisation to Agentic Flows
docs.text:
AI is now part of everyday chip design. Since about 2020, machine-learning tools have tuned P&R settings and prioritised verification runs. Since 2023, generative AI assistants answer tool questions and draft scripts and RTL. In 2025-2026, the big three launched 'agentic' AI: systems that plan and execute multi-step tasks like writing RTL, building testbenches, running regressions and debugging, with human engineers supervising.

How an agentic EDA loop works. Real EDA tools, not the language model, decide whether each step passed.

Think of it like…

First AI was a smart calculator for tuning knobs, then a helpful assistant you could ask questions, and now it is becoming a junior engineer you assign tasks to and review.

Real-world example

A verification team at a GPU company pilots an agentic flow: the agent reads the spec section for a new FIFO, writes the RTL and a cocotb/UVM testbench, runs simulation, finds a failing assertion and proposes a fix. The engineer reviews every change. Separately, the PD team's Cerebrus runs explore 200 settings combinations and cut power by 7 %. AI saves time, but humans remain responsible for signoff.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Optimisation AI: reinforcement learning explores tool settings for better PPA (DSO.ai, Cerebrus).
  2. Analytics AI: prioritises regressions, predicts congestion, clusters failures.
  3. Generative AI copilots: answer questions, write scripts, RTL and assertions.
  4. Agentic AI: multi-step agents run tools, read logs and iterate under human supervision.
  5. Humans review outputs, especially for correctness, security and IP ownership.

Who uses it

All design engineers increasingly use AI tools; CAD teams integrate them; AI/ML engineers in EDA companies build them.

Key takeaway

Be ready to discuss AI in interviews: what it is good at (exploration, triage, boilerplate) and why verification and human signoff still matter.

Going deeper

  • Optimisation AI such as DSO.ai and Cerebrus uses reinforcement learning or similar search over tool settings, launching many parallel runs; gains are real but cost compute and licences.
  • LLMs often produce RTL that compiles but is functionally wrong; agentic flows ground them by running real simulators, formal tools and linters and feeding results back.
  • Companies deploy AI on private infrastructure or under strict contracts, because RTL and PDK data are confidential and may be export-controlled.
  • Signoff stays deterministic: STA, DRC/LVS and equivalence checking remain the final judges, whatever generated the design.
  • Independent studies questioned how well Google's reinforcement-learning macro placement generalises, a reminder to compare AI claims against strong baselines.
  • Skills that make engineers effective with AI: precise specifications, verification thinking, scripting and the judgement to spot a plausible but wrong answer.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting AI-written RTL or scripts because they compile; verify them functionally and review them like a junior colleague's code.
  • Pasting proprietary RTL or PDK data into public AI tools, breaching NDAs and possibly export rules.
  • Assuming AI removes the need for fundamentals; you cannot review what you do not understand.

docs.title: 8.8 FPGAs as a Stepping Stone
docs.text:
FPGAs let you turn your RTL into working hardware on your desk in minutes, for the price of a development board. They are the best way for students to practise RTL design, debugging and timing closure on real hardware. Many ASIC engineers started on FPGAs, and FPGA prototyping is also used inside ASIC projects.

FPGA vs ASIC at a glance

FPGA ASIC Logic LUTs and fixed routing Standard cells, custom wiring Up-front cost A board, from about $100 NRE, often millions Unit cost at volume Higher Much lower Turnaround Minutes to hours Months per tapeout Typical clock About 100-500 MHz Up to several GHz Power and area Higher Lowest for the function Clocking style Global clock nets, clock enables CTS, clock gating Best for Prototypes, low volume, updates High volume, best PPA

The RTL skills transfer directly; the economics and physical details differ.

Think of it like…

An FPGA board is like a flight simulator you can take home: not a real airliner, but you learn to fly properly before getting your licence.

Real-world example

Tom buys an entry-level FPGA board. He writes a UART, a VGA controller and finally a small RISC-V CPU in SystemVerilog, synthesises them in Vivado, and debugs with the integrated logic analyser. Timing reports teach him about critical paths. In his ASIC interview, he explains how he pipelined his CPU to reach 100 MHz, and the interviewer is impressed by the hands-on experience.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Buy a beginner board (AMD/Xilinx Artix, Altera Cyclone, Lattice iCE40/ECP5).
  2. Install the vendor tool (Vivado, Quartus Prime, Radiant) or open-source Yosys + nextpnr.
  3. Build projects: LEDs, UART, VGA/HDMI, SPI, a small CPU.
  4. Simulate first, then synthesise, place and route, and program the board.
  5. Use timing reports and on-chip logic analysers to debug and close timing.

Who uses it

Students, hobbyists, FPGA engineers, ASIC prototyping engineers.

Key takeaway

Remember the differences: FPGAs use LUTs and fixed routing, so ASIC-style gated clocks and latches are discouraged on FPGAs.

Going deeper

  • FPGA fabric groups LUTs, carry chains and flip-flops into slices (AMD) or ALMs (Altera), surrounded by block RAM, DSP blocks, clock managers and high-speed transceivers.
  • A Vivado Tcl flow mirrors ASIC steps: synth_design, opt_design, place_design, route_design, report_timing_summary and finally write_bitstream.
  • FPGA timing closure teaches real STA skills: reading setup and hold slack, adding pipeline stages and writing clock and I/O constraints in SDC syntax.
  • Open toolchains built on Yosys and nextpnr support Lattice iCE40 and ECP5 and Gowin parts; Project X-Ray documents AMD 7-series bitstreams for experimental open flows.
  • Adaptive SoCs such as AMD Zynq, Altera Agilex SoC and Microchip PolarFire SoC combine hard processors with FPGA fabric, ideal for hardware-software projects.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Debugging only on the board without simulating first; waveform simulation finds most bugs far faster.
  • Carrying FPGA-only habits, such as initial register values or vendor primitives, into ASIC RTL where they do not work.
  • Ignoring timing warnings because the design seems to work on one board at room temperature.

docs.title: Try it: Open-source FPGA build for a Lattice iCE40 board
docs.text:
yosys -p "synth_ice40 -top top -json top.json" top.v
nextpnr-ice40 --up5k --package sg48 --json top.json --pcf pins.pcf --asc top.asc
icepack top.asc top.bin
iceprog top.bin

docs.title: 8.9 Scripting, Linux and Flow Automation for Chip Engineers
docs.text:
Chip engineers spend much of their day at a Linux command line, driving tools with scripts rather than buttons. Tcl controls almost every EDA tool, Python glues flows together and analyses results, Make and flow managers run hundreds of steps in the right order on a compute farm, and version control keeps every change traceable. Fluency in these skills is expected in every front-end and back-end job.

An automated nightly flow. Scripts, not people, run each step, so results are repeatable and comparable.

Think of it like…

EDA tools are the kitchen appliances; scripts are the recipes and timers that run them in order, so dinner for a thousand guests comes out the same every night.

Real-world example

Each night at Northgate Semi, a CI job pulls the latest RTL, and a Makefile launches synthesis, four P&R experiments and STA on the compute farm through the job scheduler. Tcl scripts inside each tool apply constraints and write reports; a Python script parses the timing reports, compares worst slack with yesterday and posts a chart. When a run fails, the engineer searches the log for the first ERROR line instead of reading 200,000 lines.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn the Linux shell: files, pipes, grep, sed, awk, find, environment variables and job control.
  2. Learn Tcl the way EDA tools use it: variables, lists, loops, procedures and object collections.
  3. Use Python to parse logs and reports, plot trends and connect tools together.
  4. Run flows reproducibly with Make or a flow manager, a job scheduler and pinned tool versions.
  5. Keep RTL, constraints and scripts under version control and review every change.
  6. Automate quick checks on every commit so broken changes are caught within hours.

Who uses it

Every chip engineer; CAD and flow engineers make it their speciality, and DV, PD, STA and DFT job adverts routinely list Tcl, Python and Linux.

Key takeaway

Interviews often include writing a Tcl loop over design objects or a one-line grep/awk command to pull worst slack from a report, so practise both.

Going deeper

  • Tcl spread through EDA in the 1990s; SDC, UPF and most tool shells are Tcl, so set, foreach, proc, lsort and regexp appear in constraint files as well as flow scripts.
  • Collections are not Tcl lists: commands like get_cells return handles that must be walked with foreach_in_collection or converted with get_object_name; mixing the two is a classic beginner bug.
  • Python's role keeps growing: cocotb testbenches, OpenROAD and KLayout APIs, report parsers and AI-assisted flow tools are Python, while Tcl remains the language inside each tool.
  • Compute farms schedule licences as well as servers; jobs queue when licences run out, so efficient scripts release licences promptly and checkpoint long runs.
  • Reproducibility means pinning tool versions (modules, containers or Nix), recording seeds and versions in every run log, and tagging the exact commit used for tapeout.
  • Shell essentials worth drilling: pipes and redirection, find, grep -r, sed -i, awk field printing, xargs, tail -f on a running log, and ssh with tmux for long remote sessions.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Parsing reports with fragile regular expressions; formats change between tool versions, so prefer tool query commands or APIs where possible.
  • Hard-coding paths and tool versions inside scripts; use variables and environment modules so flows move between projects.
  • Keeping personal scripts outside version control; an untracked tweak that fixed timing cannot be reproduced at the next ECO.

docs.title: Try it: PrimeTime-style Tcl: print the endpoints and slack of the five worst setup paths
docs.text:
foreach_in_collection p [get_timing_paths -max_paths 5 -delay_type max] {
    set ep    [get_object_name [get_attribute $p endpoint]]
    set slack [get_attribute $p slack]
    puts [format "%-40s %8.3f" $ep $slack]
}

# Shell: show the first error in a long log, with its line number
# grep -n -m1 "ERROR" synth.log

docs.title: 8.10 Careers in ASIC Design: Who Does What
docs.text:
Chip design offers many distinct careers. Front-end roles include architects, RTL designers and design verification engineers. Back-end roles include synthesis, physical design, STA, physical verification and DFT engineers. Supporting roles include CAD/flow engineers, analog designers, post-silicon validation, product and test engineers, and application engineers at EDA and IP companies.

The roles in a chip company. Every tier is needed for working silicon, and engineers often move between neighbouring roles.

Think of it like…

A chip team is like a film crew: writers, directors, camera operators, editors and sound engineers each master their craft, and the film needs all of them.

Real-world example

At a 300-person chip company: 15 architects, 60 RTL designers, 100 verification engineers, 50 physical design and STA engineers, 15 DFT engineers, 20 CAD engineers, 15 analog designers and 25 validation/product engineers. A new graduate joins as a DV engineer, moves into formal verification after two years, and later becomes a verification lead.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Learn the fundamentals (digital logic, CMOS, computer architecture, HDLs).
  2. Choose a direction: front end (RTL/DV), back end (PD/STA/DFT), analog, or CAD.
  3. Build hands-on projects in that direction with open-source or student tools.
  4. Apply for internships and graduate roles; network at conferences and meetups.
  5. Grow into senior, lead, architect or management roles over time.

Who uses it

Semiconductor companies, hyperscalers, EDA vendors, IP companies, foundries, OSATs, start-ups and design-service firms hire these roles.

Key takeaway

Design verification is the largest entry-level hiring area; physical design and DFT are often in high demand too.

Going deeper

  • Typical entry requirements are a bachelor's or master's in electrical or computer engineering; a master's is common for design roles and a PhD for research, architecture and EDA algorithms.
  • Most companies run parallel ladders: technical (senior, staff, principal, distinguished engineer, fellow) and management (lead, manager, director).
  • Every role scripts: Linux shell, Python and Tcl are near-universal; DV adds SystemVerilog and UVM, PD adds Tcl-heavy tool flows, and CAD adds software engineering and compute farms such as LSF or Slurm.
  • Moves between roles are common: DV to formal or architecture, RTL to architecture, PD to STA or CAD, test to product engineering, and almost any role to application engineering.
  • Hardware security (security verification, side-channel and fault-injection analysis) and AI-hardware design are fast-growing specialisations in 2026.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing your first role is permanent; many senior engineers have worked in two or three disciplines.
  • Assuming back-end roles need little coding; PD, STA and CAD engineers script all day.
  • Neglecting communication: specs, reviews and cross-team debugging are central in every chip role.

docs.title: 8.11 Your Learning Path: From Zero to Job-Ready
docs.text:
A realistic path takes you from digital logic basics to a portfolio of hands-on projects. Start with digital logic and Verilog, add computer architecture and CMOS basics, then specialise: verification, RTL, physical design, DFT or analog. Free tools and open PDKs mean you can do real projects, even a real tapeout, before your first job.

A 12-month self-study plan. About ten hours a week is enough if you finish each stage with a working, tested project.

Think of it like…

It is like learning a musical instrument: scales first (logic), then simple songs (small RTL), then pieces in a band (SoC projects), and finally performing on stage (a tapeout).

Real-world example

Months 1-3: Harris & Harris textbook and all HDLBits problems. Months 4-6: Verilator/cocotb testbenches; a UART and SPI on an FPGA. Months 7-9: SystemVerilog and UVM via online courses; a small RISC-V core. Months 10-12: Yosys and LibreLane flow on SKY130; Tiny Tapeout submission; learn SDC and read STA reports. Throughout: publish projects on GitHub and write short blog posts.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Foundations: number systems, Boolean logic, combinational/sequential circuits, FSMs.
  2. HDL: Verilog/SystemVerilog, simulation, testbenches, waveforms.
  3. Architecture and CMOS: pipelines, caches, buses; transistors, timing, power.
  4. Specialise: UVM/formal (DV), synthesis/STA/PD, DFT, or analog.
  5. Build a portfolio: FPGA projects, open-source contributions, a tapeout; then apply.

Who uses it

Students, graduates, self-learners and engineers switching from software or other hardware fields.

Key takeaway

Employers value evidence: a GitHub repo with clean RTL, a self-checking testbench and a completed flow is worth more than a list of courses.

Going deeper

  • Specialisation paths: DV (SystemVerilog OOP, UVM, SVA, coverage, cocotb), PD (SDC, STA, OpenROAD or LibreLane, Tcl), DFT (scan, ATPG, MBIST theory) and analog (Razavi, Xschem, ngspice, Magic).
  • Free verification learning sites such as Verification Academy and ChipVerify, covered in the verification chapter, pair well with EDA Playground for hands-on UVM practice.
  • A strong portfolio repository has a README with block diagram and spec, self-checking tests with coverage, CI, synthesis or timing results and waveform screenshots.
  • At about ten hours a week the twelve-month plan is realistic; consistency matters more than intensity, and finishing projects matters more than starting many.
  • Practise interview skills while learning: write RTL on paper, explain timing paths aloud and critically review your own older code.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Tutorial hopping without finishing projects; employers want evidence of completed, tested work.
  • Building designs without testing them; an untested CPU is not a portfolio piece.
  • Learning tool buttons instead of concepts; tools change, but fundamentals do not.

docs.title: 8.12 Essential Books, Conferences and News Sources
docs.text:
A handful of textbooks cover most of what an ASIC engineer needs to know, and a few conferences and news sites keep you current. Read one book per area deeply rather than skimming many. Follow industry news to understand companies, nodes and tools, which helps in interviews and career choices.

A core bookshelf, one book per area. Work deeply through one book per area rather than skimming many.

Think of it like…

Books are your foundation and toolbox; conferences and news are your window onto what the industry is building right now.

Real-world example

Laila keeps four books on her desk: Harris & Harris for digital design, Weste & Harris for CMOS VLSI, Spear & Tumbush for SystemVerilog verification, and Bhasker & Chadha for STA. She reads SemiWiki and Semiconductor Engineering weekly, watches DAC and DVCon talks online, and attends a local FOSSi meetup. In interviews she can discuss both fundamentals and current trends.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Pick one core book per area and work through its examples.
  2. Supplement with free papers (Cummings, DVCon proceedings).
  3. Follow news sites and newsletters weekly.
  4. Watch conference talks (DAC, DVCon, ISSCC, Hot Chips, ORConf, Latch-Up).
  5. Keep notes and summaries; teach others to cement learning.

Who uses it

Students, self-learners and working engineers keeping up to date.

Key takeaway

Know the classic books by author name; interviewers often ask what you have read, and recognising 'Weste & Harris' signals seriousness.

Going deeper

  • Read actively: retype and simulate the book's RTL, solve end-of-chapter problems and discuss answers with a study partner instead of reading cover to cover.
  • Much conference material is free or cheap: DVCon papers, Hot Chips slides and videos, and ISSCC and VLSI Symposium short courses are excellent learning resources.
  • Key events by area: DAC and ICCAD (EDA), DVCon (verification), ISSCC and VLSI Symposium (circuits), Hot Chips (architecture), IEDM (devices), ORConf and Latch-Up (open source).
  • Use recent editions where possible, such as the RISC-V edition of Harris & Harris, but older editions of the classics still teach fundamentals that have not changed.
  • Student tickets, volunteering and online streams make many conferences affordable; DAC, for example, runs a Young Fellows programme for students.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Collecting books instead of working deeply through one per area.
  • Learning from outdated material, such as Verilog-1995 coding style, without checking current practice.
  • Treating forum or blog answers as authoritative; check them against books, the LRM or tool documentation.

docs.title: 8.13 Interview Questions You Should Be Ready For
docs.text:
ASIC interviews test fundamentals more than tool trivia. Expect digital logic puzzles, RTL coding on a whiteboard, timing questions, CDC, verification concepts, and questions about your projects. Specialist roles add UVM, STA reports, P&R flow, DFT or analog circuit questions. Practise explaining your reasoning out loud.

A typical hiring process. The order and number of rounds vary by company, but fundamentals are tested at every technical stage.

Think of it like…

An interview is like a driving test: the examiner cares less about which car you learned in and more about whether you check mirrors, signal and handle surprises safely.

Real-world example

In a DV interview, Sam is asked to design a FIFO, write SVA for 'no write when full', explain blocking vs non-blocking, describe UVM phases and talk through a bug he found. For PD, his friend is asked to calculate slack from a timing report, explain how to fix hold violations and why CTS comes before routing. Both prepared by solving problems out loud with a friend.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Review fundamentals: logic, flops/latches, FSMs, setup/hold, CDC, power.
  2. Practise RTL coding by hand: counters, FIFOs, arbiters, FSMs, edge detectors.
  3. Prepare role-specific topics: UVM/SVA (DV), SDC/STA/P&R (PD), scan/ATPG (DFT).
  4. Prepare 2-3 project stories: problem, your actions, results, lessons.
  5. Ask good questions about the team, flow and tools.

Who uses it

Anyone applying for internships or jobs in RTL, DV, PD, STA, DFT, CAD or analog.

Key takeaway

When stuck, think aloud and state assumptions; interviewers reward structured reasoning over memorised answers.

Going deeper

  • Classic RTL whiteboard tasks: edge detector, synchronous FIFO, asynchronous FIFO pointers, round-robin arbiter, sequence-detector FSM, Gray-code counter and clock divider.
  • CDC deep-dives may ask for synchroniser MTBF ≈ e^(t_r/τ) / (T0 · f_clk · f_data); adding a flop multiplies MTBF enormously by giving more resolution time t_r.
  • DV interviews probe code versus functional coverage, virtual sequences, factory overrides, config_db, race conditions and how you would verify a given block.
  • PD interviews cover useful skew, Vt swapping, fixing congestion, antenna rules, IR drop, CTS targets and reading a timing path line by line.
  • Use a structure: clarify the question, state assumptions, sketch a diagram, solve, then check corner cases; answer behavioural questions with STAR (situation, task, action, result).

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Memorising answers without understanding them; follow-up questions expose this very quickly.
  • Listing tools or skills on your CV that you cannot discuss in depth.
  • Thinking silently; interviewers need to hear your reasoning and assumptions.

docs.title: Try it: Classic whiteboard question: rising-edge detector
docs.text:
module edge_detect (input logic clk, rst_n, sig, output logic rise);
  logic sig_q;
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n) sig_q <= 1'b0;
    else        sig_q <= sig;
  assign rise = sig & ~sig_q;
endmodule

Describe how you found and fixed a timing problem in your FPGA CPU. 'Write a Python script listing the ten worst negative-slack paths in this timing report.'

docs.title: 8.14 Landing Your First Chip Job: Employers, Hubs, CVs and Internships
docs.text:
Knowing who hires, where the jobs are and how to present your skills matters as much as technical study. Chip-design jobs cluster in a few regional hubs and are spread across chip companies, cloud and systems companies, EDA and IP vendors, foundries and design-service firms. Internships and graduate programmes are the main way in.

Where chip engineers work. Look beyond the famous names: design-service firms, IDMs and start-ups hire many graduates.

Think of it like…

Job hunting is like a tapeout: a clear spec (the role you want), solid verification (projects that prove your skills) and good packaging (a sharp CV) get you through final test.

Real-world example

Final-year student Amara targets DV roles. She lists 30 employers in her region, including chip companies, a hyperscaler's silicon team, an EDA vendor's application-engineering team and two design-service firms, and applies for internships early in the autumn. Her one-page CV leads with a GitHub project: a UART with a cocotb testbench, coverage numbers and a Tiny Tapeout tile. She lands an internship that turns into a graduate offer.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose a target role and match your projects and keywords to it.
  2. Map employers: chip companies, hyperscalers, EDA and IP vendors, foundries, design services.
  3. Apply early for internships and graduate programmes, often a year ahead.
  4. Write a concise CV leading with projects, named tools and measurable results.
  5. Network through university clubs, conferences, meetups, LinkedIn and open-source communities.

Who uses it

Students, graduates and career switchers, plus the recruiters and hiring managers who screen them.

Key takeaway

Tailor your CV to each posting: DV roles look for SystemVerilog, UVM, coverage and Python; PD roles look for Tcl, SDC, STA and a completed flow.

Going deeper

  • Large companies often recruit interns many months ahead, so update your CV and GitHub before applications open and track deadlines in a spreadsheet.
  • Applicant-tracking systems scan for keywords, so mirror the posting's terms honestly: SystemVerilog, UVM, SVA, cocotb and Python for DV; SDC, STA, Tcl and Innovus or OpenROAD for PD.
  • India hosts large design centres of many global chip and EDA companies, Taiwan concentrates foundry and IC-design firms, and Europe is strong in automotive, industrial and Arm-based design.
  • Career switchers have natural routes: software engineers to DV or CAD, FPGA engineers to RTL, physicists and materials scientists to process or yield, test technicians to product engineering.
  • Compare offers on total compensation (base, bonus, equity) and on learning: team size, tapeout frequency, mentoring and how much of the flow you will touch.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Sending one generic CV everywhere; tailor projects and keywords to each role.
  • Ignoring smaller firms and design-service companies, which often hire more graduates and give broad experience.
  • Overstating skills on your CV; interviewers probe every line and notice quickly.

docs.title: Chapter 7: Fabrication, Packaging, Test & Bring-up
docs.text: After tapeout, the design leaves the world of software and enters the factory. This chapter explains who manufactures chips, how process nodes and transistors have evolved up to 2026, what a PDK contains, and how a wafer is made step by step, including EUV lithography. It then follows the chip through yield, packaging (from simple wire-bond to CoWoS and Foveros), wafer sort and final test on ATE, lab bring-up, product qualification, failure analysis, and the global supply chain and export controls that shape the industry.

docs.title: 7.1 The Foundries: TSMC, Samsung, Intel, GlobalFoundries, UMC, SMIC, Rapidus
docs.text:
A foundry manufactures chips for other companies. TSMC is by far the largest and leads in advanced nodes. Samsung Foundry and Intel Foundry also offer leading-edge processes. GlobalFoundries, UMC, SMIC and others focus on mature and specialty nodes, and Japan's Rapidus is building a new 2 nm fab. Choosing a foundry and node is one of the biggest early decisions for any chip project.

The foundry landscape by capability. Only a handful of companies can manufacture at the leading edge; most chips are made on mature and specialty processes.

Think of it like…

Foundries are like printing houses: a few can print glossy, ultra-fine art books, while many others print excellent everyday books at lower cost.

Real-world example

A fabless company plans three chips: an AI accelerator on TSMC N3 for best performance, an automotive microcontroller on a 28 nm process with embedded non-volatile memory, and a power-management IC on a 130 nm BCD process at a specialty foundry. Each foundry has its own PDK, IP ecosystem, pricing and capacity, so the team works with three different sets of rules.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Compare nodes on PPA, cost per wafer, IP availability and maturity.
  2. Check capacity, geography and supply-chain risk.
  3. Sign NDAs and agreements to get the PDK and design rules.
  4. Use foundry-certified EDA flows and qualified IP.
  5. Plan prototypes (MPW) and production volumes with the foundry.

Who uses it

Architects, programme managers, operations/supply-chain teams and foundry account and application engineers.

Key takeaway

TSMC N2 entered volume production in late 2025; Intel 18A is in high-volume production; Samsung SF2 shipped in the Exynos 2600.

Going deeper

  • Pure-play foundries such as TSMC, UMC, GlobalFoundries and SMIC only manufacture for customers; Samsung and Intel also design their own chips, so they must convince customers that designs and data stay separate.
  • Choosing a foundry locks in much of a project: PDK, standard cells, memory compilers and interface IP are node-specific, so porting a design to another foundry means largely redoing physical design and IP.
  • Wafer prices rise steeply at each leading node; press reports put 2 nm-class wafers at roughly US$30,000, several times the price of a 28 nm wafer, so die area matters enormously.
  • Leading-edge capacity is concentrated in a handful of fabs, mostly in Taiwan; newer fabs in Arizona, Kumamoto (Japan) and Dresden (Germany) spread capacity but often run slightly older nodes.
  • A typical engagement runs: NDA and PDK access, test chips and MPW prototypes, risk production, then volume production under a supply agreement fixing prices, capacity and quality targets.
  • Foundries publish roadmaps at annual events such as TSMC's Technology Symposium and Intel Foundry Direct Connect; architects use them to decide years ahead which node a chip will use.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Comparing node names across foundries as if equal: '3 nm' at one foundry is not the same as at another, so compare density, speed, power and cost data.
  • Assuming you can switch foundry late in a project; IP, PDK and qualification ties make that a major redesign.
  • Ignoring capacity: a perfect design can still ship late if wafer or advanced-packaging capacity was not reserved in time.

docs.title: 7.2 Process Nodes and Transistor Evolution (Planar → FinFET → GAA → Backside Power)
docs.text:
Each process node brings smaller, better transistors, but the transistor's shape has changed to keep control of leakage. Planar transistors gave way to FinFETs around 22/16 nm, and FinFETs are now giving way to gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheets at 2 nm-class nodes. The next big change is backside power delivery, which moves power wires underneath the transistors.

How the transistor kept scaling. Each change in material or shape kept the gate in control of the channel as dimensions shrank.

Think of it like…

It is like improving a water tap: first a simple flat valve, then a valve that grips the pipe on three sides (FinFET), then one that wraps all the way round (GAA), and finally moving the water mains under the floor (backside power).

Real-world example

A phone SoC family shows the history: 2014 on 20 nm planar, 2016-2023 on 16, 10, 7, 5 and 3 nm FinFET, 2025-2026 on 2 nm-class GAA (TSMC N2, Samsung SF2). Intel's 18A combines RibbonFET GAA transistors with PowerVia backside power, while TSMC's A16 adds Super Power Rail backside power, now scheduled for 2027.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Planar MOSFET: gate on top of a flat channel (to about 28/20 nm).
  2. FinFET: channel raised into fins, gate on three sides (about 22/16 nm to 3 nm).
  3. GAA nanosheet: stacked sheets fully wrapped by the gate (2 nm-class).
  4. Backside power: power network on the wafer back (Intel 18A, TSMC A16).
  5. Future: forksheet and CFET (stacked NMOS/PMOS), new materials, High-NA EUV.

Who uses it

Process and device engineers, foundry technologists, architects choosing nodes, and every PD engineer who works with the rules.

Key takeaway

Know which companies call their GAA what: Samsung MBCFET, Intel RibbonFET, TSMC nanosheet.

Going deeper

  • Gate control explains each change: a planar gate touches one side of the channel, a FinFET three sides and a nanosheet all four, so leakage stays low as dimensions shrink.
  • FinFET drive strength comes in whole fins, so widths are quantised; nanosheet widths can vary between devices, giving standard-cell designers finer power-performance trade-offs.
  • Backside power moves the power grid under the transistors through nano-TSVs; it frees front-side routing tracks and cuts IR drop, but needs wafer thinning, carrier bonding and new debug methods.
  • Full-node gains are now modest: TSMC quoted N2 versus N3E as 10-15 % more speed or 25-30 % less power, with roughly 15 % more density.
  • Within one node, variants target different markets, e.g. TSMC N3E (baseline), N3P (improved PPA) and N3X (high-performance computing), each with its own PDK and libraries.
  • DTCO (design-technology co-optimisation) now delivers much of each node's benefit: shorter standard-cell track heights, single diffusion breaks and contact-over-active-gate shrink area beyond raw pitch scaling.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Believing a '2 nm' chip has 2 nm gates: node names are marketing labels, and real gate and metal pitches are tens of nanometres.
  • Assuming SRAM, analog and I/O shrink like logic; they scale far less, which is one reason chiplets mix nodes.
  • Assuming the newest node is always best: higher wafer and NRE costs and immature yields make older nodes right for many products.

docs.title: 7.3 PDKs: Process Design Kits
docs.text:
A PDK is everything a designer needs from the foundry to design for one process: device models for simulation, design rules and rule decks for DRC/LVS, technology files for P&R and extraction, layer maps, parameterised cells (PCells) for transistors and passives, and documentation. Standard-cell libraries and IP usually come alongside. Commercial PDKs need NDAs; open PDKs like SKY130 are free for anyone.

What is inside a PDK. Every EDA tool in the flow reads a different part of the same PDK, so all parts must come from one release.

Think of it like…

A PDK is like a complete kit for building furniture that fits a specific house: measurements of every room, rules about what fits where, and pre-made parts.

Real-world example

When Jun starts an analog design on GF180MCU, he installs the open PDK with Ciel, opens Xschem with the PDK's symbols, simulates with ngspice using the BSIM4 models, draws layout in KLayout with PCells, and runs the PDK's DRC and LVS decks. In industry, his colleague downloads a 22 nm PDK from the foundry portal after legal signs the NDA.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Obtain the PDK (foundry portal under NDA, or download an open PDK).
  2. Install for your tools: SPICE models, tech files, rule decks, PCells.
  3. Use PDK device models in simulation and corner analysis.
  4. Draw layout with PCells and run DRC/LVS/extraction with PDK decks.
  5. Track PDK versions; foundries release updates that may change rules.

Who uses it

Analog and digital designers, CAD engineers who install and maintain PDKs, foundry PDK teams.

Key takeaway

Always record the PDK version used for tapeout; mixing versions is a classic source of foundry rejections.

Going deeper

  • A commercial PDK supports several EDA vendors at once: SKILL PCells for Virtuoso, other PCell formats for other editors, rule decks for Calibre, IC Validator and Pegasus, and technology files for each P&R and extraction tool.
  • Transistor models use BSIM4 for planar devices and BSIM-CMG for FinFET and GAA; they include corners, Monte Carlo mismatch and layout-dependent effects such as well proximity and stress.
  • Commercial PDKs come from foundry portals under NDA and export-control screening; universities usually obtain them through programmes such as Europractice or the foundry's own university programme.
  • Version discipline matters: release notes list rule and model changes, and the tapeout checklist records the exact PDK, deck and library versions so the foundry can reproduce your results.
  • Open PDKs are built for open tools by open_pdks or IHP's scripts, producing views for Magic, KLayout, Netgen, ngspice, Xschem and OpenROAD from the foundry's source data.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing versions, such as a new DRC deck with old models or LEF, gives results that disagree; pin and record every PDK component.
  • Treating early (v0.x) models as final; silicon can miss targets if signoff is not repeated on the production release.
  • Editing PDK files locally to 'fix' errors; report issues to the foundry or CAD team instead, or tapeout checks may fail.

docs.title: 7.4 How a Wafer Is Made (Simply Explained)
docs.text:
A chip is built layer by layer on a silicon wafer through hundreds to over a thousand steps. The basic loop repeats: deposit a thin film, coat it with light-sensitive resist, expose a pattern through a mask (lithography), develop, etch away unprotected material, implant dopants where needed, strip the resist and polish flat (CMP). Transistors are made first (front-end-of-line), then the metal wiring (back-end-of-line).

The patterning loop. A leading-edge wafer goes round this loop dozens of times, with variations for each layer.

Think of it like…

It is like screen-printing a T-shirt many times over with different stencils and inks, except each layer is thinner than a virus and must line up within a few nanometres.

Real-world example

A wafer at a 5 nm fab spends about three months moving between hundreds of tools in a cleanroom. For one metal layer, it gets a dielectric deposited, resist coated, an EUV exposure, etching of trenches, copper deposited by electroplating, and CMP to polish away excess copper, leaving wires in the trenches (the damascene process). This repeats for each of more than a dozen metal layers.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Wafer preparation: polished single-crystal silicon wafers (300 mm).
  2. Front-end-of-line (FEOL): isolation, wells, gates, source/drain, transistors.
  3. Middle-of-line (MOL): contacts connecting transistors to wiring.
  4. Back-end-of-line (BEOL): metal layers and vias built with copper damascene.
  5. Passivation, bond pads/bumps, then wafer-level testing.

Who uses it

Process engineers, equipment engineers, integration and yield engineers in fabs; designers benefit from understanding it.

Key takeaway

Remember the loop: deposit, pattern (lithography), etch, implant/dope, clean, CMP — repeated for every layer.

Going deeper

  • A leading-edge logic wafer passes through well over a thousand process steps and dozens of mask layers, taking roughly three to four months from bare wafer to finished wafer.
  • Fabs track cycle time in 'days per mask layer', so every extra mask adds days as well as cost; this is one reason EUV single exposure replaced multi-patterning on critical layers.
  • Gate-all-around adds new steps: Si/SiGe superlattice epitaxy, inner spacers and a selective etch that removes SiGe to release the silicon nanosheets before the gate wraps around them.
  • Statistical process control and inline metrology (CD-SEM, optical scatterometry, overlay and defect inspection) catch drifting tools within hours, before thousands of wafers are affected.
  • Wafers travel in sealed FOUPs and mini-environments, so the air touching wafers is far cleaner than the general cleanroom, which still needs strict particle control.
  • A leading-edge fab costs tens of billions of dollars and uses vast amounts of electricity and ultra-pure water, which is why only a few companies can build one.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing fab 'front-end-of-line' with design 'front end': FEOL means building transistors, not writing RTL.
  • Thinking chips are made one at a time; whole wafers, in lots of up to 25, are processed together.
  • Assuming lithography is the only critical step; a defect from any deposition, etch, clean or CMP step can kill a die.

docs.title: 7.5 Lithography: DUV, EUV and High-NA EUV
docs.text:
Lithography is the most critical and expensive step: it defines the smallest features. Deep ultraviolet (DUV) scanners use 193 nm light, with immersion and multi-patterning to print features far smaller than the wavelength. Extreme ultraviolet (EUV) uses 13.5 nm light and is essential for leading nodes. High-NA EUV, with a larger lens aperture, prints even finer lines and is being introduced for Intel 14A and future nodes. ASML is the only EUV supplier.

DUV vs EUV vs High-NA EUV

DUV ArF immersion EUV (0.33 NA) High-NA EUV (0.55) Wavelength 193 nm 13.5 nm 13.5 nm Numerical aperture 1.35 (with water) 0.33 0.55 Optics Lenses Mirrors in vacuum Anamorphic mirrors Exposure field 26 × 33 mm 26 × 33 mm 26 × 16.5 mm Single-exposure half-pitch ~40 nm ~13 nm ~8 nm Typical use Most layers; multi-patterning Critical layers, 7 nm and below Intel 14A, future nodes Tool price Tens of millions € Over €150 million ~€350 million (reported)

Shorter wavelength or larger NA prints smaller features, at a steep rise in tool cost.

Think of it like…

Lithography is like painting fine lines: DUV is a thicker brush you can use several times in clever ways, EUV is a much finer brush, and High-NA EUV is an even finer one.

Real-world example

To print a 7 nm-class metal layer with DUV, a fab needed four exposure-and-etch passes (SAQP), adding cost and error risk. With EUV the same layer needs one exposure. Intel installed the first commercial High-NA EUV system, ASML's EXE:5200B, to prepare for 14A. Each EUV scanner costs well over 100 million euros, and High-NA systems cost considerably more.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Light passes through (DUV) or reflects off (EUV) a mask.
  2. Projection optics shrink the pattern, typically 4x.
  3. The pattern exposes resist on the wafer field by field.
  4. Resolution depends on wavelength and numerical aperture (Rayleigh criterion).
  5. Overlay must align each layer with previous ones to within a few nanometres.

Who uses it

Lithography and OPC engineers, mask shops, equipment engineers; designers feel lithography through design rules.

Key takeaway

Remember: EUV wavelength is 13.5 nm; DUV ArF is 193 nm; High-NA EUV raises NA from 0.33 to 0.55.

Going deeper

  • Rayleigh: half-pitch ≈ k1 × λ / NA. With k1 ≈ 0.3, ArF immersion (193 nm, NA 1.35) reaches about 40 nm, EUV at NA 0.33 about 12-13 nm and High-NA about 8 nm.
  • Below roughly 40 nm half-pitch, DUV needs multi-patterning (LELE, SADP, SAQP); SMIC's 7 nm- and 5 nm-class processes rely on it because EUV scanners cannot be exported to China.
  • EUV optics are all reflective: each Mo/Si mirror reflects only about 70 % of the light, so after many mirrors only a small fraction of the source power reaches the wafer.
  • Scanners shrink the mask image four times; High-NA uses anamorphic 4x/8x reduction, halving the field to 26 × 16.5 mm, so the largest dies need stitching or chiplets.
  • Throughput depends on dose: low-dose exposures are faster but suffer more stochastic defects, so resist chemistry and source power are constant battles.
  • TSMC says it does not need High-NA for A16, A14 or even its 2029 A13 and A12 nodes, while Intel plans to insert it at 14A, showing that cost per wafer, not resolution alone, drives adoption.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking EUV replaced DUV: even at 2 nm most layers are still printed with DUV, and EUV is reserved for the critical ones.
  • Equating wavelength with feature size: optical tricks print features far smaller than 193 nm, while EUV pitches are larger than 13.5 nm.
  • Assuming High-NA is a free upgrade: half-field size, shallower depth of focus and tool cost all affect design and economics.

Very large dies may need stitching or chiplets under High-NA. Nanoimprint and other alternativesCanon (nanoimprint), research groups · Process · Fabrication Alternative patterning methods pressing a template into resist. Canon ships nanoimprint tools for some memory and specialty uses. EUV light source (laser-produced plasma)ASML (Cymer) · Concept · Fabrication A high-power CO2 laser hits about 50,000 tiny tin droplets per second, creating a plasma that emits 13.5 nm light. Source power directly sets scanner throughput, so ASML raises it with each NXE generation. A single buried defect in an EUV blank could print on every die, so blanks are inspected exhaustively. Almost every EUV scanner is paired in line with a TEL track that coats and develops its wafers. Raising the exposure dose reduces missing-contact defects but slows the scanner and raises cost per wafer.

docs.title: 7.6 Yield and Defect Density
docs.text:
Yield is the fraction of dies that work. Random defects (particles, tiny flaws) kill dies at a rate described by defect density (D0, defects per square centimetre). Larger dies are more likely to contain a defect, so yield drops quickly with die size. Systematic problems (design-process interactions) also reduce yield and are fixed by learning and DFM. Yield drives chip cost directly.

Poisson yield vs die area (D0 = 0.1 per cm²). At the same defect density, an 8 cm² die yields only half as well as a 1 cm² die.

Think of it like…

Throwing darts at a board covered in stamps: the bigger each stamp, the more likely a dart (defect) hits it and ruins it.

Real-world example

With a defect density of 0.1 per cm², a 1 cm² die has about 90 % yield under the simple Poisson model, while an 8 cm² die has only about 45 %. That is why NVIDIA, AMD and others build large AI products from several smaller dies, and why they include redundant cores and memory repair to recover partially defective dies.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Measure yield at wafer sort; map failing dies across the wafer.
  2. Separate random defect yield from systematic and parametric yield loss.
  3. Use yield models (Poisson, Murphy, negative binomial) to predict yield vs die size.
  4. Diagnose failures with scan diagnosis and physical failure analysis.
  5. Improve with process fixes, DFM changes, redundancy and repair.

Who uses it

Yield engineers, product engineers, process engineers and finance/operations teams.

Key takeaway

Simple Poisson yield model: Y = e^(-A × D0), where A is die area and D0 is defect density.

Going deeper

  • Poisson Y = e^(−A·D0) assumes randomly scattered defects; real defects cluster, so the negative-binomial model Y = (1 + A·D0/α)^(−α) is preferred for large dies.
  • Gross dies per wafer: DPW ≈ π·d²/(4·A) − π·d/√(2·A). For a 300 mm wafer and a 100 mm² die this gives about 707 − 67 ≈ 640; scribe lines and edge exclusion reduce it further.
  • Overall yield multiplies stage yields (line, sort, assembly, final test), so a small loss at each step compounds into a large cost difference.
  • D0 counts only killer defects: a particle landing on empty field oxide does no harm, which is why critical-area analysis predicts yield better than raw die area.
  • Chiplets raise die yield because each die is small, but packaging adds assembly yield loss and needs known-good-die testing, so total cost must be modelled carefully.
  • Systematic yield loss, such as litho hot spots, CMP dishing or via opens, is fixed by DFM rules, redundant vias, OPC updates and process tuning rather than by a cleaner fab.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using the Poisson model for very large dies gives overly pessimistic yields; use clustering models calibrated to fab data.
  • Forgetting edge loss and scribe lines when estimating dies per wafer, making die cost look lower than reality.
  • Treating yield as only the fab's problem; design choices such as DFM, redundancy and test quality strongly affect it.

docs.title: 7.7 Packaging Basics: Wire-Bond, Flip-Chip, BGA and WLCSP
docs.text:
A bare die is fragile and tiny, so it is put in a package that protects it, connects it to the circuit board and removes heat. Traditional wire-bond packages connect pads at the die edge with fine gold or copper wires. Flip-chip packages flip the die over and connect it with solder bumps across its whole area, giving more connections and better electrical performance. Wafer-level packages are barely larger than the die itself.

Cross-section of a flip-chip BGA. Heat leaves through the top while signals and power travel down through bumps, substrate and balls.

Think of it like…

The package is like a phone case with a built-in adapter: it protects the delicate device and turns its tiny connectors into ones the outside world can use.

Real-world example

A sensor chip uses a 5 × 5 mm QFN wire-bond package costing a few cents. A phone SoC uses flip-chip on a multilayer substrate with thousands of bumps, then a package-on-package memory stacked on top. A wearable's Bluetooth chip uses a wafer-level chip-scale package (WLCSP) that is the same size as the die to save space.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Wafers are thinned (back-grind) and diced into dies.
  2. Wire-bond: die attached face-up, wires bonded from pads to lead frame or substrate.
  3. Flip-chip: bumps formed on wafer; die flipped and soldered to substrate; underfilled.
  4. Molding or lid/heat-spreader attachment; solder balls added for BGA.
  5. Package tested, marked and shipped in trays or reels.

Who uses it

Package designers, packaging/assembly engineers, signal and power integrity engineers, thermal engineers.

Key takeaway

Wire-bond = cheap, I/O at die edge; flip-chip = area I/O, better power/speed; WLCSP = smallest.

Going deeper

  • Package choice balances I/O count, power, signal speed, heat, size and cost: wire-bond suits up to a few hundred pads, flip-chip thousands, and WLCSP is limited by the die's own area.
  • Bond wires add roughly 1 nH of inductance per millimetre, causing supply bounce when many outputs switch; flip-chip bumps have far lower inductance, helping fast, high-current chips.
  • Junction temperature Tj = Ta + P × θJA: a 5 W chip with θJA of 20 °C/W in 45 °C air would reach about 145 °C, so it needs a better package or a heatsink.
  • Substrates for large chips use ABF (Ajinomoto Build-up Film) dielectric layers; substrate supply was a serious bottleneck during the 2021-2022 chip shortage.
  • Chip, package and board are co-designed: the pad or bump map is fixed during floorplanning, and package SI, PI and thermal models feed back into the chip's power grid and I/O plan.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Choosing the package at the end; pad ring, bump map and power-pin count must be planned together with the floorplan.
  • Too few power and ground pins causes simultaneous-switching noise and IR drop that no on-chip fix can fully cure.
  • Quoting θJA as a universal number; it is measured on a standard JEDEC test board and changes with your board and airflow.

docs.title: 7.8 Advanced Packaging: CoWoS, InFO, SoIC, Foveros, EMIB and HBM
docs.text:
Advanced packaging connects multiple dies with far denser and faster links than a normal package. TSMC's CoWoS places dies and HBM stacks on a silicon interposer; InFO uses fan-out redistribution layers; SoIC stacks dies with hybrid bonding. Intel's EMIB embeds small silicon bridges in the substrate, and Foveros stacks dies in 3D. These technologies are the backbone of today's AI accelerators.

Connection pitch by packaging style. Halving the pitch quadruples the connections per mm², which is why hybrid bonding enables true 3D stacking.

Think of it like…

If ordinary packaging is a house with one room, advanced packaging is a block of flats where rooms are connected by private lifts and corridors far faster than going outside and back in.

Real-world example

A leading AI GPU combines two reticle-sized compute dies and eight HBM3E stacks on a TSMC CoWoS-L package with local silicon interconnect bridges. HBM sits millimetres from the compute dies, delivering several terabytes per second. CoWoS capacity has been a major bottleneck for AI chip supply since 2023, driving huge expansions by TSMC and its partners.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Choose the integration style: interposer (2.5D), bridge, fan-out, or 3D stacking.
  2. Design die-to-die interfaces and bump/hybrid-bond maps.
  3. Integrate HBM stacks next to compute dies where bandwidth is needed.
  4. Co-design power, signal integrity, thermal and warpage.
  5. Test known-good dies, assemble, and test the full package.

Who uses it

Package architects, 3D-IC designers, foundry/OSAT packaging engineers, AI chip teams.

Key takeaway

Know the families: TSMC 3DFabric (CoWoS, InFO, SoIC), Intel (EMIB, Foveros), Samsung (I-Cube, X-Cube).

Going deeper

  • CoWoS-S uses a monolithic silicon interposer, CoWoS-R an organic RDL interposer, and CoWoS-L small silicon bridges inside an RDL interposer, allowing packages several times the reticle size.
  • HBM3E stacks use a 1024-bit interface at about 1-1.2 TB/s each; HBM4 doubles the interface to 2048 bits for up to 2 TB/s, so eight HBM4 stacks can exceed 10 TB/s.
  • Hybrid bonding joins copper pads and dielectric directly with no solder, reaching pitches below 10 µm and hundreds of times the connection density of flip-chip bumps.
  • Large AI packages can draw over a kilowatt, so substrate power delivery, warpage control and liquid cooling are designed together with the dies.
  • Every die must be known-good before assembly, because one bad die scraps an expensive package; HBM stacks and chiplets are tested, and sometimes repaired, before integration.
  • Foundries and OSATs share the work: TSMC builds the chip-on-wafer part of CoWoS and has outsourced some substrate-attach steps to partners such as ASE/SPIL and Amkor.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming chiplets are always cheaper: interposers, bonding, test and compound assembly yield can outweigh the die-yield gain.
  • Treating HBM bandwidth as free: HBM adds cost, power, heat and supply risk, and its placement constrains the floorplan.
  • Ignoring thermal coupling in 3D stacks; a hot logic die under memory can push the memory beyond its temperature limit.

docs.title: 7.9 OSATs: Assembly and Test Houses
docs.text:
OSATs (Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test companies) package and test chips for fabless companies and IDMs. They bump and dice wafers, assemble packages, run final test and ship finished parts. The largest are ASE, Amkor and JCET. Foundries like TSMC and Intel also do advanced packaging in-house, and the OSATs increasingly offer advanced packaging too.

From finished wafer to shipped chip. The chip company rarely touches the parts; data such as wafer maps and test results travel with them.

Think of it like…

OSATs are like the bindery and quality-control department after the printing press: they turn printed sheets into finished, checked books.

Real-world example

A fabless company's finished wafers travel from TSMC in Taiwan to an Amkor facility, where they are bumped, probed, diced and assembled into flip-chip BGAs, then final-tested on Advantest testers. Some products go to ASE for system-in-package modules. The company never touches the wafers; it manages everything through data and contracts.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Receive wafers from the foundry; bump if needed.
  2. Wafer sort (probe test), map good dies.
  3. Dice, pick good dies and assemble packages.
  4. Final test, burn-in if required, marking and packing.
  5. Ship to distributors or customers; return data to the chip company.

Who uses it

Operations, supply-chain and product engineers at chip companies; process, test and packaging engineers at OSATs.

Key takeaway

Remember the 'big three' OSATs: ASE (Taiwan), Amkor (US-headquartered), JCET (China).

Going deeper

  • Wafer maps travel with the wafers in standard formats such as SEMI E142, so the assembly line picks only the dies that passed wafer sort.
  • Automotive products require OSAT sites certified to IATF 16949 and a production part approval process (PPAP), with frozen process flows and documented control plans.
  • For low-cost chips, packaging and test can cost more than the silicon die itself, so test time and package choice are optimised as hard as die area.
  • Advanced packaging is the fastest-growing segment; OSATs now offer fan-out, 2.5D and SiP while foundries build CoWoS-class lines, blurring the boundary between fab and OSAT.
  • Back-end capacity is spread across Taiwan, China, Malaysia, Vietnam, the Philippines, South Korea and others, with new advanced-packaging plants being built in the US and Europe.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming the foundry returns packaged chips; most fabless companies contract assembly and test separately unless they buy a turnkey service.
  • Sending wrong or outdated wafer maps, so failing dies get packaged and shipped.
  • Designing pads or bumps without the OSAT's assembly rules, forcing late layout changes.

docs.title: 7.10 Wafer Sort, Final Test and ATE
docs.text:
Every chip is tested at least twice. Wafer sort (probe test) checks dies on the wafer using a probe card with tiny needles, so bad dies are not packaged. Final test checks packaged parts, often at multiple temperatures, and sorts them into speed or quality bins. Both use expensive automatic test equipment (ATE) from companies like Advantest and Teradyne, running test programs built from ATPG patterns, BIST and functional tests.

A typical production test flow. Each insertion catches different defects; data from all of them feeds yield analysis.

Think of it like…

Wafer sort is like checking eggs in the tray for cracks before boxing them; final test is the inspection of each sealed box before it goes to the shop.

Real-world example

A smartphone SoC's test flow: wafer sort on an Advantest V93000 at 25 °C (scan, MBIST, IDDQ, repair fuse programming), then packaging, then final test at hot and cold temperatures with at-speed scan, SerDes loopback and functional tests. Parts that pass at 3.2 GHz are binned as top tier; parts passing only at 2.8 GHz go to a lower tier. Test data from millions of parts feeds yield analysis.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Develop the test program: patterns, limits, flows and bins.
  2. Wafer sort: probe each die, run tests, program fuses, ink or map bad dies.
  3. Assemble good dies into packages.
  4. Final test (and burn-in/system-level test if needed) at specified temperatures.
  5. Bin, mark and ship; analyse test data for yield and quality.

Who uses it

Test engineers, product engineers, DFT engineers and ATE application engineers.

Key takeaway

Know the test stages: wafer sort (CP), final test (FT) and system-level test (SLT), and what each catches.

Going deeper

  • Test cost is roughly tester cost per second × test time; testers cost millions of dollars, so engineers fight for every millisecond with compression, multi-site and adaptive test.
  • Each stage catches different faults: wafer sort finds process defects and programs repair fuses and trims; final test finds assembly and speed problems; SLT catches system-level marginalities.
  • ATPG patterns leave the DFT tool as STIL (IEEE 1450) or WGL, are converted to the tester's format and run inside test programs written in Advantest SmarTest or Teradyne IG-XL.
  • Analog trimming at wafer sort adjusts bandgap voltages, oscillator frequencies and sensor offsets by blowing eFuses or OTP bits, tightening specs that process variation would spread.
  • Automotive parts are often tested at three temperatures (cold, room and hot), because their defect targets are measured in parts per million or less.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Confusing design verification with manufacturing test: DV finds design bugs once, while test screens every part for fabrication defects.
  • Setting limits too tight (yield loss) or too loose (field escapes) without characterisation data and sensible guardbands.
  • Ignoring tester limits such as channel count, vector memory and frequency when planning scan pins and pattern volume.
