docs.title: 3.14 Mixed-Signal Verification and Real-Number Modelling
docs.text:
Most chips mix digital logic with analog blocks such as PLLs, ADCs, voltage regulators and SerDes. Simulating everything at transistor level is far too slow, so verification teams model analog blocks as fast 'real-number' models inside the digital simulator, and run true analog-digital co-simulation only where accuracy matters. The aim is to catch connection, control and sequencing bugs between the two worlds.

The mixed-signal speed and accuracy ladder. Going down adds accuracy but costs orders of magnitude in simulation speed.

Think of it like…

It is like rehearsing a play with stand-ins for the expensive star actors: stand-ins are good enough for positions and timing, but the stars join for the final dress rehearsal.

Real-world example

Harbor Labs is verifying a battery-monitor chip. The 12-bit ADC, bandgap reference and regulator are written as SystemVerilog real-number models, so a regression of 3,000 UVM tests runs overnight. An automated check compares each model with its transistor schematic. Before tapeout, ten key tests rerun in analog-digital co-simulation and reveal that a trim code reaches the bandgap in reverse bit order, a bug each team assumed the other would catch.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. List every analog-digital boundary signal: supplies, enables, trims, clocks, data and status.
  2. Write behavioural or real-number models of the analog blocks and validate them against schematics.
  3. Run digital-speed regressions with the models inside the UVM or cocotb testbench.
  4. Co-simulate selected tests with the real analog netlist in a mixed-signal simulator.
  5. Check analog behaviour with assertions and measurements (ranges, settling, thresholds) and collect coverage.

Who uses it

Mixed-signal verification engineers, analog designers and DV engineers on power-management, sensor, SerDes and PLL-heavy chips.

Key takeaway

Know the speed ladder: SPICE (most accurate, slowest), FastSPICE, Verilog-AMS, real-number models and pure digital (fastest); choose the lowest accuracy that still finds the bug.

Going deeper

  • Real-number models are event-driven: values change only when an input event occurs, so continuous effects such as loop dynamics need a model that samples on a fixed time step, trading speed for fidelity.
  • SystemVerilog 2012 added user-defined nettypes with resolution functions, so several drivers on one node can be combined, for example as Thevenin sources, which plain real variables cannot do.
  • Co-simulation splits the design into a digital partition solved event by event and an analog partition solved by SPICE or FastSPICE; connect modules translate at every crossing, and their thresholds matter.
  • UVM-MS 1.0, approved by Accellera in February 2025, standardises an MS bridge module and proxy class so UVM agents can drive and sample analog quantities in reusable components.
  • Most mixed-signal bugs are mundane: swapped bus bit order, inverted enable polarity, wrong supply connection, missing level shifter or a power-up order the analog block was never designed for.
  • Model validation belongs in regression; an out-of-date model that silently diverges from the schematic is worse than no model because it gives false confidence.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Trusting behavioural models nobody has rechecked against the schematic since the analog design changed.
  • Running everything at transistor level; regressions become so slow that far too few scenarios get tested.
  • Ignoring supply and bias pins in models; real blocks misbehave when supplies are low or ramping, so good models check them.

docs.title: Try it: A real-number model of an 8-bit ADC that runs in any SystemVerilog simulator
docs.text:
module adc8_rnm (input real vin, vref, input logic clk,
                 output logic [7:0] code);
  real ratio;
  always @(posedge clk) begin
    ratio = vin / vref * 256.0;          // ideal transfer function
    if (ratio < 0.0)        code <= 8'd0;   // clip below range
    else if (ratio > 255.0) code <= 8'd255; // clip above range
    else                    code <= $rtoi(ratio);
  end
endmodule

docs.title: 3.15 Safety and Security Verification: Fault Campaigns, FMEDA Metrics and Threat Checks
docs.text:
Safety-critical and security-critical chips need extra evidence beyond 'the tests pass'. For functional safety, teams deliberately inject faults into the design and measure how many the safety mechanisms catch, feeding the numbers into the FMEDA. For security, they check that secrets cannot leak, that locked debug stays locked and that the chip resists known attacks such as glitching and power analysis.

The functional-safety fault-campaign loop. Measured numbers flow back into the FMEDA until every metric meets its ASIL target.

Think of it like…

It is like crash-testing a car and hiring a locksmith to break into it: you do not just check that it drives, you deliberately break things and try to steal it, and record how well it copes.

Real-world example

Orchid Automotive's ASIL D radar chip has ECC, lockstep cores and watchdogs. The safety team injects 1.5 million stuck-at and bit-flip faults in a fault simulator; 99.2 % of safety-relevant faults are detected, meeting the ASIL D single-point fault target of 99 %. Meanwhile the security team uses formal properties and information-flow tracking to show the boot key never reaches the debug port, and an external lab attacks samples with voltage glitches.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Safety: build the FMEDA, listing failure modes and the safety mechanism claimed for each.
  2. Generate a fault list (stuck-at and transient bit-flips) and prune faults that cannot affect safety-relevant outputs.
  3. Run the fault campaign in simulation, emulation or formal, classifying each fault as safe, detected, residual or latent.
  4. Feed measured diagnostic coverage back into the FMEDA to compute SPFM, LFM and PMHF.
  5. Security: define assets and a threat model, then verify with security properties, information-flow checks, weakness reviews and lab attacks.
  6. Package the evidence for assessors: ISO 26262 safety case, ISO/SAE 21434 work products or security certifications.

Who uses it

Functional-safety engineers, safety and security verification engineers, and teams building automotive, aerospace, industrial, payment and data-centre security chips.

Key takeaway

Memorise the ISO 26262 hardware targets: SPFM at least 90 / 97 / 99 % and LFM at least 60 / 80 / 90 % for ASIL B / C / D.

Going deeper

  • ISO 26262 random-hardware targets: SPFM at least 90/97/99 % and LFM at least 60/80/90 % for ASIL B/C/D, with PMHF below 100 FIT for ASIL B and C and below 10 FIT for ASIL D.
  • Campaigns use permanent faults (stuck-at-0/1) and transient faults (single-event upsets in flops); a fault counts as detected only if the alarm fires within the fault-tolerant time interval.
  • Campaigns can reach millions of faults, so tools combine concurrent fault simulation, emulation, test grading and formal pruning of faults that can never reach an observation point.
  • Security verification starts from a threat model listing assets (keys, lifecycle state, debug access), attackers and entry points; each asset gets confidentiality and integrity properties to check.
  • Information-flow tracking and security formal apps catch leaks functional tests miss, because a leak need not produce a wrong answer, only an observable one.
  • Open roots of trust such as OpenTitan and Caliptra publish their security verification material, giving students real examples of threat models and security properties.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Assuming high functional coverage means safety mechanisms work; only fault injection measures diagnostic coverage.
  • Claiming FMEDA diagnostic coverage from textbook tables for custom logic; assessors increasingly expect measured campaign evidence.
  • Treating security as a feature list; without a threat model nobody can tell whether verification covered what an attacker would try.

docs.title: Try it: A security assertion: debug must stay locked in the production lifecycle state
docs.text:
property p_debug_locked;
  @(posedge clk) disable iff (!rst_n)
    (lc_state == LC_PROD) |-> !jtag_unlocked;
endproperty

assert_debug_locked: assert property (p_debug_locked)
  else $error("JTAG unlocked in PROD lifecycle state");

docs.title: 3.16 Regression Management and Debug
docs.text:
A regression is the full set of tests run repeatedly, usually every night, to make sure new changes did not break anything. When tests fail, engineers debug using waveforms, logs, source browsers and increasingly AI-assisted triage tools. Debug skill, finding the root cause quickly, is one of the most valued abilities in verification.

The regression and debug loop. Every fixed bug gets a test that guards it forever after.

Think of it like…

Regression is the nightly health check-up for the design; debug is the detective work when a symptom appears.

Real-world example

Wednesday's regression shows 37 new failures. A triage script groups them into two signatures: 35 share the same error message from the scoreboard, 2 are timeouts. Aisha opens Verdi on the first group, traces the bad data back through the pipeline with its driver-tracing feature, and finds that Tuesday's commit changed a FIFO's depth parameter without updating the almost-full threshold.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Run the regression nightly (and smaller 'sanity' sets on every commit).
  2. Collect results, group failures by error signature, and assign owners.
  3. Reproduce a failing test with the same seed and dump waveforms.
  4. Trace the failure back from symptom to root cause with a debugger.
  5. Fix, re-run, and add the scenario to the regression so it never returns.

Who uses it

DV and RTL engineers daily; CAD/infrastructure teams maintain regression systems.

Key takeaway

Learn to debug systematically: start at the first error in the log, not the last, and trace data backwards through the design.

Going deeper

  • Large projects run thousands to hundreds of thousands of tests nightly on compute farms managed by LSF, Slurm or cloud schedulers, with bigger runs over weekends.
  • Triage tools strip numbers and timestamps from error messages to form signatures, so 400 failures may collapse into three unique bugs with one owner each.
  • Test ranking finds the fewest seeds that reach the same coverage, producing a quick daily regression and a full weekend one.
  • Systematic debug: reproduce with the same seed, find the first error, open waveforms around it, trace drivers backwards and decide whether the DUT or the testbench is wrong.
  • A healthy project keeps the pass rate near 100 %; flaky tests signal races or uninitialised state and must be fixed, not ignored.
  • AI-assisted tools now cluster failures, suggest suspect signals and choose which tests to run after a change, but engineers still confirm each diagnosis.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Debugging from the last error message rather than the first; later errors are usually consequences.
  • Calling a failure 'not reproducible' after re-running with a different seed or code version; always pin seed, code and tool versions.
  • Living with 'known failures' in the regression, which lets new bugs hide among the old ones.

docs.title: Try it: Find the commit that broke a test with git bisect
docs.text:
git bisect start
git bisect bad  HEAD
git bisect good rtl_freeze_v1.4
# run_test.sh exits 0 on pass, non-zero on fail
git bisect run ./run_test.sh dma_burst_test --seed 81723
git bisect reset

docs.title: 3.17 Gate-Level Simulation (GLS)
docs.text:
Gate-level simulation runs tests on the synthesised or final routed netlist instead of RTL, optionally with real delays from the layout (SDF back-annotation). It catches problems that RTL simulation and static checks can miss: reset and initialisation issues, X-propagation, scan and DFT modes, clock-gating glitches, and timing-sensitive asynchronous paths. It is slow, so teams run a targeted subset.

Running timing gate-level simulation. A small, well-chosen test list is run at the slow and fast corners on the final netlist.

Think of it like…

RTL simulation tests the recipe; gate-level simulation tastes the actual cooked dish, including how long each step really took.

Real-world example

Before tapeout, Pablo runs 40 key tests on the final netlist with SDF delays at the slow corner. One test hangs: after reset, a register without reset feeds an X into the boot FSM, which RTL simulation had hidden because of optimistic X handling. Adding a reset to that register fixes it, a bug that could have bricked every chip.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Get the gate-level netlist and the standard-cell simulation library.
  2. Optionally back-annotate delays from an SDF file produced by STA.
  3. Run a focused set of tests: reset, boot, DFT/scan, power modes, key functions.
  4. Debug X-propagation and timing violations reported by cell timing checks.
  5. Run at different corners (fast/slow) to catch both hold and setup issues.

Who uses it

DV engineers near tapeout; DFT engineers for scan pattern simulation; signoff teams.

Key takeaway

GLS is not a replacement for STA; it is a safety net for reset, X, DFT and asynchronous behaviour.

Going deeper

  • Teams usually run zero-delay GLS on the synthesised netlist early, then SDF-annotated GLS at slow and fast corners on the routed netlist, using tests chosen for reset, boot, clocks, DFT and power modes.
  • SDF (IEEE 1497) carries IOPATH cell delays, INTERCONNECT wire delays and timing-check limits, each as a min:typ:max triple selected at annotation.
  • Check the annotation log: unannotated instances or mismatched hierarchy silently leave zero delays and make the run meaningless.
  • Gate-level runs are many times slower than RTL, so short reset sequences and focused tests matter.
  • GLS catches what static checks can miss: resets hidden by RTL X-optimism, wrong DFT-mode muxing, glitchy clock muxes and wrong false-path or multicycle assumptions.
  • ATPG patterns are simulated serially (full shift) for a few patterns and in parallel (direct chain load) for the rest before going to the tester.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Treating timing GLS as timing sign-off; it checks only exercised paths, while STA checks all of them.
  • Globally disabling timing checks to silence Xs, which also hides real violations; waive only reviewed synchroniser instances.
  • Running GLS at a single corner; hold problems show at the fast corner and setup problems at the slow one.

docs.title: Try it: Back-annotating SDF delays in a gate-level testbench
docs.text:
module tb;
  logic clk = 0, rst_n = 0;
  always #1 clk = ~clk;                      // 500 MHz
  top dut (.clk, .rst_n /* , ... */);       // routed netlist
  initial begin
    $sdf_annotate("top_ss_0p72v_125c.sdf", dut, , "sdf.log", "MAXIMUM");
    repeat (10) @(posedge clk);
    rst_n = 1;
    // ... run a focused reset/boot test ...
  end
endmodule

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies
docs.text: Name What it does Example Gate-level simulation (GLS)Verification practice · Methodology · Signoff Simulating the synthesised or routed netlist with standard-cell models. GLS of the boot sequence confirms the chip comes out of reset cleanly. SDF (Standard Delay Format)IEEE 1497 (originally OVI) · File format · Signoff File containing cell and interconnect delays from timing analysis for back-annotation. The STA tool writes an SDF at the slow corner for timing-annotated GLS. Zero-delay vs timing simulationSimulation modes · Concept · Signoff Zero-delay GLS checks function only; timing GLS uses SDF delays to reveal timing-sensitive bugs. Zero-delay GLS runs fast for X-checks; SDF GLS runs on a handful of tests. Timing checks ($setup, $hold)IEEE 1364/1800 specify blocks · Concept · Signoff Built-in checks in cell models that report violations during timing simulation. A $hold violation on an asynchronous FIFO pointer flags a CDC problem. X-pessimism and X-optimismSimulation semantics · Concept · Verification RTL simulation may hide Xs (optimism); gate-level may spread Xs that real hardware would not (pessimism). An if(x) statement takes the else branch in RTL, masking an uninitialised value. Scan pattern simulationDFT practice · Methodology · DFT Simulating ATPG test patterns on the netlist to confirm they will work on the tester. The DFT team simulates a sample of serial scan patterns with SDF timing. Standard-cell Verilog modelsFoundry / library vendors · File format · Signoff Verilog descriptions of each library cell's function and timing checks. The simulator loads the library's Verilog models to simulate NAND2_X1 cells. Power-aware GLSVerification practice · Methodology · Signoff Gate-level simulation including power switches, isolation and retention from UPF. Power-aware GLS shows retention flops correctly restore state after wake-up. $sdf_annotateIEEE 1364/1800 system task · Concept · Signoff System task that reads an SDF file and applies its delays and timing-check limits to the netlist instances. $sdf_annotate("top_ss.sdf", tb.dut, , "sdf.log", "MAXIMUM") loads slow-corner maximum delays before the test starts. Notifier and timing-violation XStandard-cell Verilog models · Concept · Signoff When a setup or hold check fails, the cell model toggles a notifier that drives the flop output to X. A hold violation on one flop turns its output X, and the X spreads, pointing the engineer to the bad path. Synchroniser timing-check waiversGLS practice · Methodology · Signoff Disabling timing checks only on first-stage synchroniser flops, which legitimately see asynchronous data. A list of 85 reviewed synchroniser instances has checks disabled; all other flops keep full checking. Netlist initialisationGLS practice · Concept · Signoff Forcing or depositing values on uninitialised flops or memories so pessimistic Xs don't block a test that real silicon would pass. Flops without reset in a datapath are deposited with random values at time zero, mirroring real power-up.

docs.title: Glossary of Terms
A
docs.text: ASIC Application-Specific Integrated Circuit — a chip custom-designed for one purpose, with fixed circuits. ATE Automatic Test Equipment — large tester systems (Advantest, Teradyne) that check every manufactured chip. ATPG Automatic Test Pattern Generation — software that creates test patterns to detect manufacturing faults. AXI Advanced eXtensible Interface — Arm AMBA's high-performance on-chip bus protocol with separate read/write channels.

docs.title: B
docs.text: BIST Built-In Self-Test — on-chip logic that tests the chip itself, e.g. memory BIST.

docs.title: C
docs.text: CDC Clock-Domain Crossing — a signal passing between unrelated clocks; needs synchronisers to avoid metastability. Chiplet A small die designed to be combined with others in one package to form a complete system. Clock gating Switching off the clock to idle registers to save dynamic power. Clock skew Difference in clock arrival time between two flip-flops. CMOS Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor — logic using paired PMOS and NMOS transistors; the basis of nearly all digital chips. Coverage A measure of how thoroughly tests exercised the design (code and functional coverage) or detect faults (test coverage). CoWoS Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate — TSMC's 2.5D packaging that places dies and HBM on an interposer. CTS Clock Tree Synthesis — building the buffered network that distributes the clock to all flip-flops.

docs.title: D
docs.text: DEF Design Exchange Format — file describing a design's placement and routing. DFT Design for Test — extra structures (scan, BIST, JTAG) that make manufactured chips testable. DRC Design Rule Check — verifying that layout geometry obeys the foundry's manufacturing rules.

docs.title: E
docs.text: ECO Engineering Change Order — a small, late, incremental change to the netlist and layout. EDA Electronic Design Automation — the software used to design and verify chips. Electromigration (EM) Gradual movement of metal atoms under high current density that can eventually break wires. Emulation Running a design on special hardware at MHz speeds to verify it with real software. EUV Extreme Ultraviolet lithography — 13.5 nm light used to print the finest features at advanced nodes.

docs.title: F
docs.text: Fabless A chip company that designs chips but outsources manufacturing to foundries. FinFET A transistor whose channel is a raised fin wrapped by the gate on three sides. Flip-flop An edge-triggered storage element that captures its input on a clock edge. Formal verification Using mathematical proof instead of test vectors to show a design property always holds. Foundry A company that manufactures chips designed by others, such as TSMC. FPGA Field-Programmable Gate Array — a reprogrammable chip often used for prototyping and lower-volume products.

docs.title: G
docs.text: GAA Gate-All-Around — transistor with stacked nanosheets fully surrounded by the gate, used at 2 nm-class nodes. GDSII Long-standing binary file format for chip layout sent to the foundry; OASIS is its more compact successor.

docs.title: H
docs.text: HBM High Bandwidth Memory — stacked DRAM placed beside a processor for very high bandwidth. HDL Hardware Description Language, such as Verilog, SystemVerilog or VHDL. Hold time How long data must remain stable after the clock edge for correct capture.

docs.title: I
docs.text: IP (semiconductor) A licensable, pre-designed block such as a CPU core, PCIe controller or memory compiler. IR drop Voltage lost across the resistance of the power network, slowing cells.

docs.title: J
docs.text: JTAG IEEE 1149.1 test access port, used for boundary scan, debug and test access.

docs.title: L
docs.text: LEF Library Exchange Format — abstract physical description of cells, macros and technology layers. Liberty (.lib) File format describing cell timing, power and function at one PVT corner. Lint Static checking of RTL for errors and risky coding constructs. LVS Layout Versus Schematic — proving the layout implements the same circuit as the netlist.

docs.title: M
docs.text: Metastability An unstable state when a flip-flop samples a changing input, which may resolve late or randomly. MOSFET Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Field-Effect Transistor — the voltage-controlled switch that chips are built from. MPW Multi-Project Wafer — a shuttle where many designs share one mask set to cut prototype cost.

docs.title: N
docs.text: NRE Non-Recurring Engineering — one-time costs to design a chip and prepare it for production.

docs.title: O
docs.text: OCV On-Chip Variation — modelling of speed differences across a die in timing analysis. OSAT Outsourced Semiconductor Assembly and Test company, such as ASE, Amkor or JCET.

docs.title: P
docs.text: PDK Process Design Kit — the foundry's models, rules and files needed to design for a process. Physical design The back-end stages that turn a netlist into layout: floorplan, place, CTS, route. PLL Phase-Locked Loop — on-chip circuit that multiplies a slow reference clock into the fast clocks a chip uses. PPA Power, Performance and Area — the three key metrics every chip is optimised for. PVT corner A combination of Process, Voltage and Temperature at which a design is analysed.

docs.title: R
docs.text: Respin A new tapeout to fix problems found in silicon. RISC-V An open, royalty-free instruction set architecture implemented by many companies and projects. RTL Register-Transfer Level — describing hardware as registers and the logic between them.

docs.title: S
docs.text: Scan chain Flip-flops linked into a shift register in test mode so testers can load and read internal state. SDC Synopsys Design Constraints — Tcl-based format describing clocks, I/O timing and exceptions. Setup time How long data must be stable before the clock edge for correct capture. Signoff Final formal verification that a design meets all requirements before tapeout. Slack Required time minus arrival time on a timing path; negative slack means a violation. SoC System on Chip — a chip integrating processors, memory, accelerators and I/O. SPEF Standard Parasitic Exchange Format — file of wire resistance and capacitance from extraction. STA Static Timing Analysis — exhaustive, vector-free checking of all timing paths. Standard cell A pre-designed logic gate or flip-flop of fixed height used to build digital designs. Synthesis Automatic translation of RTL into an optimised gate-level netlist. SystemVerilog IEEE 1800 language for hardware design and verification, superset of Verilog.

docs.title: T
docs.text: Tapeout Sending the final layout data to the foundry for mask making. Tcl Tool Command Language — the scripting language built into most EDA tools; SDC and UPF are based on it.

docs.title: U
docs.text: UCIe Universal Chiplet Interconnect Express — open standard for die-to-die links inside a package. UPF Unified Power Format (IEEE 1801) — describes power domains, isolation, retention and supplies. UVM Universal Verification Methodology (IEEE 1800.2) — standard SystemVerilog testbench library.

docs.title: Y
docs.text: Yield The percentage of manufactured dies that work correctly.

docs.title: How to read this guide
docs.text: Each topic follows the same simple pattern, so you can jump to any page and understand it without reading the rest first.

docs.title: How each topic is built
docs.text:
In plain English A jargon-free explanation of what the topic is. Think of it like… An everyday analogy that makes the idea click. Real-world example A short realistic story or worked example showing it in action. How it works The key steps, in order. Who uses it The people, jobs and industries that rely on it. Key takeaway The single most important thing to remember.

Many topics include a Try it box with a safe command or snippet. Then a table lists the most important entries — with what each one does and a concrete example.

docs.title: Entry type labels
docs.text:
Concept, Tool, File Format, Standard, Language, Methodology, Company, IP, Process, Device, Hardware, Organisation, Role, Certification, Resource

Concept = an idea to understand. Tool = software you run. File format = data exchanged between tools. Standard = an official specification (IEEE, JEDEC, Accellera...). Language = an HDL or modelling language. IP = a licensable design block. Process = a manufacturing step or technology. Role = a job. Resource = a book, course or website.

docs.title: Flow stage labels
docs.text:
Spec/Architecture, RTL Design, Verification, Synthesis, DFT, Physical Design, Signoff, Fabrication, Packaging & Test, Whole Flow

Shows where in the RTL-to-GDSII journey something mainly belongs: from specification and architecture, through RTL, verification, synthesis, DFT, physical design and signoff, to fabrication, packaging and test. Whole flow = used across many stages.

docs.title: Licence labels
docs.text:
Commercial, Open Source

Shown for tools, PDKs and some IP. Commercial = paid licence from a vendor (often free or discounted for universities). Open source = freely available source code you can use and modify.

docs.title: About this guide
docs.text: This guide is for students and self-learners. Standard numbers, product names, company ownership and process-node status were checked for accuracy as of late 2026, but the semiconductor industry moves fast: acquisitions, product renames and roadmap changes happen every year. Always check vendor, foundry, IEEE, JEDEC and Accellera sites for the latest details. Product names belong to their owners.

docs.title: Chapter 4: Logic Synthesis & Design for Test
docs.text: Synthesis is where your RTL becomes real hardware: a netlist of standard cells from the foundry's library, optimised to meet timing, power and area goals described in SDC constraints. This chapter explains how synthesis works, what Liberty libraries and PVT corners are, how to write timing constraints, how static timing analysis judges them and how synthesis cuts power. It then covers Design for Test (DFT): scan chains, ATPG, compression, BIST, JTAG and the test standards that let every manufactured chip be checked in seconds.

docs.title: 4.1 How Logic Synthesis Works
docs.text:
Logic synthesis turns RTL into a gate-level netlist. It happens in three main steps: translation (reading RTL into generic logic), optimisation (simplifying and restructuring logic for speed, area and power), and technology mapping (choosing real cells from the foundry library). The tool constantly checks timing against your constraints and tries alternatives until goals are met.

Inside a synthesis run. Optimisation is driven by your constraints at every step after translation.

Think of it like…

Synthesis is like a translator turning a story into another language, then an editor tightening the prose, then a typesetter fitting it to the exact page size and font available.

Real-world example

Nadia synthesises a 64-bit multiplier for 1.5 GHz. The tool first builds a generic multiplier, then chooses a Booth-encoded Wallace-tree architecture because a simple array is too slow. It maps logic to the library's fastest cells on critical paths and small high-Vt cells elsewhere. The report shows 0 ps negative slack, 48,000 µm² area and 12 mW at the typical corner.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Read RTL, libraries and constraints (SDC, UPF).
  2. Elaborate: build generic logic and infer registers, adders, multiplexers and memories.
  3. Optimise: constant propagation, logic sharing, restructuring, resource selection.
  4. Map to standard cells, size gates, insert buffers and clock gating.
  5. Report timing, area and power; write the netlist, SDC and guidance files for the next steps.

Who uses it

Synthesis engineers, RTL designers checking PPA, and physical design engineers in integrated flows.

Key takeaway

Garbage in, garbage out: synthesis results are only as good as the RTL quality and the constraints you give it.

Going deeper

  • Translation produces a technology-independent network (for example Synopsys GTECH generic cells, or and-inverter graphs in ABC) that can be optimised before real cell delays are known.
  • Arithmetic operators are recognised as whole units and given architectures to suit timing, such as ripple or prefix adders and Booth-encoded multipliers.
  • Optimisation is constraint-driven: failing paths get faster, larger cells and restructuring, while paths with spare slack are downsized to save area and leakage.
  • Keeping hierarchy eases debug and equivalence checking, but ungrouping enables cross-boundary optimisation; tools often auto-ungroup small modules.
  • Logic with no observable effect, such as unloaded flops, is removed; surprising removals usually reveal RTL bugs like unconnected outputs.
  • Flows run an initial compile, then incremental optimisation after DFT insertion or constraint updates to fix remaining violations without starting again.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Expecting synthesis to fix a poor architecture; a long arithmetic chain needs pipelining or restructuring in the RTL.
  • Ignoring warnings about inferred latches, multiple drivers or removed registers; these often reveal real RTL bugs.
  • Over-using dont_touch, which blocks optimisation and can leave violations the tool could otherwise fix.

docs.text: Name What it does Example Logic synthesisEDA technique · Methodology · Synthesis Automatic conversion of RTL into an optimised netlist of standard cells. A 50,000-line RTL design becomes a 20-million-cell netlist in a few hours. ElaborationSynthesis step · Concept · Synthesis Building the full design hierarchy, resolving parameters and generate blocks. A FIFO with DEPTH=16 is elaborated into exactly 16 storage rows. Technology mappingSynthesis step · Concept · Synthesis Choosing actual library cells to implement the generic logic. Generic AND-OR logic is mapped to an AOI22_X2 cell. Logic optimisationSynthesis step · Concept · Synthesis Restructuring Boolean logic to reduce delay, area or power while preserving function. Common sub-expressions shared between two adders are computed once. Gate sizing and bufferingSynthesis/P&R optimisation · Concept · Synthesis Selecting cell drive strengths and inserting buffers to meet timing and fix slow transitions. Upsizing a NAND from X1 to X4 speeds a critical path by 20 ps. RetimingSynthesis optimisation · Concept · Synthesis Moving registers across logic to balance pipeline stages without changing function. Retiming shifts half a multiplier's logic into the next pipeline stage. Datapath synthesis / DesignWareSynopsys DesignWare Library; Cadence ChipWare · IP · Synthesis · Commercial Optimised arithmetic architectures (adders, multipliers, dividers) chosen automatically by synthesis. Synthesis picks a fast parallel-prefix adder from DesignWare for a critical path. Multi-bit flip-flop bankingLow-power synthesis technique · Concept · Synthesis Merging several single-bit flops into multi-bit cells that share clock circuitry. Banking 4-bit flops cuts clock power by around 10-20 % in a register-heavy block. Don't-touch and dont_useSynthesis directives · Concept · Synthesis Directives telling the tool not to modify certain instances or not to use certain cells. Clock-domain synchroniser flops are marked dont_touch so they are not optimised away. QoR (Quality of Results)Industry term · Concept · Synthesis Summary of how good a synthesis or implementation run is: timing, area, power and congestion. A tool upgrade improves QoR by 3 % area at the same timing. Resource sharingSynthesis optimisation · Concept · Synthesis Using one hardware operator for several RTL operations that never happen in the same cycle, saving area. Two additions in different branches of a case statement share one adder plus a multiplexer. Ungrouping a small decoder lets the tool merge its logic with the FSM, removing two levels of gates. A parameter disables the debug port, so 1,200 flops and their logic vanish from the netlist automatically. FSM extraction and re-encodingSynthesis optimisation · Concept · Synthesis Recognising state machines in RTL and choosing a better state encoding, such as one-hot, for speed or area. A 12-state binary FSM is re-encoded one-hot, trading 8 extra flops for a faster next-state decode.

docs.title: 4.2 Synthesis Tools: Design Compiler, Fusion Compiler, Genus, Yosys and ABC
docs.text:
Commercial ASIC synthesis is dominated by Synopsys (Design Compiler and Fusion Compiler) and Cadence (Genus). Modern tools are 'physically aware': they consider where cells will be placed so their timing estimates match layout. In open source, Yosys reads Verilog and uses the ABC engine from UC Berkeley for logic optimisation and mapping.

Three synthesis flows side by side

Synopsys DC / Fusion Cadence Genus Yosys + ABC Read RTL analyze, elaborate read_hdl, elaborate read_verilog -sv Main command compile_ultra / compile_fusion syn_generic, syn_map, syn_opt synth, dfflibmap, abc Physical awareness Topographical / native in FC iSpatial with Innovus None (OpenROAD later) Typical outputs Netlist, SDC, SVF Netlist, SDC, LEC dofile Netlist, stat report Licence Commercial Commercial Open source (ISC)

Commands differ, but every flow reads RTL and constraints and writes a netlist plus reports.

Think of it like…

Choosing a synthesis tool is like choosing a professional kitchen: the big brands have every gadget and support, while the open-source kitchen is free and great for learning, though less turbo-charged.

Real-world example

At a large company, Vikram runs Fusion Compiler, which uses the same engines for synthesis and place-and-route so timing correlates closely. At a start-up with Cadence licences, his friend uses Genus with iSpatial to predict placement. At home, Vikram synthesises his RISC-V hobby core with Yosys for SKY130 and compares the area reports.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Set up the library paths, target libraries and design files.
  2. Read RTL and constraints; elaborate the top module.
  3. Compile/synthesise with chosen effort and physical awareness (floorplan or DEF).
  4. Check reports: timing (QoR), area, power, design rule violations, unmapped cells.
  5. Write outputs: netlist, SDC, UPF, and guidance for LEC.

Who uses it

Synthesis/implementation engineers; RTL designers running quick PPA checks.

Key takeaway

Know the basic command flow of one commercial tool (read, elaborate, link, compile, report_timing, write) and Yosys's 'synth' command.

Going deeper

  • A typical commercial script sets libraries, reads and elaborates RTL, links, reads SDC and UPF, runs check_design and check_timing, compiles, inserts DFT, re-optimises incrementally and writes netlist, constraints, reports and LEC guidance.
  • Physical-aware synthesis reads the floorplan (DEF) and technology LEF so wire delays and congestion reflect real layout, reducing surprises at place-and-route.
  • Fusion Compiler shares one data model between synthesis and implementation, while Genus links to Innovus through iSpatial; both aim to keep timing correlated across steps.
  • Yosys's synth command runs a generic script (proc, opt, fsm, memory, techmap, abc); for ASICs, flops are mapped with dfflibmap and logic with abc against a Liberty file, as in LibreLane.
  • Reports to read on every run: worst paths per clock group, area by hierarchy, cell and Vt usage, power, design-rule violations and messages about latches or removed logic.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Skipping check_design and check_timing; unresolved references and unconstrained endpoints produce a netlist that looks fine but is not.
  • Comparing QoR between tools without identical libraries, constraints and corners; most differences then come from setup, not the tool.
  • Forgetting timing models for memories and analogue macros, so synthesis sees no timing on their paths.

docs.title: Try it: Synthesise a design with Yosys
docs.text:
yosys -p "read_verilog -sv counter.sv; synth -top counter; \
  dfflibmap -liberty sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib; \
  abc -liberty sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib; \
  stat; write_verilog -noattr counter_netlist.v"

docs.title: 4.3 Standard-Cell Libraries and Liberty (.lib) Files
docs.text:
A standard-cell library is the foundry's or IP vendor's catalogue of logic cells (inverters, NANDs, flops, buffers...) all with the same height so they line up in rows. Each cell comes with several 'views': a Liberty (.lib) file describing timing, power and function; a LEF file describing its physical outline; a Verilog model; and the GDS layout. Synthesis and timing tools rely on the Liberty data.

The views of one standard cell. Each tool reads the view it needs; all must describe the same cell consistently.

Think of it like…

A standard-cell library is like a LEGO catalogue: every brick has the same height, a known shape, and a data sheet saying how strong and heavy it is.

Real-world example

Kenji opens sky130_fd_sc_hd__tt_025C_1v80.lib and finds the entry for nand2_1. It lists its area, its function '!(A&B)', input pin capacitances, and tables giving delay and output transition for combinations of input slew and output load. When his synthesis run picks nand2_4 instead, it is because the table shows it is faster at the heavy load on that net.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Cells are designed at transistor level and laid out with a fixed height (track count).
  2. Characterisation simulates each cell with SPICE across slews, loads and PVT corners.
  3. Results are written as Liberty tables (NLDM, CCS or ECSM, plus LVF for variation).
  4. Synthesis and STA look up delays by interpolating these tables.
  5. Libraries come in variants: Vt flavours, track heights, and different corners.

Who uses it

Library/characterisation engineers create them; synthesis, P&R and STA engineers use them daily.

Key takeaway

Know what NLDM tables contain (delay and transition vs input slew and output load) and why each PVT corner needs its own .lib file.

Going deeper

  • A Liberty file has a library header (units, nominal PVT, slew thresholds), lookup-table templates, then one cell group per cell with pins, functions and timing/power arcs.
  • NLDM tables are commonly 7×7 or 8×8, indexed by input transition and output load; tools interpolate inside and extrapolate outside, losing accuracy at the edges.
  • Every corner needs its own .lib, so a library release can contain dozens to hundreds of files across process, voltage, temperature and Vt flavours.
  • Libraries come in threshold-voltage flavours (such as ULVT, LVT, SVT, HVT) so synthesis can trade speed for leakage path by path.
  • LVF adds sigma tables for delay, transition and constraints; generating them needs Monte Carlo-based characterisation, which is why it is costly.
  • Characterisation tools run SPICE on every cell, arc, slew, load and corner, so one advanced-node library release consumes very large amounts of compute.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Mixing libraries from different corners or release versions in one run, giving meaningless timing.
  • Ignoring extrapolation warnings when slews or loads exceed table ranges; fix the transitions in the design instead.
  • Assuming the typical (TT) library is enough; timing must close at every required sign-off corner.

docs.title: Try it: Part of a Liberty cell description (simplified)
docs.text:
cell (NAND2_X1) {
  area : 0.798;
  pin (A) { direction : input; capacitance : 0.0016; }
  pin (Y) {
    direction : output;
    function : "!(A & B)";
    timing () {
      related_pin : "A";
      cell_rise (delay_template_7x7) { values ("..."); }
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 4.4 PVT Corners, Modes and MCMM
docs.text:
Transistor speed changes with Process (manufacturing variation), Voltage and Temperature: the PVT corners. A chip must work at every combination it may meet, from a slow chip at low voltage and high temperature to a fast chip at high voltage and low temperature. It must also work in every operating mode (functional, test, sleep). Tools analyse many corners and modes at once: MCMM.

Classic slow and fast corners

Slow corner Fast corner Process SS (slow NMOS/PMOS) FF (fast NMOS/PMOS) Voltage Nominal −10 % Nominal +10 % Temperature 125 °C (or −40 °C if inverted) −40 °C (125 °C for leakage) Wire RC Cworst / RCworst Cbest / RCbest Main check Setup Hold Leakage Low Highest when hot

Setup usually fails at the slow corner and hold at the fast one, with exceptions at advanced nodes.

Think of it like…

Like a car that must start on a freezing morning in Finland and not overheat in a desert summer, with either a new or a worn engine.

Real-world example

For an automotive chip rated from -40 °C to 150 °C, Ingrid's team checks setup at the slow-slow corner, 0.72 V, 150 °C, and hold at fast-fast, 0.88 V, -40 °C. They also check 'temperature inversion', where at advanced nodes low temperature can actually be slower. With 3 modes and 12 corners, they analyse 36 scenarios in one MCMM run.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Process corners: SS, TT, FF, plus skewed SF and FS (NMOS/PMOS different).
  2. Voltage: nominal and minus/plus tolerance (e.g. 0.8 V ± 10 %).
  3. Temperature: e.g. -40 °C to 125 °C (consumer) or 150 °C (automotive).
  4. Combine with RC (wire) corners: Cworst, Cbest, RCworst, RCbest, typical.
  5. Analyse all relevant mode-corner scenarios simultaneously (MCMM).

Who uses it

Synthesis, P&R and STA engineers; library teams; foundry and product engineers define corners.

Key takeaway

Setup is usually worst at slow corners; hold is usually worst at fast corners, but advanced nodes add exceptions like temperature inversion.

Going deeper

  • A scenario combines one mode with one corner (process, voltage, temperature, RC); advanced SoCs analyse dozens across functional, test and low-power modes.
  • Corner voltages are typically nominal ±5–10 % to cover regulator tolerance and IR drop; temperatures span −40 °C to 125 °C for automotive and industrial parts.
  • Global variation is covered by corners, local variation by OCV derates or statistical models such as POCV with LVF data.
  • Wire corners matter as much as transistor corners at advanced nodes: Cworst stresses capacitance-dominated paths, RCworst stresses long resistive wires.
  • Temperature inversion at low voltage means the worst setup corner can be cold, so both hot and cold slow corners are checked.
  • Adding corners progressively—few during early optimisation, the full list at sign-off—keeps run times practical.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Closing setup only at the slow-hot corner and hold only at the fast corner, missing temperature-inversion and RC-corner exceptions.
  • Forgetting test mode as its own mode; scan shift and capture use different clocks and paths needing their own constraints.
  • Loading every scenario from the start of optimisation, slowing runs without improving results.

docs.text: Name What it does Example PVT (Process, Voltage, Temperature)Industry term · Concept · Signoff The three variables that change transistor speed and must be covered by analysis. SF means slow NMOS and fast PMOS, which stresses some flop designs. docs.title: 4.5 Timing Constraints with SDC
docs.text:
SDC (Synopsys Design Constraints) is the Tcl-based language you use to tell tools your timing goals: the clocks and their frequencies, when inputs arrive and outputs are needed, and which paths are exceptions. Synthesis, place-and-route and STA all read the same SDC. Wrong constraints are a major cause of chip failures, because tools optimise exactly what you tell them.

Writing an SDC file, in order. Clocks first, exceptions last, then check that nothing is left unconstrained.

Think of it like…

SDC is the timetable for a railway: it says when each train leaves, when it must arrive, and which lines are not used for passenger trains at all.

Real-world example

Marco writes SDC for a 500 MHz block: create_clock -period 2.0 on clk, input delays of 0.6 ns for signals coming from another block, output delay of 0.8 ns, a false path on a static configuration register, and a 2-cycle multicycle path on a slow divider. When a colleague forgot to declare a generated clock from a divider, half the design was unconstrained and STA showed false 'clean' results.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Define clocks: create_clock and create_generated_clock with periods and sources.
  2. Add clock uncertainty (jitter + margin), latency and transition targets.
  3. Constrain I/O: set_input_delay and set_output_delay relative to clocks.
  4. Declare exceptions: set_false_path, set_multicycle_path, set_max_delay, clock groups.
  5. Add design rules (max transition, capacitance, fanout) and check for unconstrained paths.

Who uses it

RTL designers write initial constraints; synthesis, PD and STA engineers refine and sign them off.

Key takeaway

Every exception (false path, multicycle) must be justified and reviewed: a wrong false path hides real failures.

Going deeper

  • Setup check: data must arrive before the capture edge minus setup time and uncertainty; hold check: data must not change until hold time after the edge that launched it.
  • I/O delays describe the outside world: with a 2 ns period and 0.6 ns input delay, the internal input path gets about 1.4 ns minus setup and uncertainty.
  • Before CTS clocks are ideal and uncertainty covers expected skew; after CTS set_propagated_clock uses real tree delays and uncertainty is reduced to jitter and margin.
  • A setup multicycle of N normally needs a hold multicycle of N−1 to move the hold check back to the launch edge.
  • set_clock_groups -asynchronous stops timing between unrelated clocks, so those crossings must be made safe by CDC design and checked with CDC tools.
  • Projects keep separate SDC sets per mode, such as functional, scan shift and scan capture, all checked by constraint-verification tools.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using false paths to hide failing paths instead of fixing them; a wrong exception becomes a silicon bug.
  • Adding a setup multicycle without the matching hold multicycle, creating huge false hold violations.
  • Missing generated clocks on dividers or muxes, leaving derived-clock paths untimed or wrongly timed.
  • Leaving inputs or outputs unconstrained; check_timing reports them and they will not be optimised.

docs.title: Try it: A fuller SDC example
docs.text:
# Clocks
create_clock -name clk     -period 2.0    [get_ports clk]
create_clock -name usb_clk -period 16.667 [get_ports usb_clk]
create_generated_clock -name clk_div2 -source [get_ports clk] \
    -divide_by 2 [get_pins u_div/q_reg/Q]
set_clock_uncertainty -setup 0.10 [get_clocks clk]
set_clock_uncertainty -hold  0.03 [get_clocks clk]

# I/O budget and environment
set_input_delay  0.6 -clock clk [remove_from_collection [all_inputs] [get_ports {clk usb_clk}]]
set_output_delay 0.8 -clock clk [all_outputs]
set_driving_cell -lib_cell BUF_X4 [all_inputs]
set_load 0.02 [all_outputs]

# Mode selection and exceptions (review each one!)
set_case_analysis 0 [get_ports scan_mode]
set_false_path -from [get_cells cfg_reg*]
set_multicycle_path 2 -setup -to [get_pins u_mac/acc_reg*/D]
set_multicycle_path 1 -hold  -to [get_pins u_mac/acc_reg*/D]
set_clock_groups -asynchronous -group {clk clk_div2} -group usb_clk

# Design rules
set_max_transition 0.15 [current_design]

docs.title: Key concepts, tools, formats, standards & companies

The same top.sdc file is used by Genus, Innovus and Tempus. create_clock / create_generated_clockSDC commands · Concept · Synthesis Define primary clocks and clocks derived from them (dividers, muxes). A divider that produces results every 4 cycles gets a 4-cycle setup multicycle. CPU clock and USB clock are declared asynchronous; CDC tools check those crossings instead. A net with 300 ps transition violates a 150 ps limit and gets buffered. A checker reports 120 unclocked registers before synthesis starts. Inputs are driven by a BUF_X4 and outputs see 20 fF, matching the neighbouring block's real cells. Synthesis assumes 0.4 ns ideal latency; after CTS, set_propagated_clock replaces it with each flop's actual arrival.

docs.title: 4.6 Static Timing Analysis (STA) Fundamentals
docs.text:
Static timing analysis checks every timing path in the design mathematically, without running test vectors. It adds up cell and wire delays along each path from a launching flop to a capturing flop and compares the arrival time with the required time set by the clock. Because it checks all paths exhaustively in minutes to hours, STA is the standard way to sign off timing.

Anatomy of one setup check (2 ns clock). Slack is what is left after the data path, clock latencies, setup time and uncertainty are counted.

Think of it like…

STA is like checking every possible route on a map against a timetable, instead of sending a car down each road to see if it arrives in time.

Real-world example

Sana's STA report shows path: clock launch 0 ps, clock latency 220 ps, flop clk-to-Q 45 ps, 14 cells and wires 1,610 ps = arrival 1,875 ps. Required: next edge 2,000 ps + capture latency 205 ps - setup 30 ps - uncertainty 60 ps = 2,115 ps. Slack = +240 ps: passes. A different path with heavy crosstalk shows -12 ps and needs fixing.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Break the design into timing paths: input-to-reg, reg-to-reg, reg-to-output, input-to-output.
  2. Compute arrival times by adding clock latency, cell delays and wire delays along each path.
  3. Compute required times from the capture clock edge, setup/hold and uncertainty.
  4. Slack = required - arrival (setup) or arrival - required (hold); report WNS and TNS.
  5. Account for variation (OCV/AOCV/POCV), crosstalk and clock reconvergence pessimism (CRPR).

Who uses it

STA engineers, synthesis and PD engineers, and RTL designers fixing critical paths.

Key takeaway

Know WNS (worst negative slack), TNS (total negative slack) and how to read a timing report line by line; it is the most common PD interview question.

Going deeper

  • STA builds a timing graph of pins and arcs, propagates arrival times forwards and required times backwards, then reports the worst paths per endpoint and path group.
  • Setup uses late (max) delays on the data path and early (min) on the capture clock; hold does the opposite, which is why OCV derates come in early and late pairs.
  • Reports list each cell and net increment with transition and capacitance; reading them line by line shows whether logic depth, long wires or clock skew dominate.
  • Hold violations do not depend on clock frequency, so they break chips at any speed; setup failures can be avoided in the lab by slowing the clock.
  • Graph-based analysis takes the worst slew at each pin and is pessimistic; path-based analysis re-times critical paths with their real slews to recover margin.
  • Sign-off STA adds crosstalk, variation and IR-drop effects on top of these fundamentals, covered in the signoff chapter.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Thinking hold violations can be fixed by lowering the frequency; only changing delays fixes hold.
  • Watching only WNS; many small failures (high TNS, many failing endpoints) can be harder to close than one bad path.
  • Treating synthesis-stage timing as final; without real clock trees and parasitics the numbers are estimates.

A path arrives 150 ps after the latch opens; STA borrows 150 ps and charges it to the following path.

docs.title: 4.7 Power-Aware Synthesis: Clock Gating, Multi-Vt and UPF
docs.text:
Synthesis does not only chase timing; it also cuts power. It automatically inserts clock gates so idle registers stop switching, uses slower low-leakage cells wherever there is spare time, and reads the UPF power-intent file to add the special cells that switchable power domains need.

Three ways synthesis saves power

Clock gating Multi-Vt swap Power gating (UPF) Attacks Dynamic power Leakage power Leakage when off Inserted by Synthesis, automatically Synthesis and P&R optimisation UPF-driven synthesis + P&R Needs Enable conditions Timing slack Power intent + control logic Costs ICG area, skew Slower cells Switches, isolation, wake time Verified by LEC, DFT checks STA Power-aware sim, LP checks

Each technique attacks a different part of the power equation and has its own cost.

Think of it like…

Like a smart building that switches off lights in empty rooms (clock gating), fits energy-saving bulbs where brightness does not matter (high-Vt cells) and installs breakers between circuits that can be turned off (isolation cells).

Real-world example

Leila synthesises a sensor-hub block for a smartwatch. With clock gating and leakage recovery enabled, the power report, using activity from a real workload, shows clearly lower dynamic and leakage power at the same 200 MHz target. The UPF adds isolation cells on every output of the switchable DSP domain, and power-aware equivalence checking confirms nothing else changed.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Provide realistic switching activity (SAIF or FSDB from simulation) and the UPF power intent.
  2. Set a clock-gating style: ICG cell type, minimum register width, test-enable connection.
  3. Synthesise for timing, then let leakage recovery swap non-critical cells to high-Vt.
  4. Check the inserted isolation, level shifters and retention cells against the power intent.
  5. Compare power reports and verify with power-aware equivalence and simulation.

Who uses it

Synthesis and low-power implementation engineers at mobile, IoT, automotive and data-centre chip companies, working with power architects.

Key takeaway

Remember the split: clock gating attacks dynamic power, while multi-Vt and power gating attack leakage.

Going deeper

  • An ICG is a latch plus an AND gate: the latch holds the enable while the clock is high, so the gated clock cannot glitch.
  • Clock networks often consume a large share of a block's dynamic power, which is why gating near the clock root saves more than gating individual registers.
  • Leakage recovery normally runs after timing is met, swapping cells on positive-slack paths to high-Vt so leakage falls without losing frequency.
  • Synthesis reads UPF to insert isolation cells, level shifters and retention flops, then writes an updated UPF; static low-power checkers verify the result before P&R.
  • Power optimisation needs realistic activity from representative workloads; default toggle rates can misrank which blocks and paths matter.
  • Glitches from unequal path delays can be a significant share of dynamic power in deep arithmetic; pipelining and path balancing reduce them.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using default toggle rates instead of real activity, which misleads both optimisation and power reports.
  • Gating tiny register groups whose ICG overhead exceeds the savings; set a sensible minimum bit-width.
  • Leaving the ICG test-enable unconnected, causing large drops in scan coverage.

docs.title: Try it: Illustrative Design Compiler-style power settings (Tcl)

    -positive_edge_logic {integrated} \
    -control_point before -control_signal scan_enable \
    -minimum_bitwidth 4
load_upf sensor_hub.upf
read_saif -input workload.saif -instance_name tb/u_dut

report_power -hierarchy

docs.text: Name What it does Example Automatic clock-gating insertionDesign Compiler, Fusion Compiler, Genus and other synthesis tools · Methodology · Synthesis Synthesis replaces a register bank's enable feedback multiplexers with one integrated clock-gating cell that stops its clock when idle. A 32-bit register loaded only when 'valid' is high gets one ICG, so its 32 flops stop toggling whenever valid is low. The library's ICG_X2 cell is chosen for gating groups of up to 64 flops. With a minimum width of 4, a lone 1-bit flag register stays ungated while 8-bit counters are gated. AND gates freeze multiplier inputs whenever the result multiplexer selects the bypass path. The controller asserts light-sleep on idle cache banks, reducing their leakage while keeping contents.

docs.title: 4.8 DFT Concepts: Faults, Scan and Controllability
docs.text:
Manufacturing is imperfect: dust, defects and variation mean some chips come out broken. Design for Test (DFT) adds extra logic so every manufactured chip can be tested quickly. The core idea is scan: in test mode, all flip-flops are linked into long shift registers so a tester can load any state, run one clock, and read the results back, making internal logic controllable and observable.

One scan test pattern. Shift is slow and long; capture is one or two fast functional clocks.

Think of it like…

Scan is like giving a car mechanic a diagnostic port: instead of guessing what is wrong from outside, they can plug in and read every sensor directly.

Real-world example

A microcontroller has 200,000 flops. Without DFT, testing internal logic from 64 pins would be practically impossible. DFT engineer Hiro replaces every flop with a scan flop and stitches them into 400 chains of 500 flops. On the tester, patterns shift in, the chip captures one functional cycle, and results shift out. The test takes 0.8 seconds per chip and detects 99.2 % of stuck-at faults.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Replace normal flops with scan flops (an extra multiplexer selects scan input).
  2. Stitch scan flops into chains between scan-in and scan-out pins.
  3. In shift mode, load test values; in capture mode, run functional clock(s).
  4. Shift out captured values while loading the next pattern.
  5. The tester compares outputs with expected values computed by ATPG.

Who uses it

DFT engineers (a distinct, in-demand role), test engineers and product engineers.

Key takeaway

Explain controllability (can I set this node?) and observability (can I see this node?): they are the foundation of DFT interviews.

Going deeper

  • Scan turns a sequential circuit into combinational test problems: ATPG only has to solve the logic between flops, because every flop can be loaded and read directly.
  • Shift cycles per pattern equal the longest chain, so test time is roughly patterns × chain length × shift period, which is why short, balanced chains matter.
  • Stuck-at coverage targets around 99 % are common; transition-fault tests add delay-defect detection, and cell-aware tests catch defects inside cells that classic models miss.
  • Scan rules need test-mode control of clocks and asynchronous resets; latches, gated clocks and combinational loops need special handling.
  • Launch-on-capture uses two functional pulses after shifting; launch-on-shift launches on the last shift edge and needs an at-speed scan enable but often gives higher coverage.
  • DFT adds area (typically a few percent), extra timing modes and high switching power during shift, so test power and scan-mode timing are signed off too.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving internally generated clocks or resets uncontrollable in test mode, making whole blocks untestable.
  • Shifting at full speed with every flop toggling, causing IR-drop failures on the tester.
  • Confusing DFT with functional verification: DFT finds manufacturing defects, not design bugs.

docs.title: Try it: What scan insertion does to a flip-flop
docs.text:
// Mux-D scan flip-flop
module scan_dff (input  logic clk, d, si, se,
                 output logic q);
  always_ff @(posedge clk)
    q <= se ? si : d;   // se=1: shift from previous flop, se=0: capture logic
endmodule
// Chain: si of flop N connects to q of flop N-1; first si = scan_in pin

A net shorted to ground behaves as stuck-at-0. Transition (delay) fault modelFault model · Concept · DFT Models a node too slow to switch in time, detected with at-speed launch and capture. A test point is added to make a deep AND-tree output observable. docs.title: 4.9 Scan Insertion and Test Compression
docs.text:
Large chips have millions of flops but only a few test pins and limited tester memory. Test compression puts a decompressor at the inputs and a compactor at the outputs of hundreds of short internal scan chains, so a few external pins feed many internal chains. This cuts test time and data volume by 10x to 100x or more. Newer approaches send test data over a packetised bus.

Scan compression architecture. A few tester pins feed hundreds of short internal chains.

Think of it like…

Compression is like zipping a big file before emailing it: you send far less data, and it is expanded at the other end.

Real-world example

An AI chip with 50 million flops would need hours per chip with plain scan. Instead, Aditi's team uses Tessent TestKompress with 4,000 internal chains of about 12,500 flops, fed through 32 scan pins. They also adopt a streaming scan network so many cores are tested in parallel over a shared bus. Test time falls to about 2 seconds, saving millions of dollars per year in tester cost.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Insert scan: replace flops, define chains, add scan enable and test-mode control.
  2. Insert compression logic: decompressor (input side) and compactor (output side).
  3. Handle X sources (memories, analog) with X-masking or bounding.
  4. Plan test access for hierarchical cores (wrappers, test buses, streaming networks).
  5. Verify DFT structures with DRC checks and simulation.

Who uses it

DFT engineers; physical design engineers handle scan-chain reordering during placement.

Key takeaway

Know why scan chains are reordered after placement: to shorten wiring, while keeping the chain lengths balanced.

Going deeper

  • Compression ratio is roughly internal chains ÷ external channels; with 8 channels feeding 800 chains, chains are about 100× shorter, cutting shift cycles and data by a similar factor minus overheads.
  • Decompressors work because ATPG patterns specify only a small fraction of bits; the rest can be whatever the decompressor produces.
  • Unknown values from uninitialised memories, analogue blocks or false paths corrupt compacted outputs, so X-masking or X-tolerant compactors are essential.
  • Chains crossing clock domains need lock-up latches; chains are usually grouped by clock domain and balanced to equal length.
  • After placement, chains are reordered using SCANDEF to cut wire length, then checked with DFT rule checks and LEC.
  • Hierarchical DFT generates each core's patterns once and retargets them at chip level, cutting ATPG run time on huge SoCs.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Pushing compression ratio too high, which can reduce coverage or raise pattern counts; find the sweet spot with trial ATPG.
  • Ignoring X sources until late; one uninitialised memory output can mask large parts of the design.
  • Mixing clock domains in one chain without lock-up latches, causing shift failures on the tester.

docs.title: 4.10 ATPG and DFT Tools: TestMAX, Modus and Tessent
docs.text:
Automatic test pattern generation (ATPG) software works out the input values that will reveal each possible fault and what the correct outputs should be. The result is a set of test patterns in a tester-ready format. The three big DFT tool families are Siemens Tessent (the market leader in DFT), Synopsys TestMAX and Cadence Modus.

The ATPG flow. Fault simulation drops easy faults so the generator can focus on hard ones.

Think of it like…

ATPG is like writing the shortest possible set of exam questions that still reveals every gap in a student's knowledge.

Real-world example

Running Tessent ATPG on a 30-million-gate block, Lin gets 4,800 compressed stuck-at patterns with 99.3 % test coverage and 6,200 transition patterns at 94 %. She exports them in STIL for the Advantest tester. When coverage on one block is low, the report shows untestable faults behind a black-boxed analog macro; adding wrapper flops fixes it.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Read the scan-inserted netlist, libraries and DFT setup (test procedures).
  2. Run DFT design rule checks (DRC) for scan chain integrity and clock control.
  3. Generate patterns per fault model: stuck-at, transition, cell-aware, path delay.
  4. Simulate patterns, compute coverage, compress and order them.
  5. Export patterns (STIL/WGL) and hand off to test engineering.

Who uses it

DFT engineers and test engineers.

Key takeaway

Know the difference between fault coverage (all faults) and test coverage (excluding untestable faults); interviewers check this.

Going deeper

  • ATPG picks an undetected fault, sets inputs so the faulty node differs from its fault value, then sensitises a path to a scan flop or output; the D-algorithm, PODEM and FAN are the classic algorithms.
  • Each new pattern is fault-simulated against all remaining faults, so most faults are detected 'for free' and the generator targets only hard ones.
  • Test coverage excludes provably untestable faults (tied, blocked, redundant) from the denominator; fault coverage keeps them, so it is always lower or equal.
  • Pattern counts grow from thousands for stuck-at to tens of thousands with transition and cell-aware models, so tester time decides which fault models a product can afford.
  • Patterns are written in STIL (IEEE 1450) with procedures for shift and capture timing, then converted by test engineers into ATE test programs.
  • Diagnosis runs ATPG in reverse: failing tester cycles are mapped to suspect nets and cells to guide failure analysis and yield learning.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Using fault coverage and test coverage interchangeably; always state which one and how untestable faults were classified.
  • Sending patterns to the tester without simulating them on the netlist with timing, wasting expensive tester debug time.
  • Adding fault models without checking pattern-count growth against tester time and memory budgets.

docs.title: 4.11 BIST, Memory BIST and Repair
docs.text:
Built-in self-test (BIST) puts a small tester inside the chip. Memory BIST (MBIST) runs patterns like March algorithms through every SRAM, which are dense and defect-prone. Logic BIST uses pseudo-random patterns and signature registers. Many memories include spare rows and columns, and repair logic programs fuses to swap in spares for faulty cells, increasing yield.

Memory BIST and repair. Repair data is found once at manufacturing test and reloaded at every power-up.

Think of it like…

BIST is like a car's self-check when you turn the key: the dashboard lights flash on and off while the car tests itself without a mechanic.

Real-world example

A GPU contains 3,000 SRAM instances. Tessent MemoryBIST controllers test them in parallel groups at power-up and on the tester. In production, 7 % of dies show a few failing bits; built-in repair analysis maps them onto spare columns and burns eFuses. Those dies become good chips, adding several percentage points of yield worth millions of dollars.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Insert MBIST controllers and collars around memories.
  2. Run March algorithms (e.g. March C-) that write and read patterns in sequence.
  3. Analyse failures and compute repair solutions using spare rows/columns (BIRA).
  4. Program repair information into eFuses; reload it at every power-up.
  5. Optionally run logic BIST in the field for safety-critical self-checks.

Who uses it

DFT engineers, memory designers, test and yield engineers; automotive safety teams.

Key takeaway

Memories often dominate yield loss because they are the densest structures; that is why repair matters so much.

Going deeper

  • March algorithms are written as elements such as ⇑(r0,w1); March C- needs 10 operations per address (10N) and detects stuck-at, transition, address-decoder and many coupling faults.
  • MBIST controllers are inserted around memory wrappers and reached through IEEE 1687 networks, so the same tests run at wafer sort, final test and in the field.
  • Logic BIST needs an X-free design because one unknown corrupts the MISR signature; test points raise coverage on random-pattern-resistant logic.
  • Repairable memories carry spare rows and columns; BIRA picks an allocation, eFuses or OTP store it, and a repair-load step restores it at every power-up.
  • Automotive SoCs run LBIST and MBIST at power-on and periodically to meet ISO 26262 latent-fault targets, often within millisecond time budgets.
  • An n-bit LFSR with a primitive feedback polynomial cycles through 2^n − 1 states, making it a very cheap pseudo-random pattern source.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Running MBIST only at slow speed; many memory defects are speed-related, so test at functional frequency.
  • Forgetting to budget fuse storage and repair-load time in the boot sequence.
  • Expecting LBIST alone to reach high coverage; random-resistant logic needs test points or deterministic top-up patterns.

docs.title: Try it: An 8-bit LFSR pattern generator and March C- in notation
docs.text:
// Maximal-length 8-bit LFSR (taps 8,6,5,4): 255 states before repeating
module lfsr8 (input  logic clk, rst_n, en,
              output logic [7:0] q);
  always_ff @(posedge clk or negedge rst_n)
    if (!rst_n)  q <= 8'h01;                               // any non-zero seed
    else if (en) q <= {q[6:0], q[7] ^ q[5] ^ q[4] ^ q[3]};
endmodule

// March C- (10N):  ⇕(w0) ⇑(r0,w1) ⇑(r1,w0) ⇓(r0,w1) ⇓(r1,w0) ⇕(r0)
// ⇑ = ascending addresses, ⇓ = descending, ⇕ = either order

docs.title: 4.12 JTAG and Test Access Standards (IEEE 1149.1, 1500, 1687)
docs.text:
JTAG (IEEE 1149.1) is a standard 4-or-5-pin test port found on almost every chip. It began as a way to test solder connections on boards (boundary scan) and became the universal access point for test, debug and programming. IEEE 1500 standardises test wrappers around embedded cores, and IEEE 1687 (IJTAG) standardises access to the many internal instruments like BIST controllers and sensors.

Layers of test access. One small JTAG port reaches everything from board pins to sensors inside each core.

Think of it like…

JTAG is the building's service entrance with a master key: engineers use it to reach any room (instrument) inside without disturbing the front door (normal operation).

Real-world example

On a new board, the factory runs a boundary-scan test through the processor's JTAG port, discovering that pin 47 is not soldered. Later, firmware engineers use the same port with a debug probe to halt the CPU. Inside the chip, an IEEE 1687 network lets test engineers start MBIST, read temperature sensors and tune PLLs through that one port.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. JTAG pins: TCK (clock), TMS (mode), TDI (data in), TDO (data out), optional TRST.
  2. A TAP controller state machine selects instruction and data registers.
  3. Boundary-scan cells at each I/O pin test board connections (EXTEST).
  4. IEEE 1500 wrappers isolate cores for independent testing.
  5. IEEE 1687 networks (described in ICL/PDL) reach embedded instruments flexibly.

Who uses it

DFT engineers, board test engineers, firmware/debug engineers and silicon validation engineers.

Key takeaway

Memorise the JTAG pins and that the TAP controller is a 16-state FSM; 1149.1 = boundary scan, 1500 = core wrappers, 1687 = IJTAG.

Going deeper

  • TMS values sampled on rising TCK edges walk the 16-state TAP controller; holding TMS high for five TCK cycles always returns it to Test-Logic-Reset.
  • Boundary-scan cells let a board tester drive and capture every pin to find opens and shorts in solder joints without physical probes.
  • IEEE 1687 networks use Segment Insertion Bits (SIBs) to open only the needed parts of a long scan path; ICL and PDL let tools retarget instrument procedures automatically.
  • IEEE 1500 wrappers isolate a core with wrapper boundary cells and a Wrapper Instruction Register, described in Core Test Language (IEEE 1450.6).
  • The same port often carries CPU debug (Arm CoreSight DAP, RISC-V Debug Module), so production parts lock or authenticate JTAG for security.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Leaving JTAG debug fully open in production parts, a common hardware security weakness; use lifecycle locks or authenticated debug.
  • Confusing boundary scan with internal scan: boundary scan tests board connections, internal scan tests on-chip logic.
  • Shipping a hand-written BSDL file that was never validated against silicon, breaking board test.

docs.title: 4.13 Test Coverage, Quality and Yield
docs.text:
Test quality is measured by coverage: what fraction of possible faults the tests can detect. Higher coverage means fewer bad chips escape to customers. Yield is the fraction of manufactured chips that pass. Testing has a cost (tester time), so teams balance coverage, test time and the quality required by the market: consumer, data-centre and automotive have very different standards.

Defect level vs fault coverage (yield 70 %). Williams–Brown model: each extra 'nine' of coverage cuts escapes about tenfold.

Think of it like…

It is like airport security: more thorough checks catch more problems but slow the queue, so the level of screening depends on how much is at stake.

Real-world example

A consumer audio chip ships with 98 % stuck-at coverage and 2 seconds of test time. An automotive brake-controller chip with the same logic needs 99.5 % stuck-at, 95 % transition, cell-aware tests, burn-in and test at three temperatures, costing four times more tester time, because one escape could endanger lives.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
1. Set coverage targets by market (consumer, industrial, automotive, data-centre).
  2. Generate patterns and measure coverage per fault model.
  3. Balance test time against quality; prune patterns that add little.
  4. Track yield and failure data from production; diagnose systematic issues.
  5. Feed learnings back into design (DFM, DFT) and process.

Who uses it

DFT, test, product and yield engineers; quality teams for automotive (AEC-Q100, ISO 26262).

Key takeaway

Know the relation: defect level falls as yield and coverage rise; high coverage matters most when yield is low.

Going deeper

  • The Williams–Brown model DL = 1 − Y^(1−T) shows that at 70 % yield even 99 % fault coverage lets about 3,560 defective parts per million escape.
  • Real escape rates are usually lower than the model predicts, because one defect often causes several faults, but the trend holds: coverage matters most when yield is low.
  • Automotive suppliers target very low single-digit DPPM by combining high stuck-at and transition coverage, cell-aware tests, IDDQ, stress tests and outlier screening such as PAT.
  • Test cost scales with tester seconds; multi-site testing and scan compression are the main levers for reducing cost per chip.
  • ISO 26262 hardware metrics—SPFM and LFM—must reach at least 99 % and 90 % for ASIL D, measured with fault-injection campaigns on the design.
  • Hyperscalers have reported silent data corruption from marginal defects in a small fraction of server CPUs, driving in-fleet testing and stronger screens.

Common mistakes & misconceptions

  • Equating high yield with high quality; yield counts how many pass, not how many bad parts slipped through.
  • Chasing the last 0.1 % of stuck-at coverage when delay or cell-aware tests would catch more real defects.
  • Treating burn-in as free; it is costly, so many products replace it with voltage stress and outlier screening.

docs.title: Try it: Compute defect level with the Williams–Brown model (Python)
docs.text: python -c "for T in (0.90, 0.99, 0.999): print(T, round((1 - 0.7**(1 - T)) * 1e6), 'DPPM at 70% yield')"
